| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| ARA-01 [OD-7I-23, conditions 1, 2] | **The ten relations**, named, never selected by schema membership: `organization.memberships`, `organization.roles`, `organization.role_permissions`, `organization.permissions`, `organization.teams`, `organization.team_memberships`, `organization.compliance_policies`, `organization.data_subject_requests`, `identity.password_reset_tokens`, `identity.oauth_identities`. `REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES` on each from `app_platform_admin`. `SELECT` is included: no frozen 6M route reads any of them, three of them carry personal data or credential material, and the rule of OD-7I-17 (no direct read where 6M has no read requirement) is applied unchanged. |
| ARA-02 [OD-7I-23, condition 5] | **Sequences, columns, partitions, views.** All ten use UUID keys; none owns a sequence and none is partitioned in `001` – `112` (static reading). The migration nevertheless walks `pg_inherits` and asserts `has_sequence_privilege` and `has_column_privilege` false for the role over every sequence and column of schemas `organization` and `identity` other than the objects it is meant to keep. The three `identity.v_platform_safe_*` views stay; they are owned by the migration role, expose no hash or secret reference, and are read-only. No view exists over the ten relations. |
| ARA-03 [OD-7I-23, conditions 5, 6] | **Functions.** `EXECUTE` on `organization.get_user_organization_ids(UUID)` is revoked from the role. No other `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `001` – `112` inserts, updates or deletes any of the ten relations: the only writers are seed statements inside migrations (`007_5B`, `096_5B2`, `104_5B3`). The assertion block scans the catalogue for any function executable by the role whose body references one of the ten relations and fails the migration if it finds one outside a governed allow-list, which is empty in V1. |
| ARA-04 [OD-7I-23, condition 5] | **`PUBLIC` and membership.** Nothing is granted to `PUBLIC` on any of the ten; no migration grants one role to another; no default privilege exists (§8.5). The role cannot `SET ROLE`. `BYPASSRLS` bypasses row policies, not table or function ACLs, which is why the ACL is the only control that binds this role. The block asserts `pg_auth_members` has no row for it. |
| ARA-05 [OD-7I-23, conditions 4, 7] | **No platform membership or role capability in V1.** No function, route or tooling capability is introduced through which a platform administrator creates, activates, promotes or removes a tenant membership, edits a role or its permissions, issues a reset or invitation token, or links an identity. No frozen contract requires one, so the allow-list of guarded maintenance operations on these relations is empty. Adding one is a new 6M function, a purpose and an owner decision. |
| ARA-06 [FROZEN; OD-7I-23, conditions 3, 8, 12] | **Tenant workflows are untouched.** `app_api` and `app_worker` keep every grant in the last column above, under the forced tenant policies of `003_5B` and `004_5B`. The frozen 6B and 6C paths therefore run exactly as designed: invitation (a `SUSPENDED` membership with `accepted_at` null plus an `INVITATION` token; 6C ADR-6C-03), acceptance (6B §21.13), member suspend, reactivate with its `accepted_at IS NOT NULL` clause, remove and leave (6C §8.6), role assignment under `role:manage` with its two OWNER guards (6C §8.4), ownership transfer as two compare-and-swap updates in one transaction (6C §8.5), custom-role management (6B §21.31 – §21.34), team management (6C §10), password reset, email verification and OAuth linking (6B §21.8 – §21.16). No route, permission string, error code or audit action changes. |
| ARA-07 [FROZEN; OD-7I-23, condition 9] | **Cache and token effects of a legitimate change** are 6B's and are restated, not changed. The access token's `role` claim is advisory and never authoritative (6B §11.1, §11.3). Every request resolves the membership and its status from the database. The compiled permission set `rbac:permissions:{org}:{user}` is cached for five minutes and is invalidated synchronously on a role assignment, a role-permission change (for every member holding that role), and a membership status change (6B §24). A removed or suspended membership is denied at step 1 on the next request whatever the token says. After IR-48 the only sessions able to change these rows are the tenant path's, which performs that invalidation; revoking the administrator's grants needs no cache action. |
| ARA-08 [7I] | **Break-glass is not an equivalent path.** A holder of the administrator database credential can call `fn_break_glass_grant` (its check is `is_platform_admin()`). That writes a grant row. Using it requires an authenticated platform-administrator API session whose user and session match the grant (6B §18.3a; `fn_break_glass_check`), which a database credential does not provide, and the row changes no PostgreSQL privilege (PAS-08). It is therefore not a way to act as a tenant member. That `is_platform_admin()` rests on a session setting is the pre-existing 6M property recorded in §8.10; the break-glass functions are not lifecycle functions and are not superseded here. |
| ARA-09 [7I] | **`owner_user_id` and ownership.** 6B authorizes on the membership's role, never on `organizations.owner_user_id`; ownership-sensitive operations in 6C are bound to "the caller is the current OWNER membership" (6C §8.5), and the frozen transfer statement updates two membership rows and does not write the column. `owner_user_id` is therefore linkage and display, not an authorization input, and no rule in this document may read it as one. The administrator cannot write it (`105_5B4`); `app_api` keeps a column grant for creation (§8.10). The inventory entry of §8.10 that named ownership transfer as a writer of the column is corrected: 6C §8.5's statement does not write it, and whether any frozen path updates it after creation is for the IR-45 enumeration. A value that disagrees with the OWNER membership grants nothing. |
| ARA-10 [7I] | **API keys.** `identity.api_keys` has been unreachable to the role since `109_5B7` except through a view without `key_hash`. A key's scopes are a ceiling intersected with what the issuing user held (6B §16.4). The administrator cannot insert a key, change scopes or learn a hash, so no API-key path forges tenant access. |
| ARA-11 [7I] | **Migration order and atomicity.** One transaction: revoke on the ten relations and any child; revoke the function; run the assertion block (`has_table_privilege`, `has_column_privilege`, `has_sequence_privilege` false for the role on the ten; `has_function_privilege` false for the function; the kept objects still held; `pg_auth_members` empty). A failed assertion aborts the migration. Roll-forward only: reverting re-opens P1-7I-R14, so a downgrade is gated like IR-09's. |
| ARA-12 [OD-7I-23, condition 6] | **What is and is not claimed.** *Prevented:* the administrator database credential creating an `ACTIVE` membership, promoting a role, widening a system or tenant role's permissions, planting a reset, verification or invitation token, linking an identity, or reading any of these rows. *Not prevented, and not claimed:* a stolen `app_api` credential can set any tenant context and write memberships and roles through the tenant path's own grants. That is RR-01, exactly as ADM-14 states for the endpoint table itself: such a credential can already update the endpoint directly, so the membership route adds nothing to it. It is not the administrator path this finding is about. |

**The counterexample, closed.** With IR-48 applied, under `app_platform_admin`, with any session setting and any break-glass grant: the `INSERT` into `organization.memberships` fails with `42501 permission denied for table memberships` before any row is written; so do the `UPDATE` of `role_id`, the `INSERT` into `role_permissions`, the `UPDATE` of `roles`, and the inserts into `password_reset_tokens` and `oauth_identities`. U has no membership in the victim organization, `get_user_organization_ids` does not return it, no token for it is issued, and step 1 of 6B §8 denies any request that names it. The endpoint is not changed and the delivery goes to the tenant's own URL. A tenant OWNER inviting a member, the member accepting, a role assignment and an ownership transfer all proceed as before under `app_api`. Until IR-48 exists every statement above succeeds, and AB-7I-01 therefore blocks the dispatcher. Tests: VT-107 … VT-110.

### 8.14 Data-subject request status authority (P1-7I-R15; OD-7I-24)

Nothing in this section exists. It is a requirement on a future governed migration (IR-49) with a controlled erratum to 5B and 6C (ERR-7I-22). The hold rules it serves are §14.7.

**Physical and frozen facts.** `organization.data_subject_requests` (`004_5B` L53 – L86) has `status` in `RECEIVED`, `VERIFYING`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `COMPLETED`, `REJECTED`, `ON_HOLD` (`chk_dsr_status`), a foreign key to the organization, forced RLS with the tenant policy, and one trigger (`updated_at`). `app_api` and `app_worker` hold table-level `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE` (L86); `app_platform_admin` holds all four (`008_5B` L38) and is `BYPASSRLS`. No trigger or function constrains a status transition. The frozen writers are five 6C routes, all issued by `app_api` as compare-and-swap statements under `data_subject:manage` (6C §13.3, §15.31 – §15.37): create, verify, hold, complete, reject. No `app_worker` writer is defined: 6C §13.1 leaves the erasure mechanics to "later phases". **5B §27 and 6C §13.2 draw `ON_HOLD` as a state that is entered and define no transition out of it; `REJECTED` is drawn from `VERIFYING` only.**

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| DSH-01 [OD-7I-24, condition 6] | **Protected fields.** `status` is a protected column: no login role writes it directly. The request's identity is immutable after insert: `organization_id`, `request_type`, `subject_contact_id`, `subject_email`, `subject_phone_e164`. A hold is scoped by those fields, so a request whose subject could be edited would move its hold. A row-level trigger rejects any change to them for every caller. |
| DSH-02 [OD-7I-24, condition 6] | **Grants.** Table-level `UPDATE` is revoked from `app_api` and `app_worker`. `app_api` keeps `SELECT`, keeps `INSERT`, and receives column-level `UPDATE` on the descriptive columns its frozen routes write that are neither `status` nor an identity field; the exact list is an IR-49 deliverable read from 6C. `app_worker` keeps `SELECT` only unless that enumeration names a frozen writer, which then receives a guarded function. `app_platform_admin` holds nothing (ARA-01). `DELETE` is held by no role. A column-level `REVOKE` under the table-level grant would do nothing (§8.6). |
| DSH-03 [7I] | **Creation.** The frozen create route stays a direct `INSERT` by `app_api`. A `BEFORE INSERT` trigger rejects a row whose `status` is not `RECEIVED` unless `current_user` is the function-owner role (the STP-03 form). |
| DSH-04 [OD-7I-24, conditions 1, 6] | **Each frozen route is one guarded `API` edge.** Verify, hold, complete and reject run inside four Organization-owned functions executable by `app_api` only, each checking `session_user`, each requiring an API action proof (STP-06) bound to `data_subject:manage`, the organization, the request and the transition, and each consuming its request identifier once. Each carries the frozen compare-and-swap statement unchanged and writes its frozen audit row (`DATA_SUBJECT_REQUEST_VERIFYING`, `_ON_HOLD`, `_COMPLETED`, `_REJECTED`) and a provenance row in the same transaction. A caller who can set `app.tenant_id` and supply a user identifier, but cannot compute the proof, is refused before any row is locked. |
| DSH-05 [OD-7I-24, conditions 3, 12, 13] | **Edges out of `ON_HOLD`.** A `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger on `status` enforces, for every caller including the function-owner role: `COMPLETED` and `REJECTED` are terminal; **from `ON_HOLD` the only permitted target is `REJECTED`**; `ON_HOLD → COMPLETED`, `ON_HOLD → IN_PROGRESS` and `ON_HOLD → VERIFYING` are not expressible. There is no resume and no new state. `ON_HOLD → REJECTED` is **not drawn in the frozen 5B §27 / 6C §13.2 diagram**, which shows `REJECTED` from `VERIFYING` only, and 6C §15.37 does not state the reject route's source states. It is therefore recorded as a controlled compatibility correction (ERR-7I-22), not asserted as already frozen. **Until the 5B and 6C owners consolidate that erratum, a held request has no exit at all and stays held**; that is the safe direction, and it is gated (AB-7I-14). The edges among the other states are the frozen ones and their matrix is an IR-49 deliverable. |
| DSH-06 [OD-7I-24, conditions 1, 2; OD-7I-26] | **The hold function is the placement of the request hold, with its scope.** In one transaction the hold function: takes the organization's hold gate exclusively (HLD-10); locks the request row; verifies the proof; calls the subject resolver of HLD-12 and obtains the contact set for the request's subject fields; appends the placement, with the subject keys and that contact set, to the journal as HLD-09 requires; inserts the `REQUEST` hold in the registry, carrying the request identifier, the subject fields copied from the locked row and the contact set; runs the frozen compare-and-swap to `ON_HOLD`; writes the audit row and the provenance row. Either all of it commits or none. A status of `ON_HOLD` without its registry row, or the reverse, is not producible by this function, and neither is a hold whose scope is still to be worked out: there is no such state. The route's request and response are the frozen ones; the function never refuses a hold because the subject matched nothing (HLD-12). |
| DSH-07 [OD-7I-24, conditions 4, 11] | **The reject function ends only that request's hold.** For a request in `ON_HOLD` the reject function, in one transaction and under the same gate and row locks, runs the compare-and-swap to `REJECTED`, marks released the single registry row whose kind is `REQUEST` and whose request identifier equals this request, and writes the frozen `DATA_SUBJECT_REQUEST_REJECTED` audit row and the release's journal record (HLD-09). It cannot name another hold: the function takes no hold identifier. It never touches a `PLATFORM` hold or another request's hold, erases nothing, cancels no other request and no erasure step, and resolves no obligation. After it commits, the subject's data is under whatever other holds and ordinary retention clocks apply. |
| DSH-08 [7I] | **Consistency is enforced, not assumed.** A deferred constraint trigger on both relations requires, at commit: a request is `ON_HOLD` if and only if an unreleased `REQUEST` hold names it. It fires for every writer, the function owner included, so a later function cannot break the pairing. The governed migration backfills a `REQUEST` hold for every request already in `ON_HOLD` before it enables the trigger. |
| DSH-09 [7I] | **Crash, retry, concurrency.** A crash before commit leaves neither the status nor the hold. A retried hold with the same proof finds its request identifier and returns the recorded outcome; with a new proof it meets the frozen guard and changes nothing. Two concurrent holds of one request serialize on the row; one wins. A hold racing a completion of the same request serializes on the row: whichever commits second re-evaluates its compare-and-swap and changes 0 rows. A hold racing an erasure is HLD-10. |
| DSH-10 [OD-7I-24] | **What is and is not claimed.** *Prevented:* any login role, with any session setting, moving a request out of `ON_HOLD` or into any state by SQL; a forged function call; release of a hold by a status change. *Not prevented, and not claimed:* a compromised API process holds the action key and can reject a held request, which is the tenant's own authority exercised by a compromised authorized workload (attacker C; RR-08). It cannot release a `PLATFORM` hold by any means. |

**The counterexample, closed.** With IR-49 applied: `UPDATE organization.data_subject_requests SET status = 'IN_PROGRESS' WHERE id = …` fails with `42501` under `app_api` and `app_worker` (no privilege on the column) and under `app_platform_admin` (no privilege on the table). The verify and complete functions refuse the edge from `ON_HOLD` whatever proof is presented. Suppose the status were changed by an authority outside every runtime role: the deferred trigger of DSH-08 aborts that transaction, and independently the registry row is still unreleased, so every erasure function still finds the hold (HLD-01, HLD-03). Until IR-49 exists the update succeeds; AB-7I-14 blocks any erasure that would rely on the hold. Tests: VT-111 … VT-114.

---
## 9. Redis ACL Design

The frozen topology is preserved: 11 durable family keys and one SIGNAL key, shared by tenants (7E §15.4; OD-7E-03 = B). No per-tenant stream and no per-group stream is introduced. What changes under OD-7I-15 is **who holds the consumer-side commands**: one stream gateway, not the consumer workloads (§9.5). Streams, keys, groups, entry format, acknowledgement timing and trimming are as frozen.

### 9.1 Rules

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| RDS-01 [FROZEN] | A stream key, partition and group are not tenant authority (7E TNY-01). Co-tenancy in a stream is transport co-location only. |
| RDS-02 [7I] | **Classification of a stream.** A durable family stream inherits the highest class of any payload routed to it (§10.2). `LS-D-VOX`, `LS-D-CRM`, `LS-D-CPN` and `LS-D-KNW` carry class `PII` or `SEN` fields. Every principal that can read a family key is therefore in the trusted computing base for every tenant's data in that family. |
| RDS-03 [7I] | No tenant-scoped principal, no API process, no operator workstation **and no consumer worker** holds a Redis credential for a stream key. The only readers of entries are the stream gateway and, during an approved group operation, the recovery operator user. |
| RDS-04 [7I] | Stream entries are not encrypted at the application layer in V1. The envelope format is frozen as `fmt` + `env` (7E ENT-01) and a ciphertext envelope would change it. Protection is TLS in transit, storage encryption of the persistence volume, ACLs and network isolation. Field-level minimization (§10) is what limits exposure. |
| RDS-05 [OD-7I-15] | **Consumer-side commands, resolving the 7E / 7F / 7G overlap.** The commands 7E SCY-05 lists for consumers are held by **one ACL user, the stream gateway's**: `XREADGROUP`, `XACK` (normal path) and `XAUTOCLAIM`, `XPENDING`, `XINFO` (the sweep of 7G RCL-04). Keys: the durable family keys and the SIGNAL key. Consumer workloads have no ACL user. Which group and key a given consumer may reach is decided by the gateway's binding registry (GWY-03), because Redis cannot decide it. This supersedes the earlier per-context consumer users, which gave nine credentials the power to name any group on a shared key (ERR-7I-08). |
| RDS-06 [7I] | **`XCLAIM` is not a consumer-path command.** 7G RCL-09 permits it only for governed repair on enumerated IDs and for idle-consumer maintenance. It belongs to the recovery operator user and is not held by the gateway. This narrows the consumer list of 7E SCY-05 (ERR-7I-05). |
| RDS-07 [7I] | The gateway user's need for `XAUTOCLAIM` implies nothing else. It has no `XGROUP` subcommand, `XADD`, `XDEL`, `XTRIM`, `XSETID`, `DEL`, `UNLINK`, `RENAME`, `EXPIRE`, `PERSIST`, `XRANGE` or any scripting command. |
| RDS-08 [7I] | The read path and the sweep use the same gateway user. Splitting them would add a credential inside one workload without adding a boundary. |
| RDS-09 [7I] | **No runtime ACL user has an all-keys pattern.** Redis ACLs have no negative key pattern. Every other Redis user of the platform (cache, rate limiter, Celery broker, token denylist) therefore has positive key patterns that cannot match `stream:global:*`. Where a client library writes unprefixed keys, a key prefix is configured so that this is possible (IR-16; HE-7K-7I-03). |
| RDS-10 [7I] | Denied to every runtime user: `MONITOR`, `KEYS`, `SCAN` on stream keys, `DEBUG`, `CONFIG`, `ACL`, `EVAL` / `EVALSHA` / `FUNCTION` / `SCRIPT`, `FLUSHALL` / `FLUSHDB`, `MIGRATE`, `RESTORE`, `DUMP`, `SWAPDB`, `REPLICAOF`, `CLUSTER` write subcommands, `XDEL`, `DEL` and `UNLINK` on stream keys. `MONITOR` and `DUMP` would expose payloads. |
| RDS-11 [7I] | The built-in `default` user is disabled. Administrative access to Redis is an infrastructure break-glass identity outside every runtime workload; its use is logged and alerted (HE-7J-7I-04). It is never the path for a recovery operation (7G AUT-06). |
| RDS-12 [FROZEN] | Stream bodies are never logged or placed in metrics by the adapter, the SIGNAL publisher, the trim worker or provisioning (7E SCY-03). |
| RDS-13 [7I] | **Credentials.** One credential per ACL user, from the secret manager, readable only by its workload. Rotation is by a second password on the same user (Redis permits several), deployment of the new one, then removal of the old; no restart-coupled cutover. A suspected theft is contained by removing the password and forcibly closing that user's connections. |
| RDS-14 [7I] | **TLS and network.** TLS on every connection, with certificate verification (7E SCY-04). The Redis nodes accept connections only from the workload network segments of the users defined below. |
| RDS-15 [7I] | **Failover.** ACL definitions are per node and are not propagated by the cluster bus. Every primary and replica carries the identical ACL set, applied from one governed source. A node whose ACL digest differs from the governed digest is not allowed to take traffic, and a mismatch is an alert. A promoted replica without the ACL set would either refuse all workers or accept the default user; both are prevented by this parity rule (IR-17). |
| RDS-16 [FROZEN + 7I] | **`noeviction`.** The durable cluster's `noeviction` policy is inherited unchanged (7E §13). Its security consequence is availability: when memory is full, `XADD` fails and publication stops rather than data being evicted. Only two users can add to durable keys, so a tenant cannot fill the durable keyspace through Redis. Bounding SIGNAL growth so that it cannot starve durable publication is 7K's (HE-7K-7I-03). |
| RDS-17 [7I] | **Observation exposure (corrected in the second remediation; F-7I-22).** `XINFO GROUPS`, `XINFO CONSUMERS` and `XPENDING` (summary and ID-range forms) reveal entry IDs, counts, idle times and consumer names: class `INT`, no payload. **`XINFO STREAM` is not payload-free: its reply includes the stream's first and last entries with their fields.** The earlier text granted bare `XINFO` to the reconciler, trim, provisioning and health-probe users and called it payload-free; that was wrong. Redis 7 ACLs select subcommands, so those four users receive `XINFO GROUPS` only (the `groups` subcommand selector of `xinfo`), which is all that 7E TRM-02 and the reconciler need. `XINFO STREAM`, `XRANGE`, `XREADGROUP` and `XAUTOCLAIM` return payloads, and only the gateway and recovery-operator users hold any of them (the gateway needs `XINFO STREAM` for the first-entry ID of 7G RCL-06). The subcommand selector and the reply shapes are stated from the Redis 7.2 command reference, not from an executed test (VT-16). |
| RDS-18 [7I] | **DLQ.** Redis is never the DLQ (7G LDG-03). No ACL user needs, and none has, a dead-letter key. |

### 9.2 Matrix 6 — Redis users, commands, key patterns

`D` = `stream:global:d:*`; `D(ctx)` = the durable family keys a context subscribes to (7E §29.3); `S` = `stream:global:s:*`.

| User | Workload | Allowed commands | Key pattern | Explicitly denied | Credential |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Relay publisher | Outbox relay | `XADD`, `WAITAOF`; read-only `CLUSTER SLOTS` / `CLUSTER SHARDS` / `CLUSTER INFO`, `INFO`, `COMMAND INFO`, `PING` | `D` | Every read of an entry; `XTRIM`; every `XGROUP`; `S` | Relay workload |
| Class-D signal publisher | Conversation runtime | `XADD`; `PING` | `S` | `D`; every read; `WAITAOF` | Voice runtime workload |
| Stream gateway | Stream gateway workload, on behalf of the nine consuming contexts (identity, compliance, crm, campaign, billing, analytics, voice, knowledge, integrations) | `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, `XAUTOCLAIM`, `XPENDING`, `XINFO STREAM` / `GROUPS` / `CONSUMERS`; read-only cluster and `PING` | `D`, `S` | `XCLAIM`; `XADD`; `XDEL`; `XTRIM`; `XRANGE`; every `XGROUP` | Gateway workload only (GWY-13) |
| Consumer workers | — | **None.** No ACL user exists for them | — | Everything | No Redis credential for a stream key |
| Obligation reconciler | Event-sweeper workload | `XINFO GROUPS`; `XPENDING` in the summary form and in the ID-range form `XPENDING <key> <group> <id> <id> 1` (ACC-16) | `D` | `XINFO STREAM` and every other command that returns an entry; `XACK`; `XAUTOCLAIM`; `XADD`; every `XGROUP` | Sweeper workload |
| Stream provisioning | Deployment job | `XGROUP CREATE` (with `MKSTREAM`); `XINFO GROUPS` | `D`, `S` | `XGROUP DESTROY`, `SETID`, `DELCONSUMER`, `CREATECONSUMER`; every read of an entry; `XADD` | Deployment pipeline; short-lived |
| Trim / maintenance | Trim worker | `XINFO GROUPS`, `XPENDING`, `XTRIM`, `PERSIST`, `TTL` | `D`, `S` | `XINFO STREAM` and every other read of an entry; `XADD`; `XDEL`; every `XGROUP` | Trim workload |
| Repair publisher (R4, R5) | Event-operations tooling | `XADD`, `WAITAOF`; read-only cluster | `D` | Everything the relay is denied | Tooling workload; retrievable only while an approved R4 / R5 operation is `RUNNING` (OPA-11) |
| Recovery operator | Event-operations tooling | `XGROUP DESTROY`, `XGROUP SETID`, `XGROUP DELCONSUMER`, `XCLAIM`, `XPENDING`, `XINFO`, `XRANGE` | `D` | `XADD`; `XDEL`; `XTRIM`; `DEL`; `S` | Tooling workload; retrievable only while an approved group operation is `RUNNING` (OPA-11) |
| Health probe | Relay, gateway, trim, tooling (consumer workers probe the gateway, not Redis) | `PING`; `XINFO GROUPS` (a non-claiming, payload-free probe in the sense of 7D HO-7E-02) | `D`, `S` | `XINFO STREAM`; everything else | Each of those workloads |

Rows: 10, of which 9 are ACL users and one records that consumer workers have none. Concrete users in V1: 9 (the earlier design had 16, nine of them consumer users).

### 9.3 What ACLs cannot do, and what covers the remainder

| Limitation | Consequence | Covered by |
|---|---|---|
| No scoping by consumer-group name | Any holder of a group command on a key can name any group on it. `XACK` removes another group's pending entry and its trim pin. `XAUTOCLAIM` takes ownership of it. **`XREADGROUP … NOACK` naming the other group advances that group's cursor and creates no pending entry at all**, so an obligation can vanish without an acknowledgement; removing `XACK` alone would not close this | **Prevention against a consumer:** consumers hold no group command; the gateway issues them for the caller's registered groups only (GWY-01 … GWY-06). **Detection and recovery against everything, the gateway included:** obligation accounting in PostgreSQL (ACC-01 … ACC-20). Naming conventions and alerts are signals only and are not relied on as prevention |
| No restriction of the `NOACK` argument | `NOACK` on a durable group cannot be denied by ACL (7E GRP-07, 7F RDL-03 are conventions) | The gateway constructs the command and never adds `NOACK` for a durable group (GWY-05); a `NOACK` read by any other route is caught by accounting |
| No restriction of command arguments | `XADD … MAXLEN` trims; `XCLAIM` options 7G prohibits (`FORCE`, `LASTID`, `RETRYCOUNT`, `IDLE`) cannot be denied by ACL | CI check of command construction (7G IO-7G-05); only two users hold `XADD` on `D`; stream-length-drop detection; RR-03 |
| No per-tenant scoping inside a key | Any reader of a family reads all tenants | RDS-02, RDS-03: the only reader is the gateway; RR-02 |

**HRD-01 [REC].** Optional hardening for the high-risk Billing consumer: before applying an entry, compare it with the authoritative outbox row through a guarded function that returns only (`organization_id`, `event_type`, payload digest) for an `event_id`. It detects a forged or altered entry while the row exists (7 days after publication). It is not required for any invariant here; it costs one primary-key read per event and is handed to 7K and 7L (HE-7K-7I-07).

### 9.4 Incident containment

| Event | Immediate action | Preserves |
|---|---|---|
| A consumer's gateway credential suspected stolen | Revoke that identity at the gateway; issue a new credential to the workload | Durable entries stay pending and are redelivered; the thief could reach only that context's own groups |
| Gateway Redis credential suspected stolen, or gateway compromised | Remove the password; close its connections; consumers idle; run the obligation reconciler over the exposure window before resuming | Publication continues (the relay is independent); entries stay pending; any obligation removed in the window surfaces as an unaccounted obligation and is recovered (ACC-05). Confidentiality of entries read in the window is treated as disclosed for incident handling |
| Relay or repair credential suspected stolen | Remove the password; pause publication (7D transport gate behaviour); compare stream contents of the exposure window with the outbox by `event_id` | Outbox rows remain the source of truth; unknown entries are identified by the comparison |
| ACL parity alert | Remove the node from service; re-apply the governed ACL set | — |
| Administrative break-glass used | Alert; post-incident review of every command issued | — |

### 9.5 The stream gateway (OD-7I-15)

Nothing in this section exists. It is a design; the errata it needs are ERR-7I-08 … ERR-7I-10, and consumer activation is blocked by AB-7I-10 until it is built and tested.

```
Redis durable keys ──(gateway ACL user)── stream gateway ──(authenticated, per-context)── consumer worker
                                              │                                              │
                                              └── evidence check + accounting row ──► PostgreSQL ◄── handler transaction (7F, unchanged)
```

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| GWY-01 [OD] | **One mediating workload.** Every `XREADGROUP`, `XAUTOCLAIM`, `XPENDING`, `XINFO` and `XACK` on a stream key that serves a consumer is issued by the stream gateway. It is a workload of the modular monolith (ROL-03), has no tenant-facing surface and performs no business processing. |
| GWY-02 [OD] | **Consumer authentication.** Each consuming context's worker workload authenticates to the gateway with a server-controlled workload credential issued through the secret manager, over mutually authenticated TLS. The identity never comes from an event, a request, a header a tenant can influence, or a value the caller states about itself. |
| GWY-03 [OD] | **Binding registry.** A governed, code-owned registry maps each consumer identity to its logical groups, the physical keys those groups subscribe to (7E §29) and the operations it may request. It is derived from the 7E group registry and the 7F handler-contract admission; it is loaded at gateway start; a malformed or unreadable registry stops the gateway (CLS-06 pattern). A change is a `PLATFORM_CONFIG_CHANGED` audit event. |
| GWY-04 [OD] | **No authority from the caller.** A request selects one of the caller's own registered groups by its registry identifier. The gateway resolves the Redis group name and keys itself. A group or key that is not bound to the caller is refused before any Redis command is built, and the refusal is a security signal. An acknowledgement request carries the **delivery token** the gateway issued with the entry (CEV-01): authenticated by a key only the gateway holds, and binding the consumer identity, group, key, entry ID, the envelope's `event_id` and `organization_id`, and the generations in force. A caller never submits a raw entry ID, key or group for acknowledgement. |
| GWY-05 [OD] | **Commands the gateway builds.** `XREADGROUP GROUP <group> <member> … STREAMS <key> >` without `NOACK` for a durable group; with `NOACK` only for the registered SIGNAL group (7F SIG-7F-02). `XAUTOCLAIM` with the frozen minimum idle time, after the trimmed-prefix pre-check of 7G RCL-06, for the caller's group only. `XACK` under GWY-08. It never issues `XCLAIM`, any `XGROUP`, `XADD`, `XDEL`, `XTRIM` or `XRANGE`, and its user does not hold them. |
| GWY-06 [OD] | **Members.** Consumer names stay per worker instance (7E GRP-06). The gateway assigns the member name from the authenticated identity and instance; a caller cannot read or acknowledge as another member's name, and cannot join a group it is not bound to. |
| GWY-07 [FROZEN] | **The 7F pipeline is unchanged and stays in the worker.** Validation D-01 … D-10, the tenant-context sequence, the idempotency guard, the handler and the owner transaction run in the consumer worker exactly as frozen. The gateway forwards `fmt` and `env` unchanged and reads from the envelope only `event_id`, `event_type` and `organization_id`, for the handle and for accounting. It does not parse a payload. |
| GWY-08 [OD] | **Acknowledgement authorization.** For an acknowledgement request on handle `h` the gateway obtains, through a guarded database function that returns a state and no data, the durable evidence for (`group`, `event_id`, `organization_id`), in this order: (a) a **completion record** for (`group`, `event_id`) written by the owning context's principal in the handler's transaction, whose delivery token the gateway itself verifies (CEV-08). **A guard row is not evidence.** The 7F guard still decides, inside the worker, whether the handler runs; it no longer decides whether the gateway may acknowledge (OD-7I-18, condition B-3); (b) a **recovery case** in a state in which 7G permits acknowledgement (PAT-01, PAT-07, RTY-10), identified by event, or by (group, key, entry ID) where no event identity could be parsed; (c) **known-unsubscribed**, computed by the gateway from the handler contract in force for that group and type, never asserted by the caller; (d) for the two IC-5 groups, the completion record of kind `EXTERNAL_WRITE_ATTESTED` (GWY-09). It then inserts the accounting row (ACC-01) in one database transaction, and only after that commit issues `XACK`. With no evidence it refuses, and the entry stays pending. |
| GWY-09 [OD] | **CON-01 and CON-08 (IC-5), CON-03 and CON-09 (IC-4).** These groups have no per-event guard row. CON-03 and CON-09 recompute from authoritative state inside one owner transaction, and since OD-7I-18 that transaction also writes the completion record (CEV-07), so they are acknowledged under GWY-08 (a) like any transactional consumer. CON-01 and CON-08 perform an absolute external write with no owner transaction; the stream entry is their durable intent (7F EXT-04, unchanged). After the write definitively succeeds, the member records a completion of kind `EXTERNAL_WRITE_ATTESTED` in a short transaction under its context principal with its delivery token, and the gateway records the accounting row as kind `ATTESTED`. **An attestation is a durable statement by that group's own member, bound to a real delivery, that the frozen boundary of 7F XAK-01 was reached. It is not independent proof of the external effect and no rule reads it as one** (condition B-9). It cannot be made for another group. A compromised member can attest falsely only about its own group's work, which it could equally leave undone; that is ordinary application correctness, not a cross-group privilege. The independent check is ACC-08. |
| GWY-10 [FROZEN + OD] | **Order.** Durable success boundary in the owner transaction (7F XAK-01, XAK-05; 7G PAT-01) → evidence check → accounting commit → `XACK`. Acknowledgement is never earlier than 7F permits; it is now also never without a durable accounting row. A zero result and a lost reply are handled as 7F XAK-08, XAK-09 and 7G PAT-05, PAT-06. |
| GWY-11 [OD] | **Crash and concurrency.** Gateway crash before the evidence check: nothing changed. After the accounting commit, before `XACK`: the entry is still pending, is redelivered, takes the duplicate path, and the accounting insert is a no-op on its primary key. After `XACK`: complete. Two members acknowledging the same entry: one accounting row, two harmless `XACK` (7F CDP-05). The gateway holds no per-entry state that must survive a restart: pending entries are in Redis, evidence and accounting are in PostgreSQL. A delivery token is verified by key, not by instance, so a completion recorded under a token that an earlier instance issued is still valid evidence (CEV-11). An *acknowledgement request* is honoured only for an entry the requesting member currently owns in the PEL; otherwise the worker reads again or the sweep reclaims the entry. |
| GWY-12 [OD] | **The gateway is not a data-access mechanism.** Its database principal has no table privilege and `EXECUTE` only on the evidence-check and accounting functions, which return states and identifiers (INV-04). It sets no tenant context, holds no key-service permission, resolves no secret but its own credentials, stores no entry, and never logs `env` (RED-02). An entry exists in the gateway only in memory while it is forwarded. |
| GWY-13 [OD] | **Credential hardening.** The gateway's Redis credential is readable in the secret manager by the gateway workload identity alone. Redis accepts connections only from the network segments of the relay, the SIGNAL publisher, the gateway, the trim worker, provisioning, the reconciler and the tooling; **not** from consumer-worker segments. Rotation follows RDS-13. Per-context consumer credentials toward the gateway rotate with overlapping validity. |
| GWY-14 [OD] | **No alternate path.** A consumer cannot reach a group command because, together: (1) no ACL user other than the gateway's holds `XREADGROUP`, `XACK` or `XAUTOCLAIM` on a stream key, and the recovery-operator user (`XCLAIM`, `XGROUP`) is retrievable only by the tooling workload while an approved operation is `RUNNING` (OPA-11); (2) the `default` user is disabled (RDS-11); (3) no other Redis user's key pattern matches a stream key (RDS-09); (4) scripting is denied to every runtime user (RDS-10), so no script can issue the command for it; (5) the network policy of GWY-13; (6) the secret-manager policy of GWY-13; (7) ACL parity on every node (RDS-15). Each item has a test (VT-70). |
| GWY-15 [OD] | **Availability.** At least two gateway instances per region in separate failure domains ([REC]; counts and sizing are 7K's). An instance failure loses nothing (GWY-11). With every instance down: consumers idle, entries stay pending and pin the trim watermark, and **publication continues**, because the relay does not use the gateway and never waits for a consumer. No event publication depends synchronously on consumer or gateway availability. |
| GWY-16 [OD] | **Preserved boundaries.** The gateway takes no part in 7G recovery authorization. R2 and R3 still feed entries to the 7F pipeline under their approvals; R4 and R5 still publish through the repair publisher; governed group operations still use the recovery-operator user. A recovery worker reaches a group only as a registered identity like any other consumer. |
| GWY-17 [OD] | **Cost, stated for 7K.** Per read batch: one additional in-region round trip. Per acknowledgement batch: one additional round trip, one evidence read and one accounting insert per (group, event). Publication: nothing added. The gateway is a new capacity bottleneck and a new availability dependency of consumption. No figure is asserted here; latency and throughput budgets are HE-7K-7I-08. |
| GWY-18 [OD] | **What is not claimed.** A compromised gateway, or a holder of its Redis credential, can read all entries and change any group's state (T-7I-21, RR-02). The design does not prevent that. It ensures such a change cannot silently lose an obligation, because the accounting row requires durable evidence that the gateway cannot create (ACC-10), the reconciler works from PostgreSQL records the gateway cannot write (the relay's position record, the group registration), and every unaccounted pair reaches a recovery case by a PostgreSQL-clock deadline even if Redis state is falsified or unreadable (ACC-17). A compromised gateway can mint delivery tokens; it cannot record a completion, because that needs a context principal (CEV-14). |

### 9.6 Obligation accounting and reconciliation (OD-7I-15)

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| ACC-01 [OD] | **Accounting record.** One durable row per (logical group, `event_id`), or per (logical group, physical key, entry ID) where no event identity could be parsed: `organization_id`, evidence kind (`COMPLETION`, `CASE`, `UNSUBSCRIBED`, `ATTESTED`; the earlier `GUARD_PROOF` kind is withdrawn, GWY-08), consumer identity, entry ID, time. Insert-only, through the gateway's function. No runtime role has a table privilege on it. It holds identifiers only (class `PID`) and no payload. |
| ACC-02 [OD] | **The owed set.** Every group acknowledges every entry delivered to it, whether or not it has a handler for the type (7E GRP-08). The owed set of a recorded position (ACC-13) is therefore every durable group whose registration record covers that position on that physical key (ACC-15). Whether the group has a handler obligation for the type is a separate, frozen question (7F `A(g, E)`; canonical provenance HCG-28) that the gateway answers as `UNSUBSCRIBED`; it does not remove the transport obligation. No judgement about "who should care" is made by the reconciler. |
| ACC-03 [OD] | **Reconciliation is PostgreSQL-first.** A guarded function lists, by identifier only, the (outbox row, group) pairs of `PUBLISHED` rows that have neither an accounting row nor a recovery case, each with its recorded positions and their PostgreSQL record times. It never returns a payload. |
| ACC-04 [7I] | **Transport comparison: withdrawn and replaced (P1-7I-R09).** The first remediation compared the ID time of the group's trim bound with the row's `published_at`. That test is unsound (see "Why the time comparison fails" below) and is deleted. The comparison is now made on the exact recorded position (ACC-13 … ACC-16) and is backed by a deadline that uses no Redis state (ACC-17). |
| ACC-05 [OD] | **Recovery without an invented outcome.** For an unaccounted obligation (classified `GONE` under ACC-16, or past the deadline of ACC-17), one PostgreSQL transaction: captures the outbox row under the frozen source-capture contract of 7G DSR-12 as encrypted replay material; opens a recovery case for (group, `event_id`), class `V`, state `PARKED`, reason `OBLIGATION_UNACCOUNTED` (ERR-7I-10); raises a security signal. The case is then recovered by the unchanged 7G R2 path under its unchanged authorization (dual control for the high-risk groups, OPA-07): the captured bytes go through the 7F pipeline to that group's handler, and the handler's guard decides between `ALREADY_COMMITTED` and processing. The reconciler writes no handler result, no acknowledgement and no resolution. A class `V` case cannot be rejected (7G DAU-02). |
| ACC-06 [OD] | **Cleanup interlock.** A `PUBLISHED` row is deletable only when its frozen 7 days have passed **and** every group of its owed set has an accounting row or a recovery case. This narrows the frozen predicate in the manner of 7G ILK-01 and never widens it; it reads PostgreSQL only (7G ILK-08). Its effect on retention is that a row can outlive 7 days while a registered group is behind or while the reconciler has not run; that extension is bounded by the group-lag bound 7K sets (HE-7K-7I-06) and is alerted. It is applied by the guarded cleanup of IR-07 and is a controlled erratum to 7D CLN-03 and 7G ILK-06 (ERR-7I-10). |
| ACC-07 [OD] | **Reconciler failure is safe.** If the reconciler does not run, rows are held by ACC-06, not lost. Its watermark age is an alert (HE-7J-7I-09). It is idempotent: the case identity is (group, `event_id`), and a second run finds the case. |
| ACC-08 [OD] | **Independent check of attested groups.** For CON-08 the Voice owner's verification, run in the owner's context under the event's tenant context: the recording row is terminally `DELETED` and the exact object key is absent. For CON-01 the Identity owner's verification: a denylist entry exists for each JTI that has not expired. A failed check is treated as ACC-05. Repeating either write is harmless by definition of IC-5. For CON-03 and CON-09 the effect is a recomputation that cannot be attributed to one event; a re-drive converges and is the recovery, and no per-event verification is claimed. |
| ACC-09 [OD] | **Cause-independent.** The same accounting catches a gateway defect or compromise, a Redis group-state regression, an ungoverned `XDEL`, a mistaken governed operation and administrative break-glass. It does not depend on consumer names, on alerts, or on knowing who issued a command. |
| ACC-10 [OD] | **Forgery limits.** Accounting rows are written only by the gateway principal; the function checks `session_user`. A consumer worker cannot write one. The gateway cannot manufacture a completion record or a case: the first is written only by a context principal inside `fn_record_completion`, the second only by the 7G ledger functions, and the gateway principal can execute neither. Position records are written only by the relay and the repair publisher; registration records only by governed provisioning and retirement. What was recorded here as RR-06 (forged owner evidence under the shared worker credential) is closed by OD-7I-18 (§8.8, §9.7). |
| ACC-11 [OD] | **Retention.** Accounting rows and position records are kept until their outbox row is deleted and [REC] 30 days beyond, then purged by the maintenance principal (RET-25, RET-26). Registration records are kept as history (7F HCG-16 pattern). |
| ACC-12 [FROZEN] | SIGNAL entries are not accounted: loss is permitted and the group reads with `NOACK` (7F SIG-7F-02). |
| ACC-13 [7I] | **Transport position record.** A durable, insert-only relation of publication positions: `event_id` (the outbox row), topology generation, physical key, Redis entry ID, publisher kind (`RELAY`, `REPAIR`), and `recorded_at` from the database clock. It is written by the relay **in the same transaction that marks the row `PUBLISHED`**, through a superseding mark-published function that takes the confirmed `transport_ref` (7E ENT-05: `<physical key>/<entry ID>`) and the generation as additional arguments; the compare-and-swap of `077_5J1` is carried over unchanged. A call that presents a confirmed entry for an existing row records the position **whether or not its compare-and-swap wins**, so a relay whose lease expired still leaves a record of the entry it really appended; only the winner changes the row's status. The repair publisher records the positions of R4 and R5 publications the same way, through the ledger's functions. No runtime role has a table privilege on the relation. It holds no payload (class `PID`). This persists what 7D TPT-10 and 7E ENT-05 say is never persisted: controlled erratum ERR-7I-13. |
| ACC-14 [7I] | **Identity rules.** `event_id` remains the only business-event identity. An entry ID is never an `event_id`, never a dedup key, never an ordering key across keys, never placed in an envelope, and never read by the relay to decide whether to publish (7D TPT-02 and TPT-10's decision rule, 7E ENT-04, 7C ID-03, all unchanged). Accounting, completion evidence and cases stay keyed by (group, `event_id`). A position record only answers one question: *where in which key did the transport copy of this event land*. It is stored beside the outbox, not in the outbox row. |
| ACC-15 [7I] | **Group registration record.** A durable PostgreSQL record per (logical group, physical key, topology generation): the start position the group was created at (`0` for every V1 group, 7E BST-01; the explicit position of a governed later registration, BST-04), and, when a governed retirement closes it (7G §38), the boundary position and the operation reference. It is written in the governed provisioning, key-onboarding (7F TKO-01) and retirement operations, by the tooling principal, with an audit row; the gateway and the consumers cannot write it. **Coverage:** a registration covers position `R` on its key when `start < R` and it is either open or closed at a boundary `≥ R`. A pair of a retired group at or below the boundary stays owed until it has an accounting row or the retirement operation's recorded disposition as a case (7G DAU-05); a position above the boundary, or at or below a later group's start, is not owed by that group. This is the per-group admission evidence the reconciler needs; it mirrors, and does not replace, 7E's registry and 7F's handler-contract record. |
| ACC-16 [7I] | **Exact-position classification, payload-free.** For an unaccounted pair (event `E`, group `g`) and each recorded position (`K`, `R`) that `g`'s registration covers, the reconciler issues `XINFO GROUPS K` and reads `g`'s `last-delivered-id` `L`; and, when `R ≤ L`, `XPENDING K g R R 1`. Entry IDs are compared as IDs (two unsigned integers), never as times. Result: `R > L` → **`UNDELIVERED`** (the cursor has not reached the entry); `R ≤ L` and the range query returns `R` → **`PENDING`** (delivered, not acknowledged); `R ≤ L` and the range query returns nothing → **`GONE`** (delivered or skipped, and no longer pending). A key or group that does not exist yields `GONE`. Redis unreachable yields `UNKNOWN`. The pair as a whole is `GONE` only when **every** covered position is `GONE`; it then goes to ACC-05 at once. Otherwise it waits, under ACC-17. `GONE` is exactly the state the trim watermark treats as acknowledged (7E TRM-05), which is why no accounting row there means the obligation left Redis without evidence. No later entry is needed to reach this verdict: it compares one stored ID with the group's cursor. |
| ACC-17 [7I] | **Deadline backstop, PostgreSQL clock only.** Every unaccounted pair has an age: database `now()` minus the earliest `recorded_at` of its positions (or the row's `published_at` if, against ACC-13, no position exists). A pair older than the obligation deadline `T_obl` goes to ACC-05 **whatever ACC-16 reports**: `UNDELIVERED` (the entry may have been trimmed or deleted ahead of the cursor, or the group is stalled), `PENDING` (a claim that is never completed), or `UNKNOWN`. Both timestamps come from one clock, and no Redis value enters the decision. `T_obl` is 7K's value; it must exceed the group-lag bound of HE-7K-7I-06, so a healthy but slow group does not produce cases, and it must be below the ACC-06 alert bound. A case opened for an entry that later arrives is harmless: the normal delivery is processed and accounted, and the case's R2 then finds the completion and resolves as already committed. This rule, not ACC-16, is what guarantees detection against a gateway or a Redis that reports false state. |
| ACC-18 [7I] | **Duplicate publication and the confirmation / persistence crash.** (a) Relay crashes after `XADD` is confirmed and before the mark call: entry `R1` exists with no position; the row is reclaimed and republished as `R2`, which is recorded. Processing either entry accounts the pair, because accounting is by `event_id`. Losing `R1` alone is harmless while `R2` is live; losing `R2` is detected on `R2`. An unrecorded entry can therefore only add a delivery, never hide a loss. (b) Lease expiry with both relays confirming: both positions are recorded (ACC-13); the pair is `GONE` only when both are. (c) The mark transaction commits and its reply is lost: the row is `PUBLISHED` with its position; the retry is a no-op and the position insert is idempotent on (`event_id`, key, entry ID). (d) Confirmation fails or is unknown (7D PRB-05): no position is recorded and the row is not marked; 7D's unknown-outcome handling is unchanged. **Invariant:** a row is `PUBLISHED` only in a transaction that also recorded a position whose entry was confirmed durable before that transaction began. |
| ACC-19 [7I] | **Generations and keys.** A position names its own topology generation and physical key, so one event published to keys of two generations has two positions with their own registrations and owed sets. Before an old-generation key is retired every pending entry on it has a 7G terminal disposition (7G TPG-05); an unaccounted pair on a key that no longer exists classifies as `GONE` and becomes a case, which is the conservative result. A handler-contract cutover (7F CUT-1 … CUT-9) changes `A(g, E)` and not the transport obligation, so it changes no owed set here. The reconciler never infers a position, a generation or an origin from an ID's value, a time or a UUID (7G DSR-13). |
| ACC-20 [7I] | **Concurrency and atomicity.** The capture-and-case transaction takes the row lock of 7G DSR-12 (a), which conflicts with deletion, and inserts the case under its (group, `event_id`) identity. A concurrent accounting insert by the gateway may also commit; both then exist, the cleanup interlock is satisfied, and the case resolves through R2 as already committed. A concurrent cleanup blocks on the row lock and then finds the case. Two reconciler runs converge on one case. A reconciler crash between classification and capture leaves the pair listed for the next run. The classification the reconciler stores is advisory history; the decisions of ACC-05, ACC-06 and ACC-17 re-read PostgreSQL. |

**Why the time comparison fails (the reviewed counterexample).** Redis appends entry `E` with ID `R`. The relay confirms durability. PostgreSQL then sets `published_at = P`, with `P` later than the instant encoded in `R`, by the confirmation wait at least and, after a relay crash and reclaim, by a lease timeout or more. A subverted gateway issues `XREADGROUP … NOACK`, or `XACK`, for the group. The group's cursor is now `R`, it has no pending entry, and no further entry arrives. 7E TRM-02 gives `bound(g)` = the ID immediately after `R`. The withdrawn test asked whether the *time* of that bound exceeds `P` plus a margin. It does not, and it never will: the bound moves only when a later entry is delivered, and none exists. The pair is reported as "group merely behind" indefinitely, while ACC-06 holds the outbox row and nothing recovers the obligation. The test also compared a Redis node's clock with PostgreSQL's, and treated an entry ID as a timestamp, which 7E ENT-04 forbids.

**The counterexample, closed.** The same sequence under the corrected rules: the mark-published transaction stored (`event_id`, generation, key, `R`). The reconciler lists the pair as unaccounted, reads the group's `last-delivered-id` (`R`), finds `R ≤ L`, asks `XPENDING K g R R 1` and receives nothing: `GONE`. It captures the still-retained outbox row under DSR-12 and opens one `PARKED` class `V` case. R2 delivers the bytes to the owning handler through the unchanged 7F pipeline; the guard applies the effect once and the completion record makes the result verifiable. Had the subverted gateway also falsified what the reconciler could learn from Redis, or had Redis been unreachable, the pair would reach the same case at `T_obl` (ACC-17). The outbox row could not have been cleaned up meanwhile (ACC-06). A compromised campaign worker cannot start the sequence at all: it has no Redis credential and no route (GWY-13, GWY-14), and the gateway refuses any group it is not bound to (GWY-04). Tests: VT-70 … VT-73, VT-78 … VT-81.

### 9.7 Delivery-bound completion evidence (P1-7I-R11, part B; OD-7I-18)

Nothing in this section exists. It needs a controlled erratum to 7F (ERR-7I-14) and a case reason in 7G (ERR-7I-15).

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| CEV-01 [OD-7I-18] | **Delivery token.** With every entry it delivers to an authenticated member, the gateway issues a token: a message-authentication code under the gateway's token key over a fixed-format encoding of: the purpose label `7i-delivery-v1`; the consumer identity (context and member name); the database principal bound to that context; the logical group; the topology generation and physical key; the entry ID; the envelope's `event_id` and `organization_id` (or the platform-scope marker); the handler-contract generation the member was admitted under (7F HCG-03); the delivery count reported for the entry; issue time and expiry. The encoding length-prefixes each field. This is the delivery handle of GWY-04, now specified (conditions B-1, B-2). |
| CEV-02 [OD-7I-18; OD-7I-19] | **Two codes, two keys.** A token carries two authentication codes over the same fields. The **gateway code** is under a key that lives in the secret manager, is readable by the gateway workload identity alone and is never stored in PostgreSQL; only the gateway can verify it, at acknowledgement (CEV-08). The **database-verifiable code** is under a second key that the gateway also holds and that PostgreSQL holds in the protected relation of STP-10, so that `fn_record_completion` and the `EVENT` transition functions can verify a delivery *before* they write (STP-05). No login role can read either key. Consumer workloads, the relay, the tooling and every database principal cannot mint a token (B-7). Forging an acknowledgement needs both keys; forging a write needs the database key, which no runtime credential can read. Keys have versions and IDs; a retired version is kept verify-only while any retained completion record cites it (the KEY-14 pattern), and is then destroyed. |
| CEV-03 [OD-7I-18] | **Completion record.** One insert-only row per (logical group, `event_id`): `organization_id`; origin (`GATEWAY_DELIVERY`, `RECOVERY_ITEM`); outcome (`COMMITTED`, `EXTERNAL_WRITE_ATTESTED`); the token as presented, or the operation-item reference; the writer's `session_user`; the commit time. No runtime role has any table privilege on the relation. It holds identifiers only (class `PID`). |
| CEV-04 [7I] | **Not an idempotency guard.** No handler reads a completion record to decide whether to process. The domain-owned guard of 7F §13 and §28 decides, unchanged (CTX-11). The record answers a different question, for a different reader: *may the transport copy be acknowledged*. 7F EID-08 ("no ledger for uniformity") is a rule about guards and stays true; the added row is acknowledgement evidence and its cost is stated in CEV-15. |
| CEV-05 [OD-7I-18] | **The only writer.** `fn_record_completion(group, event_id, organization_id, token)` is `SECURITY DEFINER`. It raises unless: `session_user` is the principal registered for that group's owning context (a governed table written by the migration, PRV-19); `organization.current_tenant_id()` equals the organization argument (or both are the platform scope); the token's group, `event_id`, organization and principal fields, read as claims, equal the arguments and `session_user`; the token's database-verifiable code verifies (CEV-02; STP-05); and the token's expiry is later than the database clock. It then inserts with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. It is granted to the nine context principals and to no other role (PRV-28 assertion). The gateway code is checked separately, by the gateway alone (CEV-08). A holder of a context's database credential with no genuine delivery can therefore not even record a completion. |
| CEV-06 [OD-7I-18] | **Atomic with the effect.** A database-transactional handler calls the function inside its owner transaction, after its guard has won and with its effects, so the guard, the effects, any emitted outbox row and the completion record commit together or not at all (7F TXA-01, extended by one statement; B-4). **Which transactions record one depends on what the guard can tell (CEV-06a).** |
| CEV-06a [7I] | **Event-keyed and state-keyed guards.** (i) *Event-keyed* guards identify the event itself: the IC-1 ledgers and the IC-2 keys derived from `event_id` (CON-04, CON-06, CON-07, and CON-10 once its claim exists). "Already present" there means *this event* was claimed before, so the claiming transaction must have left a completion record. The duplicate path writes nothing, and a present guard with no record is CEV-09. (ii) *State-keyed* guards test the owner's current state and do not name the event: IC-3 (CON-05, CON-11), the organization-level IC-2 key of CON-02, and IC-4 (CON-03, CON-09). By frozen design they absorb logical duplicates (7F EID-08): a transition that finds the row already at or beyond its target is a correct, effect-free outcome, whoever advanced the row. For these the handler's transaction records the completion **whether or not the transition won**, because the record means "the owning context's transaction evaluated this delivered event and committed its decision". CEV-09 does not apply to them. The completion record does not, by itself, show who advanced such state; that is established by §8.9, under which a guard column can be written only by a function that verified an authorized cause (OD-7I-19). |
| CEV-07 [OD-7I-18] | **Per class.** IC-1, IC-2, IC-3: as CEV-06. IC-4 (CON-03, CON-09): written in the recompute transaction; these consumers thereby gain per-event acknowledgement evidence without gaining a guard. IC-5 (CON-01, CON-08): no owner transaction exists; after the external write definitively succeeds (7F EXT-04) a short transaction records outcome `EXTERNAL_WRITE_ATTESTED`. That record proves an authenticated member of the owning context, holding a real delivery, declared the boundary reached. It proves nothing about the external store; ACC-08 remains the independent check (B-9). |
| CEV-08 [OD-7I-18] | **Verification at acknowledgement.** The evidence function returns the completion row for (group, `event_id`) to the gateway principal. The gateway accepts it only if: the authentication code verifies under a retained key version; the purpose label matches; the token's group and `event_id` and organization equal those of the entry being acknowledged; the token's context is the owning context of the group; and the row's writer is that context's registered principal. The token's entry ID and key may differ from the entry being acknowledged (a duplicate delivery of the same event), provided the key is one the group is registered on. Expiry is not re-applied at verification: it limited when the completion could be *recorded*, and a committed record does not lapse (B-5). |
| CEV-09 [OD-7I-18] | **An event-keyed guard with no completion.** The handler's event-keyed guard (CEV-06a i) reports "already processed", and no acceptable completion record exists (a forged ledger or effect row; a row written under another role). The gateway refuses. The worker does not retry indefinitely: it parks the entry through the ledger worker function as a class `V` case for (group, `event_id`), reason `COMPLETION_EVIDENCE_UNATTRIBUTED`, with material (7G PAT-01), and the case is then the acknowledgement evidence. The case cannot be rejected (7G DAU-02). An R2 would meet the same guard and is not a resolution; the case is resolved only by the owning domain's reconciliation (R6), which establishes what the effect should be and repairs it under its own authority. A security signal is raised. Nothing is acknowledged on the forged row, and nothing is discarded. |
| CEV-10 [OD-7I-18] | **Replay, substitution, cross-group use (B-6).** Re-presenting a token for its own (group, event): a no-op conflict. Presenting it for another event, group or organization: refused in the function by field equality, and would fail the gateway's code check if the fields were altered. Two groups of one context (Campaign CON-05 and CON-11; Compliance CON-02 and CON-03) cannot use each other's tokens, because the group is bound. A token cannot be obtained without being an authenticated, registered member of that group at the gateway. A stolen database credential alone therefore yields no acceptable evidence for any group; a stolen gateway identity alone cannot write a row. |
| CEV-11 [7I] | **Crashes, duplicates, stale claims, expiry (B-8).** Crash before the owner commit: nothing exists; the redelivery carries a fresh token and is processed. Crash after commit, before acknowledgement: the redelivery takes the duplicate path and the original record verifies, whichever gateway instance issued its token. A stale claim taken over by another member: the new delivery has its own token; if the first member's transaction commits late, the guard arbitrates as 7F §19 specifies and exactly one record exists. Token expiry before a slow handler commits: the function raises, the transaction rolls back, the entry is redelivered with a fresh token; the expiry is a 7K value above the handler time budget. In no branch is an obligation acknowledged without a record or lost for want of one. |
| CEV-12 [7I] | **Generation changes.** The token carries the handler-contract generation for attribution; admission and revalidation remain 7F HCG-02 … HCG-04. A record committed under generation *n* stays valid after a cutover, because the obligation is fixed by origin provenance (7F HCG-28 … HCG-30), not by the current generation. A topology-generation change is covered by the key in the token and by CEV-08's registered-key condition. |
| CEV-13 [7I] | **Recovery items.** R2 and R3 feed the 7F pipeline by an internal path, not through the gateway (GWY-16). Their handler transaction records the completion with origin `RECOVERY_ITEM`; the function verifies **in the database**, under the item's lock, that the operation item exists, is running, and targets that group, event and organization, and it commits with the item result (7G). No gateway token is involved and none can be substituted for it. |
| CEV-14 [7I] | **What each compromise yields.** Database credential of another context: nothing (CTX-03; CEV-05). Database credential of the same context without its gateway identity: for an event-keyed guard, a row with no token, hence CEV-09; for a state-keyed guard, nothing: the guard column is not writable and the transition function demands a verifiable token (§8.9). Gateway keys: tokens, but no row. `app_api`: no write on the event-keyed guards (CTX-03 lists none for it) and, on the state tables of CON-02, CON-05 and CON-11, only the `API` edges and only with an action proof it cannot compute from the database credential alone (STP-06). Platform-administrator credential: no `EXECUTE` on the function and no guard column. Both credentials of one context, or a compromised API process: that workload's own authority (RR-08; attacker C). |
| CEV-15 [7I] | **Cost, stated for 7K (HE-7K-7I-10).** One insert per (group, event) in every handler transaction; one token computation per delivery and one verification per acknowledgement; one evidence read; storage for the records. **Retention (RET-27):** at least the consumer's guard evidence horizon (7F §31) and at least the life of the outbox row plus 30 days; for state-guarded consumers, whose horizon is unbounded, a 7K value. The failure direction of early purge is safe and visible: a later duplicate becomes a `COMPLETION_EVIDENCE_UNATTRIBUTED` case, never a silent acknowledgement. |
| CEV-16 [7I] | **What is not claimed.** The record shows that a transaction of the owning context committed while holding a genuine delivery of that event. It does not prove the handler's code was correct, and for IC-5 it does not prove the external write. Outside the guard columns of §8.9 it does not prevent a holder of a context's own database credential from writing false data into that context's own tables (RR-01); it prevents that data from being accepted as proof that a delivery was handled. |

**The counterexample, closed.** (1) An attacker steals the Campaign consumer's database credential. (2) It sets a tenant context of some organization: allowed, as before. (3) It tries to insert Billing's `usage_events` row with the event's idempotency key: `42501`, because the Campaign principal holds no write privilege on a Billing guard object (CTX-03). Suppose instead the stolen credential is Billing's own, without Billing's gateway identity, and the row is inserted. (4) The genuine delivery reaches Billing's consumer; its guard reports a duplicate. (5) The gateway looks for a completion record for (billing group, event): none exists, because the attacker could not obtain a token for that delivery and `fn_record_completion` rejects a call without one. Acknowledgement is refused. (6) The worker parks a `COMPLETION_EVIDENCE_UNATTRIBUTED` case with the event's bytes; Billing's reconciliation finds a usage row that no delivery produced and corrects it. The business effect is not silently absent, the obligation is not acknowledged on forged evidence, and the forgery is on record. Until IR-40 and IR-41 exist the original sequence succeeds, and AB-7I-11 therefore blocks every durable consumer. Tests: VT-85 … VT-90.

---
## 10. Event Classification and Redaction

### 10.1 Classes

Nine classes. A field has exactly one. A record, entry, body or material copy inherits the highest class of anything it contains, in the order `SEC` > `SEN` > `PII` > `FIN-P` > `FIN-T` > `PID` > `INT` > `TEN` > `OPS`.

| Class | Name | Definition | Examples in the catalogue |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OPS` | Public operational metadata | Carries no tenant business meaning and identifies no one | `event_type`, `event_version`, closed enum codes, error codes from a known list |
| `TEN` | Tenant-confidential business information | Business facts of one organization that identify no natural person | campaign and agent identifiers, field-name lists, counts, organization name, tool names |
| `INT` | Platform-internal operational information | How the platform runs; not the tenant's and not for the tenant | provider and model references, worker identity, claim state, egress rule code, pinned address, stream entry IDs |
| `PID` | Personal identifier or linked attribute | An opaque identifier of a natural person or of that person's interaction, or an attribute that is personal only through such an identifier. **Not anonymous**: it is linkable while the owning record exists | `contact_id`, `call_id`, `conversation_id`, `appointment_id`, `user_id`, consent status, appointment times, body hashes |
| `FIN-T` | Tenant financial information | Amounts the tenant itself is entitled to see, including the customer's own authoritative billed spend and a ratio computed only from such amounts | invoice totals, deal values, usage thresholds, EV-097 `total_cost` and `roi_pct` on a billed basis |
| `FIN-P` | Platform-confidential financial information | Provider procurement cost, wholesale rate, margin, spread, internal rates, **and any figure derived from them, a ratio included** | never in any event (7A BIL-05; 6L DEC-6L-02, §26.2); `billing.cost_entries` amounts; a campaign cost summed from them |
| `PII` | Direct personal information | Identifies or contacts a natural person by itself | phone numbers, names, email addresses, file names that may contain names |
| `SEN` | Sensitive personal or call content | What was said or derived from it, and free text that may quote it | transcript and utterance text, summaries, recordings, tool arguments and results, free-text reasons |
| `SEC` | Restricted security or credential information | A secret, a bearer capability, or an identifier whose disclosure weakens a security control | tokens, signing secrets, presigned URLs, token identifiers, URL query strings, storage locators of sensitive media |

`PID` deserves its sentence: an identifier, a hash or a pseudonym is classified by its actual re-identification risk and its retention basis, and is never treated as anonymous because it is opaque (OD-7I-06 condition 5). A UUID that still joins to a contact row is personal data for as long as the join works.

### 10.2 How each class maps to enforcement

| Class | Internal durable event | Stream entry | Outbox / ledger metadata columns | Replay material | Logs and traces | Metric labels | External (webhook, plugin) | Field-level encryption at rest | Erasure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `OPS` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, where the value set is closed and small | Yes | No | None |
| `TEN` | Yes | Yes | Identifiers only | Yes | Identifiers only; never free values | No | Only if the topic's allow-list names it | No | With the organization |
| `INT` | Yes, where a frozen binding has it | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, internal sinks only | Closed sets only | **Never**; never on a tenant surface | No | Operational retention |
| `PID` | Yes | Yes | Yes (case identity, aggregate reference) | Yes | Internal restricted sinks only; never a tenant-visible log | **Never** | Only if the topic's allow-list names it | No (storage-level) | Follows the owning record; identifiers survive a tombstone only where the owner's retention keeps them |
| `FIN-T` | Yes | Yes | No | Yes | No | No | Only the billing topics, exactly as 6K §45.1 | No | Financial retention of the owner |
| `FIN-P` | **Never** | Never | Never | Never | Never | Never | **Never** | — | — |
| `PII` | Only where a frozen V1 binding already carries it (MIN-01) | Yes (same bytes) | **Never** | Yes, encrypted | **Never** | **Never** | Only the fields 6J §40.2 names, for the topics it names | **Yes** in material and processing inputs | Erased when erasure is due (§14) |
| `SEN` | Free-text reasons only where a frozen V1 binding carries them; content **never** | Same | **Never** | Yes, encrypted | **Never** | **Never** | **Never** | **Yes** | Erased when erasure is due |
| `SEC` | **Never**, except the one frozen non-bearer identifier of EV-001 | Same | **Never** | Only as part of EV-001 | **Never** | **Never** | **Never** | Yes where stored | With the credential's own lifecycle |

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| CLS-01 [7I] | The classification of every event field is recorded in a code-owned **classification manifest** keyed by (`event_type`, `event_version`, field path), alongside the 7C schema manifest (IR-20). A field without an entry is treated as `SEN`. |
| CLS-02 [FROZEN] | The exclusions of 7C §19.3 and 7B §24 are absolute for every version: no token, credential, secret-manager value, presigned URL, raw media, transcript or utterance text, raw provider payload or card data. |
| CLS-03 [7I] | A whole event type is **PII-bearing** when its V1 payload has at least one `PII` or `SEN` field. In V1 these are EV-004, EV-019, EV-021, EV-024, EV-025, EV-038, EV-049, EV-087, EV-088, EV-091 and EV-092. Every other durable type is **identifier-only**. This distinction drives OD-7I-06. |
| CLS-04 [7I] | Bytes that could not be parsed (`CONSUMER_UNIDENTIFIED`, `TRANSPORT_INTEGRITY`) are of unknown content and are treated as `SEN` everywhere: encrypted, never logged, never shown unmasked by default. |
| CLS-05 [7I] | **Necessity.** A field is in an event only if a current or catalogued consumer needs it and cannot obtain it from the owner by identifier. Where §10.3 marks a field "not needed by any current consumer", MIN-02 applies. |
| CLS-06 [7I] | A malformed or unknown classification value fails closed: the manifest fails to load, and the producer or serializer that depends on it does not start. It never defaults to a lower class. |
| CLS-07 [7I] | **DLQ sensitivity** (7E HE-7I-04). An entry moved out of a PEL into the ledger becomes replay material and takes the class of its content under CLS-03 / CLS-04. |
| CLS-08 [7I] | A storage locator of sensitive media (an object key of a recording) is class `SEC`: it is not a credential, but together with storage access it yields the media. It is never in a log, a metric, a tenant surface or an external body. |
