| RET-22 | Erasure-step records, hold records, capability grants (in PostgreSQL) | [REC] as long as the audit rows that cite them are hot | — | — | — | Hold and step records carry identifiers only | [7I] |
| RET-23 | Backups | Deployment value (7K). 3F §11 currently states 7 days of point-in-time recovery, 30 days of daily snapshots and 1 year of weekly snapshots | Contain earlier copies until they age out | — | A hold never extends a backup | ERA-20; restore only into quarantine | [LATER]; 3F |
| RET-24 | Erasure journal records (object storage) | Until every backup, recovery range and replica that predates the record's completion or withdrawal has left restorability, plus a margin: completion time + the longest backup retention + [REC] 30 days. Hold records: while the hold is active, then the same horizon. All object versions expire together | — | — | A hold on the journal itself is possible under `retention.hold.manage` | Not erased on request: the record is what prevents resurrection. It holds identifiers only, encrypted, and is disclosed as residue (ERA-18) | [OD] OD-7I-13 |
| RET-25 | Obligation accounting rows | Until the outbox row is deleted, plus [REC] 30 days | — | — | Unchanged | Not altered (identifiers only) | [OD] OD-7I-15 |
| RET-26 | Transport position records; group registration records | Positions: with their outbox row, plus [REC] 30 days. Registrations: kept as history | — | — | Unchanged | Not altered (identifiers and transport positions only) | [7I] ACC-13, ACC-15; ERR-7I-13 |
| RET-27 | Completion records | At least the consumer's guard evidence horizon (7F §31) and the outbox row's life plus [REC] 30 days; a 7K value for state-guarded consumers | — | — | Unchanged | Not altered (identifiers and a delivery token; no payload) | [OD] OD-7I-18; CEV-15 |
| RET-28 | Subject index (HLD-16): heads; edges, current and ended; merge links | An edge lives while its source row exists, or any content-bearing event-store row still carries that attribution, or it lies on a path to an unreleased hold. Then it is removed by the maintenance principal. Ending an edge does not remove it: an ended edge is evidence and still links (HLD-21). A contact's `KEY` edges, current and ended, go when the contact has been erased and the last content-bearing row attributed through it has gone; they are not kept for the life of the tombstone row | — (identifiers, keyed digests with their key version, transition provenance; no content) | — | Not removed while it could decide a hold | Entries of an erased subject go when the last attributed row has gone; a subject's erasure is not complete while they remain. The key version an edge was written under cannot be retired while the edge exists (HLD-20) | [OD] OD-7I-26, OD-7I-27; HLD-16 |
| RET-29 | Retention-decision records, exceptions, association releases, determinations, seal records and unauthorized-retention incident records (HLD-18, HLD-21, HLD-22) | The life of the row they concern, then 5J §20 as audit evidence. An incident record's interval is never shortened or rewritten | — (identifiers, hold references, deadlines, occurrence times, operators, reason and evidence references, escalation history; no content) | — | Unchanged | Not altered | [OD] OD-7I-26, OD-7I-27, OD-7I-28 |
| RET-30 | Sealed content (HLD-22; §14.7a) | **No retention period: its approved limit has already passed.** It exists only until a disposition: a proven hold (then until that hold ends), an exception (until its expiry, then unauthorized again) or lawful erasure. While none exists it is unauthorized overdue retention (RR-10), of no bounded duration | Sealed; no ordinary reader | Not replayable, not deliverable, not exportable | A hold proven for it keeps it. Nothing else does | Erased at once on a lawful determination, or when no hold it was assessed against remains | [OD] OD-7I-28 |

Rows: 30. No row states an indefinite period, **and one row is not bounded**: RET-30 has no period because it is already past one. It is unauthorized retention accepted as a residual (RR-10), not a longer period, and this matrix does not present it as a limit. An unattributed row that HLD-18 keeps past its clock does not change its row here: its retention period is the one stated, and what keeps it is a proven hold, or a separate dual-controlled exception that expires, or nothing that authorizes it at all, in which case it is sealed and recorded as an unauthorized-retention incident (HLD-22); never a longer period. Since OD-7I-16 the journal of RET-24 holds a record for every time-erased row as well as for request-driven erasures: encrypted identifiers and lifecycle states of those rows persist for the backup-restorability horizon, about one year under 3F's current schedule, which is longer than the 30 / 90 days the rows themselves live. That is the price of restore safety, was put to the owner, and is part of LR-05. The three rows with no age limit are bounded by state, not left open: RET-08 by the 90-day hold expiry, RET-11 by resolution, RET-18 by the bounded processing-attempt count. **Since OD-7I-29 and OD-7I-30:** "under an active hold" in this matrix means a hold of either kind whose effective state reaches the row (HLD-11). And the body clock of each row is also the end of its ordinary use: once it has run, no ordinary path reads or uses the content, whether a hold keeps it, a pass has sealed it, or no pass has run (CAG-01). A hold changes how long content is preserved. It never changes how long it may be used. Coverage certifications, their acceptance records and the legacy flags of HLD-24 are kept on the terms RET-29 and RET-28 set for decision records and index heads.

### 14.3 Erasure principles

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| ERA-01 [7I] | **Erasing personal content is not deleting proof of processing.** After any erasure in this section the following remain for their own retention: identity of the row or case, its state and history, the SHA-256 of what was erased, category codes, timestamps and the erasure reference. |
| ERA-02 [OD-7I-06] | Identifiers, pseudonyms and hashes that remain are class `PID`. They are kept only for the retention of the row that holds them and are never described as anonymous. A body hash covers a body that contains unique event and request identifiers, so it cannot practically be reversed by enumeration; it is still treated as linkable. |
| ERA-03 [FROZEN + OD] | **Erasure never resolves an obligation** (7G RPM-12, PRT-06; INV-09). It does not mean the event succeeded, was rejected or became terminal. It never produces `RESOLVED`, `NOT_OWED`, `NOT_APPLICABLE`, `DELIVERED` or `CANCELLED`. |
| ERA-04 [7I] | Erasure in the event pipeline is one part of a data-subject request, which is the Organization context's aggregate (6C §13). 7I defines what the event stores do when asked; it does not define the request workflow, its verification or its deadlines. |
| ERA-05 [7I; OD-7I-13] | **Crash-safe, idempotent and journaled.** Each (request, store) pair is a durable **erasure step** in PostgreSQL: organization, request reference, store, the subject's resource references, status, attempt count, completion evidence (counts), and its **journal state** (JRN-06). A step is executed by guarded functions that are safe to repeat: erasing an already-erased row changes nothing and reports it. A worker crash leaves the step open and it is resumed; the request is not reported complete for a store until that step is `VERIFIED`. **The step ledger alone is not restore-safe**: it lives in the database and returns to the past with it. No erasure function runs unless the step's intent is already durable in the independent journal of §14.8. **A row an erasure function does not erase because a hold applies is recorded on the step or batch as `SKIPPED_HELD`, with the reason and the hold or decision record concerned; it is never counted as erased, and a step with such a row is never `VERIFIED` or reported complete** (HLD-18). A row sealed at its limit is recorded as `SEALED_UNDECIDED` on the same terms (SEAL-02). |
| ERA-06 [7I] | **Subject resolution.** The owning contexts resolve the subject to resource references before their own erasure runs: the contact identifier and the identifiers of that contact's calls, conversations, appointments, deals and campaign-contact rows. The event stores are searched by organization and those references: deliveries by `event_id` of events whose aggregate is one of them; cases by (`organization_id`, `aggregate_type`, `aggregate_id`). The ledger therefore records the validated envelope's aggregate reference on the case (IR-24). That is envelope metadata, not payload, so 7G LDG-06 is respected. The same mapping, kept as a standing subject index (HLD-16), is what scopes a hold of either kind that has subject scope (HLD-11): an erasure and a hold resolve a subject to rows in one way, from one source, so they cannot disagree. Every content-bearing row of the event stores carries an attribution reference from creation (HLD-17). |

### 14.4 An erasure request, stage by stage

| # | Where the subject's data is | What the erasure does | What it must not do | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ERA-S1 | **Pending outbox row** | Nothing. The row is a publication obligation and is published unchanged | Delete, edit or skip the row | The row ages out 7 days after publication, or later only under the accounting interlock (RET-01). The step records the expected expiry. The one exception is a row made stale by a database recovery (JRN-15) |
| ERA-S2 | **Event already published**, in a stream | Nothing to the entry | `XDEL`, trimming out of order | The entry leaves by safe trim. Port-read fields of a later fan-out are `null` because the owner record is already tombstoned (XPL-06) |
| ERA-S3 | **Consumer retry** (case `OPEN_RETRY`, entry pending) | Nothing to the entry. No material exists yet | Acknowledge, park or resolve because of the erasure | The handler runs against the tombstoned owner state and returns its true result. If it later parks, the material is erased as S4 |
| ERA-S4 | **Parked or poison case with PII-bearing material** | Erase the material in one transaction; `material_state = ERASED_UNDER_PRIVACY_RULE`; reason `PRIVACY_MATERIAL_ERASED`; erasure reference; history entry; state → `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` (7G T-13) | Resolve the case; set any terminal resolution | Raw replay is no longer possible. The owning domain reconciles (7G R6) |
| ERA-S5 | **Recovery case with a valid owed obligation and identifier-only material** | Nothing now. The material holds identifiers and quantities only | Erase it early, which would force a reconciliation for no privacy gain | Kept until resolution and within 90 days of parking (RET-12). The step records that it was examined and why it was kept |
| ERA-S6 | **Captured replay material** (R4 source) | As S4 or S5 by its class. An item of a running operation that needs it gets `SOURCE_MISSING` | Fabricate a source | The operation's result records it |
| ERA-S7 | **Webhook delivery `PENDING` or `DELIVERING`** | Nothing while the delivery is owed. The body is erased in the same transaction that makes the row terminal | Cancel the delivery; erase the body under an active claim | Bounded: the frozen schedule ends within days; a held delivery ends at the 90-day hold expiry (RET-08). The step stays open and visible until then |
| ERA-S8 | **Delivered or dead-lettered history** | Erase body and preview at once; keep row, hash, history, category | Delete the row; alter history records | `body_state = ERASED`. Replay of that row is refused |
| ERA-S9 | **Replay descendants** | Every row with the same (`organization_id`, `event_id`) is treated in one pass: root, descendants, and deliveries to other endpoints | Leave a sibling copy | All copies gone or scheduled under S7 |
| ERA-S10 | **Callback processing input** | Terminal `FAILED`: delete at once. Not terminal: wait for the terminal transition, then delete in it | Delete owed work | Bounded by the processing-attempt limit |
| ERA-S11 | **Audit entry** | Nothing | Rewrite an immutable row | Rows written by 7I contain no personal content by construction (RED-10). `actor_name` is LR-04 |
| ERA-S12 | **Backup copy** | Nothing to the backup. The erasure is already recorded in the independent journal, which a restore cannot rewind | Edit a backup; rely on the erasure-step ledger inside the restored database; rely on a row's own clock to re-erase it after a restore | ERA-20; §14.8 |

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| ERA-07 [OD] | An undispositioned outbox `FAILED` row of a PII-bearing type is a publisher recovery case whose replay source is the row (7G RPM-04). When erasure is due, or 90 days after the case was parked, a guarded function replaces the payload with a tombstone and records the digest; the case moves to `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` and the producing owner reconciles. The row and its interlock are otherwise untouched. |
| ERA-08 [OD] | Material of a PII-bearing type (CLS-03) is erased when a linked subject's erasure is due (S4). Identifier-only material is kept until its case resolves, inside RET-12 (S5). Material of unknown content (CLS-04) cannot be linked to a subject; it is reached by the 90-day cap, by OD-7I-11 and by organization-level erasure. While a hold that can make a row uncertain exists in its organization (HLD-11 c: a hold of either kind with subject scope or a `RESOURCE` reference), such material is in the uncertainty set: it cannot be shown not to be the held subject's, so the cap does not erase it and it follows the decision procedure of HLD-18. |
| ERA-09 [OD] | Once material is erased every replay path that depends on it is disabled: the case is not an R2 candidate, and a plan that names it gets `SOURCE_MISSING`. Nothing reconstructs it from logs, traces, audit rows or mutable domain state (7G RPM-08). |
| ERA-10 [OD] | A webhook body is erased by a guarded function that acts only on a **terminal** row, only for a step or batch whose intent is durable in the journal (INV-23), and removes the body and the preview together. The terminal-only restriction is never relaxed for a restore: a row restored as non-terminal is first brought to its journaled terminal state (JRN-25) and only then erased. Earlier lawful erasure (a subject's request) and the lineage and cancellation clocks all use this one function. |
| ERA-11 [OD] | A body is never erased while its delivery is `PENDING` or `DELIVERING`. Past any deadline, a non-terminal delivery keeps exactly what its obligation needs, the body, and nothing is added to it; the open erasure step is its explicit reconciliation record. |
| ERA-12 [7I] | **Transactional erasure of material.** One transaction, under the case's row lock: verify the case is `PARKED` (or `REPLAYING` → wait, ERA-15); verify no hold; delete ciphertext and wrapped key; set `material_state` and the erasure reference; compare-and-swap the state; write the history entry and the audit row. Either all of it commits or none. |
| ERA-13 [7I] | A case in `OPEN_RETRY` or `HOLD` has no 7G transition to `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` by erasure (T-13 is from `PARKED` and `REPLAYING`). Its material, where a crash-loop hold stored some, is erased when the case parks, which the isolation limit bounds (7G CLP-06). No new transition is invented. |
| ERA-14 [7I] | A case already in `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` keeps its state; only `material_state` and the erasure reference change. |
| ERA-15 [OD-7I-10] | **Reference interlock.** Material referenced by an operation that is `APPROVED`, `RUNNING` or `PAUSED` is not erased. The wait is bounded: an approval expires in 24 hours (OPA-11); a running item completes; a paused operation older than a bound ([REC] 72 hours) releases its unstarted items with result `CANCELLED`, which leaves their cases `PARKED` (7G CAN-03) and frees the reference. Then the erasure runs. |
| ERA-16 [7I] | **Tenant isolation of cleanup.** Every erasure function selects by organization and reference, or by a predicate on the row's own clock. A subject-driven erasure of organization A cannot reach a row of B: the function takes the organization from the erasure step, which was created under A's tenant context. |
| ERA-17 [7I] | **Organization erasure.** When an organization's data is deleted under the frozen organization lifecycle, its event-pipeline copies go with it: bodies, previews, processing inputs, material (unresolved cases keep their metadata and move to `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` only where an obligation to another party survives; an obligation owed to the erased organization itself is resolved by the owner's reconciliation as superseded), then its KEKs (KEY-18). Organization erasure runs only under an approved organization-erasure operation for a `CANCELLED` organization (§8.12; OD-7I-20); the integration-connection anonymization of `061_5I` is one of its scoped steps. |
| ERA-18 [7I] | **Transport residue is stated, not hidden.** A stream entry cannot be removed on request. The erasure step records, per family, the time by which the trim watermark is expected to pass the entry, and the request's completion evidence lists transport and backup residue with their expected expiry. A trim pin that holds a PII-carrying family beyond a bound is an alert and is handed to 7K for a governed limit (HE-7K-7I-06). |
| ERA-19 [7I] | **Replicas.** Read replicas follow the primary; an erasure is complete there when replication has applied it. The step's completion evidence is taken on the primary. A replica that is **promoted** while it may lack committed transactions is a recovery to an earlier point and is subject to INV-18 exactly like a backup restore; a replica is attached to a restored primary only after that primary is reconciled. |
| ERA-20 [7I; OD-7I-13] | **Backups and recovery.** A backup is immutable and is not edited; it ages out under backup retention. **The restored database's own erasure-step ledger is never the source of what must be re-erased**, because it was restored to the same earlier point. The source is the independent journal. Every recovery that can lose committed transactions (backup restore, point-in-time recovery, promotion of a lagging replica) starts in quarantine, re-applies every journal record later than the recovery point, **including the time-based erasure records and the lifecycle reconciliation of rows restored to an earlier state (JRN-24, JRN-25)**, runs every time-based erasure pass, proves journal completeness, and only then is activated (§14.8; INV-18). Re-running the time-based passes alone does not reconstruct earlier deletions and is not relied on for that. If completeness cannot be proved the environment stays quarantined. Whether retaining erased data inside encrypted, access-restricted backup media for the backup-retention period is acceptable is a legal-review item (LR-05). |
| ERA-21 [7I] | Erasure never recreates data. No function restores an erased body, input or material from a log, a trace, a ticket or business state. |
| ERA-22 [7I] | **Best-effort residue** (7D HO-7I-04). The frozen owner contracts leave object deletion (6F §23.4) and secret purge (6J §42.1, §42.3) best-effort. Their classification is unchanged. 7I adds a detective and corrective control: a periodic reconciliation that lists objects with no referencing row and secret-manager entries with no referencing row, and removes them (IR-26). |
| ERA-23 [7I] | A data-subject erasure is not reported complete while ERA-22's residue for that subject's objects is known to exist. |

### 14.5 Replay material lifecycle (OD-7I-06, 09, 10, 11, 12)

Two clocks that must not be confused:

| Clock | Measured from | Governs | Set by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Evidence horizon** | The event's `occurred_at` | Whether a consumer may process the event through its normal handler | 7F §31: CRM 30 days, Billing and Analytics 90 days, state-guarded consumers unbounded |
| **Material retention** | The case's `parked_at` | How long the stored bytes exist | OD-7I-09: 90 days |

The 90 days is a data-minimization limit. It is **not** a replay entitlement and **not** a reason to close a case.

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| MRL-01 [OD-7I-09] | Replay material of an unresolved case is erased no later than 90 days after `parked_at`, through ERA-12, unless an earlier erasure applies or a recorded hold pauses it. |
| MRL-02 [OD-7I-09] | The erasure uses the frozen RPM-12 path: `material_state = ERASED_UNDER_PRIVACY_RULE`, reason `PRIVACY_MATERIAL_ERASED`, erasure reference, state `RECONCILIATION_PENDING`. Case identity, event provenance, owning context, grant references, obligation status and history are kept. |
| MRL-03 [OD-7I-09] | **The reliability trade-off, stated.** A state-guarded consumer (CON-01, 02, 03, 05, 08, 09, 11) has no fixed evidence horizon, so an event parked for one of them could in principle be replayed after any delay. Erasing its material at 90 days converts an otherwise replayable event into a reconciliation by the owning domain. That cost is accepted by OD-7I-09 in exchange for a bounded lifetime of parked personal data. No consumer is thereby given a "90-day replay limit": a ledger-bound consumer's raw replay ends at its own horizon, which may be much earlier. |
| MRL-04 [7I] | An alert-grade signal is raised 14 days before a case's material deadline, per case owner (HE-7J-7I-08), so that a fix and an R2 can be attempted first. |
| MRL-05 [OD-7I-10] | After `RESOLVED`, material is erased no later than 7 days after `resolved_at`. Metadata, digest, provenance and history keep the frozen 90 days. Payload erasure is never recorded as, or confused with, deletion of the case. |
| MRL-06 [OD-7I-10] | **Backfill reopening is preserved.** A later authorized R3 that reopens a case (7G T-18) stores fresh replay-complete material in the same commit as the item result (7G BKL-14, T-17 / T-18). It never depends on the erased copy. |
| MRL-07 [7I] | **Compatibility with 7G RPM-10.** RPM-10 says material is retained at least while the case is non-terminal; RPM-12 is its one exception, "where a frozen privacy rule requires". OD-7I-09 is an owner-approved privacy rule and is applied through RPM-12, so the state machine is unchanged. The exception is recorded as a controlled erratum to the wording of RPM-10 and RPM-12 (ERR-7I-03); 7G is not edited. |
| MRL-08 [OD-7I-09] | **No material is destroyed while a separate obligation still needs it without that obligation being preserved.** Material is per case (7G LC-3). Where one material record is referenced by more than one case or by a captured source (7G PCL-02), it is erased only when the last reference permits, and each referencing case that loses it takes the RPM-12 transition for itself. |
| MRL-09 [OD-7I-11] | **Day 83, `CONSUMER_UNIDENTIFIED` cases.** A system job runs D-01 … D-07 on the stored immutable bytes with the current build, inside the decrypting service, and records the result on the case history. It emits no bytes and holds no disposition capability (OPA-17). |
| MRL-10 [OD-7I-11] | **If it now validates:** permanent rejection is refused (7G DAU-09). The case becomes an R2 candidate with a trusted identity, and its origin and obligation are verified by the normal R2 path. If it is still unresolved at day 90 it follows MRL-01 as an identified case, which has an owning domain. |
| MRL-11 [OD-7I-11] | **If it still fails:** a human holder of `recovery.case.disposition` may record `PERMANENTLY_REJECTED_WITH_REASON` only with proof of **permanent** invalidity. A failure of the current decoder alone is not proof. Proof is all of: (a) the failure is structural under 7G FC-01 or FC-02 (entry shape, `fmt`, unparseable `env`, duplicate keys, invalid envelope field); (b) an independent second validation path, not sharing the decoder's implementation, reaches the same verdict; (c) no validator-defect incident is open for that group (7G IMP-07); (d) the recorded proof category. FC-06 conditions (an unknown type or version that a deployment could cure) are never proof. |
| MRL-12 [OD-7I-11] | A legitimately rejected case's material is erased at the earlier of 7 days after resolution and the 90-day limit. |
| MRL-13 [OD-7I-11] | The day-83 run, a concurrent R2, a disposition and an erasure are serialized by the case row lock and compare-and-swap on state (7G RSM-02). Re-running the job is harmless: it appends an equal result. A revoked capability or erased material makes the disposition fail closed. |
| MRL-14 [OD-7I-12] | **Day 90, still failing, permanence unproven or undispositioned.** The material is erased (ERA-12). The case moves to `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` with `PRIVACY_MATERIAL_ERASED`. It is **not** rejected, not resolved and not closed by age. Its digest, consuming group, observations and history remain and it stays discoverable by authorized operators. |
| MRL-15 [OD-7I-12] | **Owner-window reconciliation.** The owning domain of the consuming group investigates the observation window (first to last observation of the case, 7G LC-2) using independently trustworthy evidence: producer state, the outbox where rows still exist, its own domain ledgers, and processing evidence. It states the window and the limits of its completeness. It does not infer an event identity from the untrusted bytes or the digest; it does not claim the unknown event was processed; it invents no event ID, organization, origin record or handler result. Obligations it discovers are processed through its own separately authorized reconciliation. |
| MRL-16 [OD-7I-12] | **Terminal resolution.** `OWNER_RECONCILED` is permitted for such a case only when that owning domain records durable evidence that the obligations of the window are reconciled or accounted for: the sources examined, the verification scope and any remaining uncertainty. A completed checklist or the fact of erasure is not evidence. Where the evidence is insufficient the metadata-only case remains `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` with no terminal deadline. |
| MRL-17 [OD-7I-12] | This needs a narrowly scoped controlled erratum to 7G §24.4 (ERR-7I-04): for a `CONSUMER_UNIDENTIFIED` class `I` case whose material was erased under the approved privacy rule, and only for that, `OWNER_RECONCILED` recorded by the consuming group's owning domain under `recovery.reconciliation.record` becomes a permitted resolution. It gives general operators nothing, does not bypass DAU-09, does not extend to other class `I` cases, and is enforced in the guarded ledger transition (7G MR-18). **Until that erratum is governed and the transition implemented, such cases stay open**; nothing here activates it (AB-7I-08). |

### 14.6 Class `I` resolution after this document

| Case | State of material | Permitted terminal resolution | By whom | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Class `I`, material present, still fails re-validation, permanence proven | Present | `PERMANENTLY_REJECTED_WITH_REASON` | Holder of `recovery.case.disposition`; plus the owning domain's acknowledgement where the identity is trusted and owed | [FROZEN] 7G DAU-03, DAU-09; MRL-11 |
| Class `I`, material present, now validates | Present | Any R2 result | R2 executor | [FROZEN] 7G §24.4 |
| Class `I` with a trusted identity, material erased | Erased | Owner reconciliation as an identified case | Owning domain | [FROZEN] 7G T-13, T-14 |
| `CONSUMER_UNIDENTIFIED`, material erased | Erased | `OWNER_RECONCILED`, evidence-bound; otherwise none | Consuming group's owning domain | [OD] OD-7I-12; ERR-7I-04; gated |
| Any class `I`, material erased | Erased | `PERMANENTLY_REJECTED_WITH_REASON` is **not** available (DAU-09 cannot run) | — | [FROZEN] |

### 14.7 Legal hold

Frozen sources define two hold signals: a data-subject request in `ON_HOLD` (6C §13.2) and a suppression with reason `LEGAL_HOLD` (4I §8.6), both checked before an erasure executes (4I §9.3). They are subject-level. No frozen source defines how a hold reaches copies in the event stores, so 7I defines that and nothing wider.

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| HLD-01 [FROZEN; OD-7I-24] | A request in `ON_HOLD` starts no erasure step, and an erasure step already registered for it does not erase. The status is not trusted by itself: it is written only by the guarded functions of §8.14, and it is paired, in the same transaction, with a `REQUEST` hold in the registry (DSH-06, DSH-08). The registry is what an erasure function reads (HLD-11). |
| HLD-02 [7I; OD-7I-24] | **Hold registry: the one authoritative effective hold state.** Two kinds of record, in one relation on which no login role has any privilege. **`PLATFORM`:** a hold that must preserve event-pipeline copies, recorded as (organization, scope, reason reference, placing identity, review date), where the scope is one or more of: `ROW` references (a store and a row identifier), `RESOURCE` references (a resource type and identifier) and subject fields (a contact identifier, a phone number, an email address), which the placement turns into a contact set and typed clear keys exactly as a request hold's are (HLD-12, HLD-23; OD-7I-29); placed and released under `retention.hold.manage` with a second approver, and audited. **`REQUEST`:** the hold of one data-subject request, recorded as (organization, request identifier, the request's subject fields); placed only by the request's hold function and released only by that request's reject function (DSH-06, DSH-07), each a tenant-authorized, proof-verified 6C action. The two kinds are separate rows with separate writers. No request transition can create, alter or release a `PLATFORM` hold, and no platform operation releases a `REQUEST` hold. The registry holds identifiers and each hold's subject fields only. **One attribution model serves both kinds** (HLD-11): the kinds differ in who may place and release them, and never in how a subject is matched to a row. |
| HLD-03 [7I; OD-7I-24] | Every erasure and content-bearing purge in this document, request-driven or time-based (lineage, cancellation, `FAILED` input, material cap, post-resolution, row purge, organization erasure), excludes rows to which the effective hold state of HLD-11 applies. The exclusion is evaluated **inside the erasure function, in the erasure's own transaction, after it has taken the hold gate of each affected organization in share mode** (HLD-10). A hold placed concurrently therefore either commits before the erasure reads and prevents it, or waits for the erasure to commit and finds the data already gone. There is no third order. |
| HLD-04 [7I] | **A hold introduced during an erasure.** Steps already completed are not reversed, and cannot be. Steps not yet started do not start. The request records which stores were erased before the hold. |
| HLD-05 [OD-7I-09] | **No unbounded retention through a hold, and no release by the passage of time.** A `PLATFORM` hold has a review date; an expired review date raises an alert and **the hold stays in force** until explicitly released or renewed, each of which is a dual-controlled, audited act. A `REQUEST` hold has no review date and never lapses: it ends only with its request's rejection (DSH-07), and its age is alerted. A hold never exists without a registry record, and "the case is still unresolved" is never a hold. |
| HLD-06 [7I] | A hold preserves data. It does not authorize access: material under hold stays encrypted and subject to §13.5. |
| HLD-07 [7I] | A hold conflicts with an erasure request only in the sense that one waits. Which prevails in law is not decided here (LR-03); the engineering rule is that a recorded hold pauses erasure and the conflict is visible on the request. |
| HLD-08 [7I] | **Holds and keys.** A hold on a record is a reference to the key version that wrapped it. A held record therefore blocks retirement of that version for as long as the hold lasts (KEY-19 b), whatever the standard retention of the record's kind. Releasing the hold does not by itself destroy anything. |
| HLD-09 [OD-7I-13] | **Holds are journaled.** A hold placement is appended to the journal before the registry row commits, and a release after it commits, so the safe direction on any crash or restore is preservation: a restored database receives every later hold before any later erasure is re-applied (JRN-10). This applies to both kinds: a `REQUEST` hold's placement is appended inside the hold function's transaction before it commits (DSH-06), and its release after the reject commits. If the journal cannot confirm the placement, the hold function fails and the request is not `ON_HOLD`; that is safe because no erasure can commit without the journal either (INV-23), and the tenant retries (FS-39). |
| HLD-10 [OD-7I-24, conditions 8, 9; OD-7I-26] | **The hold gate: one lock that every participant takes.** Each organization has one gate row in the registry's schema, created with the organization and backfilled by the migration. **Exclusive** (`FOR UPDATE`): placing a hold of either kind, releasing one, rejecting a held request, a contact merge through the superseding merge function (HLD-12), and recording a retention decision, an exception, a determination or an association release (HLD-18, HLD-21), or a coverage certification or its acceptance (HLD-24). **Share** (`FOR SHARE`): every erasure function, every content-bearing purge and the sealing function (SEAL-03), for each organization whose rows it will touch, in the transaction that erases, before it evaluates HLD-11. The gate is taken first, before any other row lock, in ascending organization identifier where a batch spans organizations, and it is held to commit. The erasure functions are guarded functions of the maintenance, restore and owning-context principals; the gate is taken inside them, so there is no writer that erases without it. In `READ COMMITTED` a statement that follows a lock wait sees every row committed before it began, so an erasure that waited for a placement reads the new hold. The gate is held only for the length of one short transaction; it serializes, and it is never a retention delay: nothing holds it across a wait for a person or another process. |
| HLD-11 [OD-7I-24, conditions 7, 10; OD-7I-26; OD-7I-27, conditions 3, 11, 12; OD-7I-29] | **Effective hold state.** A row is held when **any** of these is true, evaluated by one database function that the erasure functions call under the gate, after they have locked the row itself. (a) **Explicit reference:** an unreleased `PLATFORM` hold of its organization names the row itself by a `ROW` reference, or names by a `RESOURCE` reference a member of *Res(R)* as defined below, so that a hold on a deal reaches a note on that deal. (b) **Attributed rows:** the row is *subject-linked*, as defined below, to an unreleased hold of its organization that has subject scope. **The kind of the hold is not a term of the link:** a `PLATFORM` hold placed for a phone number, an email address or a contact is matched by the same traversal as a `REQUEST` hold, and was not before the seventh remediation (P1-7I-R20). (c) **Uncertain rows:** the row has no usable attribution reference, or some edge its evaluation needs cannot be verified (HLD-19, HLD-20), or its evaluation meets a legacy head and HLD-25 applies; and an unreleased hold of either kind that has subject scope or a `RESOURCE` reference exists in its organization; and no recorded determination says the row is unrelated to every such hold (HLD-18). A hold that carries `ROW` references only makes no row uncertain: a row either is the one named or is not. (d) For a request-driven step, the driving request is `ON_HOLD`, or another request whose subject shares a contact or a key with it is. (e) A request of that organization is `ON_HOLD` with no unreleased `REQUEST` hold naming it, which DSH-08 makes unreachable; if ever found, that request is treated as a hold whose scope the function computes at that moment from the request's own subject fields with the same resolver, and an integrity alarm is raised. **The subject link, exactly.** Every term is evaluated inside one organization: the organization is taken from the locked row and is part of every index key, so no step can cross tenants. Let *R* be the row's attribution reference (HLD-17). *Res(R)* is *R* and every resource reached from it by `PARENT` edges (a note on a deal reaches the deal). *Con(R)* is every contact named by a `CONTACT` edge of a member of *Res(R)*. *Id(c)* is *c* and every contact joined to it by `MERGED_INTO` edges, followed in both directions to a fixed point. A hold *H* has a contact set *H.C* and typed clear keys *H.K*. *D(v, k)* is the digest of key *k* under index key version *v* (HLD-20). *R* is linked to *H* when one of three paths exists. **(b1) Direct key:** for some *k* in *H.K*, some non-retired *v* and some *r* in *Res(R)*, *D(v, k)* equals a `KEY` edge of *r* written under *v*. **(b2) Contact:** for some *c* in *Con(R)*, *Id(c)* and *H.C* share a contact. **(b3) Contact identity key:** for some *c* in *Con(R)*, some *c′* in *Id(c)*, some *k* in *H.K* and some non-retired *v*, *D(v, k)* equals a `KEY` edge of the contact *c′* written under *v*. Edges are used whether current or ended. A path all of whose edges are current is a **current** path; any other is **historical**. A row with a current path to *H* is held by *H* without qualification. A row whose only paths to *H* are historical is held by *H* as well, unless a recorded association release for that row and that hold exists (HLD-21). **Reading discipline.** The function first locks, `FOR SHARE` and to commit, the index head of every member of *Res(R)* in (type, identifier) order and then of every contact of the closure in ascending identifier, repeating until the set stops growing; only then, in a later statement, does it read their edges. A writer that adds or ends an edge holds that head exclusively (HLD-16). An identity or association change therefore either committed before the read and is seen, or cannot commit until the erasure has. **A row attributed to a subject that no hold reaches by (b1) – (b3) is not held by (b), (c) or (e), whatever holds exist in its organization, and whatever their kind.** A subject-scoped platform hold is therefore never an organization-wide retention exemption: an unresolved identifier is a hold with an empty contact set and its keys, which reaches what carries those keys and nothing else. The one qualification is a `FROM_T0` organization, where a row that meets a legacy head is not thereby shown to belong to a different subject (HLD-25). The former clause that held every row of an organization while a hold was "unresolved" is withdrawn (P1-7I-R17): there is no unresolved state. The result is a union: a status and a registry row can each hold data alone, and neither can release what the other holds. **One result per row and per erasure transaction.** The function returns a single verdict, held or not held, with the list of holds that produce it, each with its kind and its basis: `ROW`, `RESOURCE`, path b1, b2 or b3 and whether current or historical, uncertain, or request status. The erasure acts on the verdict alone. A rejection, a release, a determination or an association release removes one entry from that list and never another, so a tenant's rejection of its request cannot take a row out of a platform hold, and the release of a platform hold cannot take it out of a request hold. Expiry of a review date is not a term of this function. Organization erasure is the one operation that any hold of the organization blocks entirely (OEA-06). |
| HLD-12 [OD-7I-26; OD-7I-24, conditions 9, 10; OD-7I-27, condition 11] | **A hold's subject scope is fixed when it commits. There is no resolution phase.** This rule is written for a request hold and governs the subject fields of a `PLATFORM` hold in the same words, with the differences HLD-23 lists. All contexts share one PostgreSQL database, so resolving a subject is a query in the hold's own transaction, not a call that can be unavailable. The hold function calls a CRM-owned resolver, a `SECURITY DEFINER` function that returns contact identifiers and nothing else, which returns for the request's organization: the contact named by `subject_contact_id` if that row exists; every contact whose `phone_e164` or `secondary_phone_e164` equals `subject_phone_e164`; every contact whose `primary_email_normalized` equals the normalized `subject_email`. A hold is never refused, never left pending and never reported as scoped when it is not: the scope **is** the contact set and the keys, and both are complete at commit by definition. **Merge.** The installed merge function is the body of `097_5D5`, which replaced `093_5D2`'s with a different marker payload and nothing else. It locks the two contact rows, smaller identifier first; re-points deals, tasks, notes and appointments to the survivor; leaves activities, lead-score records, consent, campaign, call and memory rows on the merged-away contact; gives the survivor the other contact's secondary phone and email only where its own are empty; and leaves the merged-away row with its own identifiers and an immutable `merged_into_contact_id`. A hold therefore cannot rely on the survivor carrying the held key, or on the child rows having moved. It relies on the merge link: the two contacts are one identity for HLD-11, whichever of them the hold names and wherever a row is attached. The superseding function (by `CREATE OR REPLACE`, the `097_5D5` precedent) is that body unchanged, preceded by one statement that takes the hold gate exclusively, so its order is gate, then the contact rows in the frozen order; it also adds the survivor to the contact set of any hold that names the merged-away contact, as a recorded fact on the hold. **The proof does not depend on that addition, nor on the function being the path taken:** a merge recorded by a direct update of `merged_into_contact_id`, which the frozen grants permit once per contact, writes the same link through the contact trigger and is followed in the same way. Nothing ever removes a contact or a key from a hold. **Tenant isolation:** the resolver takes the organization from the locked request row and matches contacts of that organization only; a key equal to another organization's contact matches nothing, and the index is keyed by organization throughout. **Changed identifiers and aliases:** a contact stays in the set after its phone number or email changes, and the hold's original keys stay in force, so both the old and the new identity of a held contact are covered; a secondary phone number is a key like the primary. A contact that acquires a held key after placement is reached through its identity-key edge from the commit of that change, and stays reached after it gives the key up, because the ended edge still links (HLD-16, HLD-21). The erasure placeholder `+99000000000`, `[erased]` and a null value are never keys. **Coverage evidence:** the hold records, with its scope, the verified state of the subject index for every inventoried relation at that moment (HLD-19); a hold is committed only when all of them are verified. |
| HLD-13 [OD-7I-24, condition 10; OD-7I-26] | **Request scope versus subject scope.** A `REQUEST` hold pauses erasure of its subject's data, not only the steps of its own request: a second erasure request for the same subject does not erase while the first is held (HLD-11 d). It does not pause another subject's requests, and it does not pause time-based cleanup of rows attributed to other subjects, at any time, including the moment it is placed. A hold preserves; it grants no access (HLD-06), creates no retention entitlement beyond itself, and decides nothing about which right prevails in law (HLD-07; LR-03). A `PLATFORM` hold with subject scope has the same reach by the same paths and the same limit: its subject's rows, the rows that cannot be shown not to be its subject's, and nothing else of the organization (HLD-23). |
| HLD-14 [7I] | **Owner-context erasure is bound to the same rule.** The erasure of a subject's rows in the owning contexts (contacts, calls, recordings, documents and the rest) is outside this document's design, but it is the same erasure for the purpose of a hold. Every owner-context erasure function, existing or future, must take the gate in share mode and call the effective-hold function of HLD-11 in its transaction, and must be registered as an erasure step (ERA-05; IR-24). The frozen functions `knowledge.fn_docver_gdpr_erase` and `knowledge.fn_document_gdpr_delete` (`081_5F4`) exist today, are executable by `app_api`, `app_worker` and `app_platform_admin`, and contain no hold check; they are superseded with that check, and the administrator's grant on them is withdrawn, by IR-49. Until every such function is bound, no data-subject erasure is executed in any context (AB-7I-14). |
| HLD-15 [7I; OD-7I-27, condition 13] | **Lock order.** Hold gate (share or exclusive) → the request row, for the 6C functions → the row being erased or sealed, in the 7H order organization → lineage anchor → delivery → endpoint, or the case row lock for material → the index heads the effective-hold function reads: resource heads by (type, identifier), then contact heads by ascending identifier (HLD-11). Placement, release, rejection and decisions hold the gate, the request row and registry rows only, and no delivery, case, organization or contact row, so they cannot be part of a cycle with an erasure. Two placements for one organization serialize on the gate. The superseding merge takes the gate exclusively and then the contact rows in the frozen order, so a merge and an erasure of one organization never overlap. **What is not ordered, and does not need to be for safety:** a tenant-path transaction takes no gate and locks a head only inside the trigger of the row it writes. One that writes two indexed rows can meet an erasure in the opposite head order; PostgreSQL then aborts one of the two. An aborted erasure has erased nothing and is retried (ERA-05); an aborted tenant write returns the existing retryable error. No such interleaving erases a held row, because the result of the effective-hold function is used only by a transaction that still holds every head it read. Determinism is claimed for the gate participants, not for every tenant write. |
| HLD-16 [OD-7I-26, §1; OD-7I-27, conditions 1, 12, 13] | **The subject index.** A standing structure, with no privilege for any login role, read only through the effective-hold function and the resolver. **Heads.** One row per (organization, resource type, resource identifier), where a contact is itself a resource of type `CONTACT`. A head carries no data; it is the lock point for that resource's edges. **Edges**, each keyed by (organization, source head, kind, target): `CONTACT` (the source belongs to that contact identifier); `KEY` (the source carries that subject key: its kind, `PHONE` or `EMAIL`, the digest, the index key version and the normalization version, never the clear value; HLD-20); `PARENT` (the source belongs to another resource, whose edges it inherits); `MERGED_INTO` (source contact, target contact). **An edge is never deleted and never rewritten.** It is created *current*. When the row no longer carries that reference or value the edge is *ended*, once and one-way: the end time and the transition's provenance are written to it (the transaction, the session principal, the relation and statement kind, whether the merge function was the caller, and the edge that replaced it), and a trigger on the index rejects every other change. An ended edge is the immutable evidence of the association: original contact, replacement contact, authoritative transition and transaction. It still links (HLD-11), which is why editing a reference or an identifier takes nothing out of a hold. **Writers.** Only row-level triggers, owned by the migration role, on the relations of a governed inventory, **in the transaction that writes the row**. A trigger takes the organization from the row itself, never from a session setting; locks the head, creating it if absent; and adds or ends edges with idempotent inserts, so a retried or replayed write adds nothing twice. A trigger is a property of the relation, not of a code path: an import, an ingestion, a replay, a merge, a background task and a direct statement all pass through it, and a failure of the trigger fails the write, so no unindexed resource can be created. **The inventory starts from the SQL as read** and is completed and classified under IR-50: `crm.contacts` (`020_5D`, `093_5D2`), with `KEY` edges for `phone_e164`, `secondary_phone_e164` and `primary_email_normalized`, and `MERGED_INTO` when `merged_into_contact_id` is set; deals, appointments, lead-score records, consent records and suppressions (`021_5D`, `023_5D`, `024_5D`), with `CONTACT`, and `KEY` for a suppression's own number; **tasks, notes and activities (`022_5D`), which the fifth remediation's list omitted**, with `CONTACT` where `subject_type` is `CONTACT`, `PARENT` to the deal where it is `DEAL`, and nothing where it is `COMPANY`; call sessions and conversations (`011_5C`, `012_5C`), with `CONTACT` from `contact_ref` and `KEY` for the two numbers; campaign contacts and their identities (`030_5E`, `098_5E1`), with `CONTACT` and `KEY`; memories (`045_5G`), with `CONTACT`. A row with a null organization (a platform or regulatory suppression) belongs to no tenant and is not indexed. A resource whose content lives in object storage is attributed through the row that holds its storage reference, and its objects follow that row. The mapping to the aggregate types of 7B is an IR-50 deliverable. **Never a key:** the erasure placeholder `+99000000000`, `[erased]`, `[ERASED]` and null. Indexing them would join every erased contact into one identity. **Index writes take no gate.** Their ordering against an evaluation comes from the head lock (HLD-11), and against a merge from the merge's gate (HLD-12). The index is class `PID`. Entries are removed under RET-28 only. Reads by the two functions are not audited individually; every decision taken on it is (HLD-18, HLD-21). |
| HLD-17 [OD-7I-26; OD-7I-27] | **Attribution reference on every content-bearing row.** So that a row can be looked up in the index when its turn to be erased comes, possibly long after the event's outbox row is gone, each row carries from creation the validated envelope's aggregate reference: outbox rows already do (`aggregate_type`, `aggregate_id`, `077_5J1`); delivery rows and lineage anchors record it at fan-out; recovery cases record it under IR-24, and material is attributed through its case. A callback processing input is encrypted and its receipt row carries no resource reference (`062_5I`); the processing workload, which decrypts it at the first attempt, records in that attempt's transaction the platform resource the input names, or the index keys of the two numbers of a provider-originated call (CBI-02), **whether or not processing then succeeds**. A row whose reference is absent, whose aggregate type is unknown, or whose reference finds no index entry is **unattributed**. An aggregate type that the inventory marks as not contact-linked (an organization, a plan, an invoice) is attributed to no contact and is not held through the subject scope of any hold (a `ROW` or `RESOURCE` reference of a `PLATFORM` hold can still name it): the frozen request subject is a contact or contact details (5B ADR-5B-007). Unattributed is a fail-safe default, not a convenience: it is what a row is until evidence says otherwise. A row attributed through an edge that has since ended is **attributed**, not unattributed: its historical links are evaluated by HLD-11 and reviewed by HLD-21. Number keys recorded for a callback carry the index key version they were digested under (HLD-20). |
| HLD-18 [OD-7I-26, §4; OD-7I-27; OD-7I-28] | **Uncertain material and the decision procedure.** *Uncertain* rows are those of HLD-11 (c): unparseable replay material (CLS-04), an input that failed before any reference was recorded, a row whose aggregate type the inventory does not classify, a row whose evaluation meets an unverified relation or an unusable key version; those held by a hold only through a historical path (HLD-21); and, in a `FROM_T0` organization, those that meet a legacy head and that no path links to the hold assessed (HLD-25). They cannot be shown not to be a held subject's, so they are never classified as unrelated by default, and while a hold they are assessed against exists, of either kind, no clock and no request-driven step erases them. **The retention deadline of each row stays the one approved for its kind; nothing in this rule moves it.** **A decision record opens before the deadline**, not at it: the retention pass opens one, per row, as soon as it finds an uncertain row in an organization with an unreleased hold that can make it uncertain (HLD-11 c), whatever time the row has left (for a 7-day input, its first day). The record names the row, its store and owning context, its deadline, why it is uncertain, the holds assessed, the approvals a decision needs and an operational owner. **Its status says which of six things is true, and they are never merged.** `PENDING_INVESTIGATION`: the deadline has not passed; the row is inside its approved retention and nothing is exceptional. `HOLD_APPLIES`: two reviewers recorded, with evidence, that the row is a named hold's subject's data; it is retained **because an established hold requires it**, as that hold's row, until the hold ends. `EXCEPTION_AUTHORIZED`: an approved, time-limited retention exception is in force (below). `ERASURE_DETERMINED`: two reviewers recorded that the row is unrelated to every hold assessed; it is erased at once by its ordinary journaled function. `CLOSED_NO_HOLD`: every hold it was assessed against has ended; it is erased by its clock, which has already run. `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED`: the deadline has passed and none of the above is true. **That last status is not an authorization of any kind** (HLD-22). A row whose retention is governed by another, independent obligation is in none of these: a delivery still owed keeps its body under ERA-11, and a row named by a `PLATFORM` hold is held by HLD-11 (a); neither is described as an exception. **Who decides.** Every decision is taken by two different humans holding `retention.hold.manage`, a requester and an approver, each bound by an operator action proof as in OEA-04, in a function that takes the gate exclusively and writes its audit row in the same transaction. One person, the same person twice, a forged proof and any login role are refused. **Lawful erasure may be determined only on evidence**: an attribution that the day-83 re-validation produced (MRL-09) and that maps the row to a subject no hold reaches, or a dual-controlled inspection of the content (SEAL-08; §13.5). It is refused for a row that a current path links to a hold: a determination cannot waive a hold; it can only record that a hold does not reach this row. A determination is per hold; a hold placed later reopens the question for rows still present. **An exception** is its own record and is not a `PLATFORM` hold: one row, a purpose from a closed list, a reason reference, an evidence reference and an **expiry** ([REC] at most 30 days). At the expiry it stops being an authorization, by the clock and whether or not any job runs: the status the function reports is computed from the record and the time. It is never renewed automatically, and no scheduler creates one. A further exception for the same row is a new dual-controlled act. It is refused if its evidence reference equals that of any earlier exception for the row; refused beyond a cumulative [REC] 90 days without the recorded approval of the named privacy owner as a third proof; and **refused for everyone beyond a cumulative cap** ([REC] 180 days). Past the cap the only decisions left are that the hold applies or that the row is lawfully erased: continued retention can no longer be given the appearance of approval. A `PLATFORM` hold is not a substitute: its function refuses a reason that cites a retention-decision record, because a platform hold records a preservation duty that exists independently of this uncertainty (HLD-02). **If nobody decides**, HLD-22 applies. A row whose non-involvement is established by its attribution is never in this procedure and keeps its normal schedule. |
| HLD-19 [OD-7I-26, §1 condition 8; §2 conditions 7, 8] | **An index that is incomplete or unavailable is never read as "no match".** Each inventoried relation has a verification state in the database, per organization where the backfill is organization-scoped: `VERIFIED` once the backfill and the completeness assertion have passed, and `UNVERIFIED` from the moment a periodic completeness check, a failed trigger installation, a restore, or a newly inventoried relation says otherwise. While any relation is `UNVERIFIED` for an organization: (a) **hold placement fails**, for a request hold and for the subject scope or a `RESOURCE` reference of a platform hold alike; a platform hold that carries `ROW` references only reads no index and is placed regardless. The hold function raises before it changes anything; the request is not `ON_HOLD`, no registry row exists, and the route answers with the existing server-error class of the frozen envelope, which is retryable. No success is returned for a hold whose coverage is not established, and no new state or error code is introduced (the STP-14 treatment of an internal failure). (b) **Erasure that depends on that part of the index is refused in the same period**, whether or not any hold exists: a row whose attribution falls in an `UNVERIFIED` relation is treated as unattributed and, in addition, is not erased even when the organization has no hold, because a tenant may be trying to place one and failing. Rows attributed through `VERIFIED` relations are unaffected and keep their schedules. A row that reaches its limit in this period opens a decision record like any other (HLD-18), with reason `INDEX_UNVERIFIED`. This is a platform fault state, alerted as an incident from its first moment; it is not a mechanism for resolving any hold, and no hold ever puts an organization into it. **What coverage means after OD-7I-27.** The completeness assertion covers heads, current edges of every kind, and merge links, which are re-derivable in full from `merged_into_contact_id`. Ended edges are not re-derivable from source rows: they exist only in the index, are backed up and restored with the database, and are never removed by a rebuild. **Stated limit:** identity history from before the index was backfilled, an earlier number of a contact or an earlier contact of a resource, is not known to the index and is not claimed; merge lineage is the exception. What that limit means for readiness, and how a row that depends on it is classified, are HLD-24 and HLD-25 (OD-7I-31): the limit is recorded per organization, and a missing edge from before it is never read as "no earlier history". An index key version that cannot be read is treated like an unverified relation for every row whose evaluation meets an edge of that version (HLD-20). |
| HLD-20 [7I; OD-7I-27, condition 12] | **Index key versions: a rotation never unlinks a subject.** **Semantics.** A subject key is a pair (kind, value). Normalization *N* is one database function per kind, used by the triggers, the resolver and the hold function alike. `PHONE` is the E.164 string that the frozen checks already require of a stored number. `EMAIL` is the normalization that produces `primary_email_normalized`; its single definition, and its equality with the application's, are an IR-50 deliverable and a tested gate. *N* is total: a value that is not canonical is compared as its exact bytes, and can then equal no canonical stored value. The digest is *D(v, k)* = HMAC-SHA-256 under index key version *v* over (organization, kind, normalization version, *N*(value)). Two digests are compared only when version, kind and normalization version are equal, and then by bytes. **Versions** live in the protected key relation of STP-10, each `WRITE` (exactly one), `VERIFY` or `RETIRED`. **A hold is version-independent:** it stores its keys in clear (HLD-12), and the effective-hold function digests each under every `WRITE` and `VERIFY` version when it evaluates. Nothing on a hold is migrated at a rotation; a hold placed before a rotation matches edges written after it, and the reverse. **Rotation** is one transaction of a guarded function of the maintenance principal under a governed change: the new version becomes `WRITE` and the old `VERIFY`. **Concurrent writes** need no dual-writing: a trigger that read the old version and commits after the rotation leaves an edge under a `VERIFY` version, which is compared like any other. **Re-derivation** is optional and add-only: the rebuild function writes new-version `KEY` edges for the values rows carry now; an old edge may be removed only in a transaction that has computed both digests from the same clear value and found the new edge present. Ended edges, and edges that outlive their row, cannot be re-derived, because the clear value is gone; they stay under their version. **Retirement** of a version requires that no edge under it exists in the database and that no restorable backup contains one, established by the reference count of KEY-19 and decided under dual control with a journaled record. Until then it stays `VERIFY`, however old; a version can stay in use for as long as a contact with an ended identifier exists. That is the cost of never unlinking, and it is stated. **Unavailable key.** If the `WRITE` version cannot be read, a trigger that must write a `KEY` edge raises and the row write fails; the relation is `UNVERIFIED` and hold placement fails closed (HLD-19 a). If a `VERIFY` version cannot be read, every row whose evaluation meets an edge of that version is uncertain (HLD-11 c), is not erased, and opens a decision record with reason `INDEX_KEY_UNAVAILABLE`. A missing key is never read as "no match". **Compromised key.** The version is marked, a rotation is made at once and re-derivation is run. The old version stays `VERIFY`: matching is not weakened by disclosure, because no login role can write the index. What is lost is the secrecy of the digests under that version against someone who can also read the index or a backup, and that exposure lasts until its edges age out. It is an incident and is not described as closed by the rotation. **Restore.** The key relation and the index are in one database and return to the same point together, so they stay mutually consistent; holds are re-applied from the journal with their clear keys and match whatever versions the restored index holds. **Erasure.** When a subject's rows are erased their edges go under RET-28, and with the last edge goes the reference that pins a version. A change of normalization function is handled as a rotation: a new normalization version, both compared, the old retired on the same rule. |
| HLD-21 [OD-7I-27] | **Historical associations: held by default, released only on evidence.** A re-pointed resource, a contact whose identifier changed and a recycled number each leave an ended edge (HLD-16). **(1) Not discarded.** The ended edge still links, so a re-pointing by a tenant-path credential, an identifier edit and a merge take nothing out of a hold, whether the hold was placed before the change or is placed after it (conditions 3, 11). **(2) Not permanent proof.** A changed `contact_id` shows neither that the former subject's information is still in the resource nor that it has gone (condition 7). A row that a hold reaches only through historical paths is therefore *uncertain* for that hold: it is held, and it enters the decision procedure of HLD-18 with reason `HISTORICAL_ASSOCIATION`, its record naming the hold and each edge of the path with its provenance. The question put at the deadline is whether the resource still contains the held subject's information (condition 4). **(3) Three outcomes.** *It still does:* `HOLD_APPLIES`; the hold is preserved for the row (condition 8). *It is proven unrelated:* an **association release**, recorded by two different holders of `retention.hold.manage` (condition 5) in a guarded function under the exclusive gate, citing all four kinds of evidence: the verified content of the resource, by dual-controlled inspection; the lawful purpose of the retention; the historical identity evidence, that is the ended edges and their provenance; and the current authoritative associations (condition 6). The function refuses a release whose only evidence is the edge change, and refuses any release while a **current** path links the row to that hold. A release is a record beside the edges, for one row and one hold; the edges are untouched. The row then follows its normal schedule, subject to every other hold, each assessed separately (condition 9). A hold placed later is assessed afresh: an earlier release does not bind it. *It is uncertain, or nobody decides:* the row is never assumed unrelated; at the deadline HLD-22 applies (condition 10). **(4) Unification is not reassignment.** When the merge function re-points a deal from the merged-away contact to the survivor, the old edge is ended and the new one is current, and the two contacts are one identity by their `MERGED_INTO` link. The path through the survivor is current, so the row is plainly held and no review opens. A re-pointing between contacts that no merge link joins is a reassignment and is reviewed. The index does not have to be told which is which. **(5) Scope.** This rule applies to a hold of either kind that has subject scope (OD-7I-29, condition 5). It decides hold applicability for content-bearing event-store rows and binds every owner-context erasure function through HLD-14. It adds no route, no request state and no CRM behaviour (condition 14). |
| HLD-22 [OD-7I-28] | **Past the limit with no valid decision: preserved, sealed, declared.** When an uncertain row's deadline passes and its record is neither `HOLD_APPLIES` nor an unexpired `EXCEPTION_AUTHORIZED`, or when an exception expires, the row is not erased and no hold is released. It is sealed (§14.7a) and its record is `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED`. **Nothing authorizes that retention.** It is not a legal hold, not an extension of the retention period and not evidence of compliance. A named owner, an alert, an open task and an incident ticket are accountability; they are not authority. It is an **unauthorized-retention incident**, dated from the instant the authorization ran out, and it lasts until two authorized people decide or every hold assessed ends. **This design does not bound that time and does not claim to.** Software cannot compel a human decision, and the owner has accepted the residual rather than have possibly held evidence destroyed automatically (OD-7I-28; RR-10). |
| HLD-23 [OD-7I-29] | **A `PLATFORM` hold with subject scope: same attribution, separate authority.** **Placement.** The platform hold function, callable by the tooling principal, verifies two operator action proofs of two different holders of `retention.hold.manage` (OEA-04), takes the organization's gate exclusively, and, when the scope carries subject fields, calls the CRM resolver of HLD-12 in that transaction for the named organization. It stores the contact set and the typed clear keys, normalized by the function of HLD-20, with the coverage evidence of HLD-19 and HLD-24, the journal record of HLD-09 and the audit row, and commits. An identifier that matches nothing gives an empty contact set and its keys. That is a valid hold, complete at commit, and it reaches a contact created, edited or merged later through paths b1 and b3 exactly as a request hold does. `ROW` and `RESOURCE` references are stored as given, after a check that each names a row or a resource type of that organization; a reference to a contact is stored as a contact identifier in the subject scope, so that merged identity applies to it. **What is the same as for a request hold:** the traversal of HLD-11 (direct key, contact, merged identity in both directions, identity key, parent resource, current and ended edges, every non-retired index key version); the head-locking discipline; the uncertainty rule of HLD-11 (c) and the decision procedure of HLD-18; the historical-association review of HLD-21; sealing under HLD-22; the placeholder exclusion; the organization as part of every key, so that the same phone number in another organization matches nothing. **What is different.** (1) *Authority:* placed, renewed and released only by its own functions under two operator proofs. The request functions of §8.14 cannot name it, and no tenant action, request transition or elapsed time changes it. (2) *Scope is immutable:* nothing is added to or removed from a platform hold after it commits. A wider preservation duty is a further hold, placed under its own dual control. The merge function writes its survivor annotation beside the hold as an add-only fact, as it does for a request hold; the annotation is not read by HLD-11, which follows the `MERGED_INTO` edge whether or not the annotation exists. (3) *Release:* dual-controlled, audited and journaled after it commits (HLD-05, HLD-09). It releases that hold only. A row it alone held then follows its own clock; if that clock has already run, the next pass erases it through its ordinary journaled function, or by disposition if it is sealed (SEAL-10 iii). (4) *Determinations and association releases against it* are taken by two different holders of `retention.hold.manage`, as for any hold: for a platform hold that is the same authority that could release the whole hold, exercised for one row, on the evidence HLD-18 and HLD-21 require, and never while a current path links the row to it. (5) *A request hold stays the tenant's.* No platform function releases, narrows or rejects a `REQUEST` hold. A determination that a row is unrelated to a request hold is the item-level decision OD-7I-26 approved; it is dual-controlled and writes a tenant-scoped audit row (§19.4), so it is never silent. **What cannot bypass it.** A contact created after placement, an identifier edit, a re-pointing and a merge each write or end an index edge in their own transaction under the head lock, and the erasure reads under that lock (HLD-11, HLD-16), so the order argument of §28.9 holds for a platform hold word for word. An index-key rotation changes nothing on the hold, which keeps its keys in clear (HLD-20). A restore re-applies the hold from the journal with its scope, and the reconciler re-runs the resolver against the restored data and takes the union, before any erasure record is re-applied (JRN-10; VT-136). **No route.** Platform holds are placed through the internal tooling under `retention.hold.manage` as before; no public legal-hold or data-subject route, state or error is added or changed. |
| HLD-24 [OD-7I-31] | **Coverage certification: what the index may be relied on for.** An index head for every current row proves that current state is indexed. It proves nothing about what a row carried, or belonged to, before the index existed. Each organization therefore has one certification record, in a protected relation with no login-role privilege, written under the exclusive gate and journaled, in exactly one of three states. **`NOT_CERTIFIED`:** the default for an organization that existed before the index migration. The organization is treated as `UNVERIFIED` in every relation (HLD-19): placement of a hold with subject scope or a `RESOURCE` reference fails closed, and no erasure or content-bearing purge that depends on the index runs. **`FROM_ORIGIN`:** every inventoried relation carried its index trigger, in this database, before the organization's first row in that relation. It is established by construction and by evidence, never by assertion: the organization row was inserted by a transaction that began after the index migration committed; the certification row is written by a trigger in that same creating transaction, as the gate row is (HLD-10); and it records the inventory version in force. **`FROM_T0`:** the organization held rows in at least one inventoried relation before that relation's trigger was installed. The record carries T0, the commit time on the database clock of the transaction that installed the last such trigger for that organization, and the boundary of each relation. It is immutable. **What the backfill writes, and what it does not.** For a `FROM_T0` organization it writes heads, the edges that current rows carry, and merge lineage in full from `merged_into_contact_id`, which is immutable once set (`093_5D2`). It writes no ended edge, no earlier phone number or email, no earlier contact of a resource and no merge that the rows do not record: none is known, and none is inferred or invented. **Authoritative history sources, as read.** Merge lineage: yes. Anything else: no. `crm.contacts` has no version column and no history relation (`020_5D`). `updated_at` equal to `created_at` is not evidence that a row never changed: the table-level `UPDATE` of `020_5D` L76 covers `created_at`, so a tenant-path credential can make them equal. Audit rows are not contracted to carry identifier values (RED-10; a 4,096-byte snapshot, `072_5J`). The activity types of `022_5D` record no identifier change. A backup holds earlier states at isolated instants and is not mined for history: doing so would restore personal data outside quarantine (INV-18). **Legacy flags.** At certification each head that existed at T0 in a relation whose identifier or reference columns are updatable under the frozen grants receives an immutable flag: `KEY_HISTORY_UNKNOWN` on a contact (`phone_e164`, `secondary_phone_e164`, `primary_email_normalized`), `ASSOCIATION_HISTORY_UNKNOWN` on a resource whose contact or parent reference is updatable (deals, tasks, notes, appointments, campaign contacts; the list is completed by the IR-50 inventory, and a relation it has not classified is flagged). A flag never clears. A head created after T0 never has one. **Conditions under which the index is certified for an organization.** All of: (1) a trigger on every relation of the recorded inventory version; (2) the backfill complete and the completeness assertion of HLD-19 passing for every relation; (3) an index key in `WRITE` and the normalization equivalence of HLD-20 proven; (4) every content-bearing event-store row of the organization carries an attribution reference, or is counted as unattributed (HLD-17), in which case it is uncertain and never treated as unrelated; (5) for `FROM_T0`, the legacy flags written and the classification rule of HLD-25 implemented and tested; (6) for `FROM_T0`, an **acceptance record**. **The acceptance** is for one organization. It is recorded by two different holders of `retention.hold.manage`, one of them the named privacy and security owner, each with an operator action proof, and it states T0, the relations concerned and the limit accepted, in the words of RR-11. It is a precondition of the certification state and nothing else: HLD-11, the decision functions, the deadline function and the guard of §14.7b never read it, so it cannot override a hold, a statutory duty or a retention limit, and it is never an exception under HLD-18. **Transitions.** `NOT_CERTIFIED → FROM_T0`; `FROM_ORIGIN → FROM_T0`, a demotion, which happens when a relation is added to the inventory after the organization already had rows in it, or when a rebuild had to re-derive an index whose ended edges were lost (a rebuild cannot restore them; HLD-19), with T0 set to that event; and any state `→ NOT_CERTIFIED` on a failed assertion. A trigger on the relation refuses every other change. **`FROM_T0 → FROM_ORIGIN` is not expressible**, by anyone, at any later time, however many rows have aged out. **The index-first gate (AB-7I-16).** In production the index migration is applied before an organization can write an inventoried relation, so that an organization is born `FROM_ORIGIN` and RR-11 does not arise for it. Whether any deployed database already holds tenant data is not known to this document and is not assumed: the certification is decided per organization from the evidence above. A restore returns certification, flags and index to one point together; the reconciler re-applies later certification records from the journal before any hold or erasure record. |
| HLD-25 [OD-7I-31] | **Legacy rows: a missing historical edge is not evidence of no history.** In a `FROM_T0` organization the effective-hold function evaluates a row as HLD-11 says, and then, for each unreleased hold *H* that no path links the row to, applies this rule. The row is **uncertain for *H***, with reason `LEGACY_HISTORY_UNKNOWN`, when either is true. (i) *Unknown earlier keys:* *H* has at least one key, and the row's closure, *Con(R)* extended by merged identity, contains a contact head flagged `KEY_HISTORY_UNKNOWN`. That contact may have carried the held number or address before T0, and nothing records whether it did. (ii) *Unknown earlier association:* *H* has subject scope or a `RESOURCE` reference, and *Res(R)* contains a head flagged `ASSOCIATION_HISTORY_UNKNOWN`. That resource may have belonged to a held contact, or to a held parent, before T0. **Not uncertain by this rule:** a row whose closure contains no flagged head, which is every row that reaches only contacts and resources created after T0; any row, for a hold with `ROW` references only; a row that a path does link to *H*, which is simply held, by a current or a historical path as usual. **What follows is the approved procedure, unchanged:** the row is not erased by any clock or step while *H* is unreleased; a decision record opens before its deadline (HLD-18) naming the flagged heads and T0; at the deadline two reviewers record that the hold applies, or release the row for that hold on the four kinds of evidence of HLD-21, or authorize a time-limited exception; if nobody decides it is sealed and is an unauthorized-retention incident (HLD-22). **"The index shows no edge" is refused as the evidence for a determination or a release**, exactly as an edge change alone is refused (HLD-21), because the absence is the thing that is unknown. **The cost, stated plainly.** In a `FROM_T0` organization, while a hold with a key is unreleased, every content-bearing row that reaches any contact that existed at T0 waits for an item-level decision. That can be most of the organization's contact-linked rows. It is not the organization-wide pause that OD-7I-26 removed: each row has a recorded reason, a deadline, a decision record and an exit, rows of contacts created after T0 are unaffected, and no state is waiting to be "resolved". It is nevertheless wide, it loads the decision queue, and where nobody decides it becomes RR-10. The owner chose it over treating missing history as none (OD-7I-31), and it is the reason for the index-first gate. It is recorded as CNF-7I-30 and RR-11, not as closed. **Owner contexts** are bound through HLD-14: an owner-context erasure function calls the same effective-hold function and receives the same verdict. |

### 14.7a Sealed overdue retention (OD-7I-28; P1-7I-R19)

Nothing in this section exists. It is a requirement on a future governed migration and on the decrypting and tooling services (IR-51), with a controlled erratum to record shapes of 7G, 7H and 6J (ERR-7I-25). Sealing changes where content is and who can reach it. It changes no obligation, resolves nothing and authorizes nothing. Since the seventh remediation sealing is the second of two layers.
