The first is the content access guard of §14.7b, which denies ordinary access from the deadline itself and does not depend on any pass having run (P1-7I-R21; OD-7I-30).

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| SEAL-01 [OD-7I-28, conditions 1, 2, 15] | **Sealing is by absence, not by a flag.** In one transaction the content of the row leaves its store: a delivery's body and preview (`payload_json` and `last_response_body_preview` become SQL null); replay-material ciphertext and its wrapped key; callback processing-input ciphertext and its wrapped key; a PII-bearing outbox payload, replaced as ERA-07 replaces it with the digest kept. It is written, encrypted under a data key wrapped by a KEK of purpose `SEALED_CONTENT`, to a **sealed vault** relation on which no login role has any privilege. A seal record (organization, store, row, deadline, decision record, time) is written beside it. Every ordinary reader then finds no content, because there is none in the place it reads: the tenant's delivery read, the dispatcher's fenced load, the replay function, the replay executor, the material view, the callback processor, an export, a diagnostic query, and a direct `SELECT` under any role. No reader has to remember to check a flag. **That is true only once the pass has run.** Before it, the content is still in its store, and what denies it is the guard of CAG-01 and the privileges of CAG-06, not absence. |
| SEAL-02 [condition 19] | **No obligation and no state is resolved.** A delivery row keeps its terminal status; its `body_state` is `SEALED` (PBR-10), never `ERASED`. A recovery case keeps its state, its history and its obligation: sealing never produces `RESOLVED`, `PERMANENTLY_REJECTED_WITH_REASON`, `OWNER_RECONCILED`, `NOT_OWED` or any other resolution (ERA-03; 7G RPM-12). A resolution that does not read the material, such as the owning domain's reconciliation, stays available on its own frozen terms. The erasure step or batch records the row as `SEALED_UNDECIDED`, never as erased, and is never `VERIFIED` (ERA-05). How a sealed case's material is shown in the frozen 7G material record is ERR-7I-25 and is decided here only this far: bytes absent, seal reference present, and no existing state value reused to mean it. |
| SEAL-03 [conditions 1, 18] | **The sealing function** is a guarded function of the maintenance principal, run by the retention pass that would otherwise have erased the row. Its transaction: the seal's intent already durable in the journal (SEAL-07) → the gate, in share mode → the row lock → HLD-11 and the decision record re-evaluated under those locks (a row that nothing holds any longer, or that is determined unrelated, is erased; a row kept by a proven hold or by an unexpired exception is sealed with that basis and no incident, SEAL-14; a row whose deadline has moved because an operation now references it is left) → vault insert → content removal → seal record → decision status → incident record → audit row. All of it commits or none. Repeating it for a sealed row changes nothing and reports that. A kill at any statement leaves the row unsealed with its intent pending, and the next pass seals it. **Stated, and corrected (P1-7I-R21):** sealing happens at the first pass after the deadline, as erasure would have. If the pass is not running, the content stays physically in its store past the deadline. The sixth remediation left it readable there by every ordinary path. It no longer is: from the deadline, on the database clock, no function returns it and no login role can select it (CAG-01, CAG-06), whether or not the pass, the journal or the vault is available. The incident is still dated from the deadline (SEAL-04). **The pass and the guard use one deadline function and one clock** (CAG-02, CAG-03, CAG-11): the pass acts on a row only when the clock has reached its deadline, and the guard returns content only while it has not. |
| SEAL-04 [conditions 6, 7] | **The incident record** is insert-only and is written in the sealing transaction: the row, its store and owning context; the original deadline; **the occurrence time, which is the deadline itself or the expiry of the last exception, never the time of detection or of sealing**; the reason for the uncertainty; the holds assessed; the approvals a decision needs; the operational owner. Escalations are appended to it. Its interval ends only with a disposition and is never shortened, rewritten or backdated: an exception authorized later starts when it is authorized and leaves the unauthorized interval before it on the record. |
| SEAL-05 [conditions 8, 9, 20] | **Escalation is mandatory, and it is not a resolution.** At occurrence the privacy and security owner is notified and the formal incident workflow is entered (LR-09, LR-10). While the incident is open it is escalated again at intervals ([REC] 7, 30 and 90 days, then every 90) to named roles of increasing seniority, each escalation appended with its recipient. Acknowledging an alert, closing a ticket or assigning an owner changes no status: the record stays `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED` until a decision function, or the end of the holds, changes it. Open incidents are counted, with their ages, in a periodic compliance record. No resolution time is promised. Whether the incident must be notified to anyone, and when, is a legal question that recording it does not answer. |
| SEAL-06 [conditions 2, 3] | **No re-entry.** With the content absent: the public replay route refuses with the existing `422 WEBHOOK_REPLAY_NOT_ALLOWED` (PBR-07, PBR-10); a sealed case is not an R2 candidate, and a plan item that names it ends as a missing source, as for erased material (ERA-09); a redrive of a sealed outbox row is refused; the callback processor has no input to claim. Nothing therefore writes the content to a stream, republishes it, hands it to a consumer or sends it to an endpoint. An entry of the original event that is already in a stream is untouched and leaves by trim, as before (RR-05). The same refusals apply from the deadline to a row that is not yet sealed, through the guard (CAG-04, CAG-08). |
| SEAL-07 [condition 17] | **Restore.** A seal's intent is appended to the journal before the sealing transaction commits, and its completion after, as for an erasure (JRN-06). A database recovered to a point before a seal has the content in its store again. It is quarantined, and the reconciler re-applies holds, then seals, then erasures, before any workload starts (JRN-10; INV-18). A seal whose journal record exists is re-applied whatever the restored decision record says. Event bodies, material and inputs are not in object storage in V1 (STO-04), so there is no object version to reactivate; the journal's own objects hold identifiers only. **Not prevented, and stated:** a backup taken before the seal contains the unsealed content until that backup ages out, exactly as it contains erased content (RR-05). It is reachable only by a governed restore into quarantine. |
| SEAL-08 [conditions 4, 5, 16] | **Access.** One inspection function exists, for the tooling principal. It needs a request by one holder of `retention.hold.manage` and an approval by a different one, each with an operator action proof, bound to one decision record or, for content sealed under a proven hold (SEAL-14), to that hold's record, valid at most 60 minutes, with a purpose from a closed list of privacy and legal purposes. The rules of MAT-03 … MAT-10 apply unchanged: re-validation on each access, audit before release, the tenant-scoped access row, tooling session only, no download, fail closed. `recovery.material.view` does not reach sealed content, and no support, replay or diagnostic capability does. |
| SEAL-09 [conditions 15, 16] | **Keys and isolation.** The `SEALED_CONTENT` KEK is per organization, as the other purposes are. It is used for unwrap only by the decrypting service, on a verified inspection grant or a disposition. Its versions follow KEY-19: a vault entry pins the version that wrapped it. The vault is keyed by organization, and the sealing, inspection and disposition functions take the organization from the locked row. This purpose, and the index key of HLD-20, are additions to the hierarchy of §12.1; they are specified here and delivered by IR-51 and IR-50, and §12.1's table is not restated. |
| SEAL-10 [conditions 10, 11, 14, 18] | **Sealing is one-way; the exits are dispositions.** Sealed content never returns to its store. (i) `HOLD_APPLIES`: it stays sealed as that hold's row until the hold ends, and is then erased. (ii) `EXCEPTION_AUTHORIZED`: it stays sealed until the expiry, and is then `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED` again from that instant. (iii) `ERASURE_DETERMINED`, or every hold it was assessed against has ended: the vault entry is deleted and the row is marked erased by its ordinary journaled erasure function, in one transaction, idempotently. No elapsed time erases it, and no elapsed time releases a hold. |
| SEAL-11 [conditions 12, 13] | **Exceptions cannot disguise it.** The exception rules of HLD-18 apply to sealed rows unchanged: hard expiry, no automatic renewal, no repeated evidence, privacy-owner approval past the first bound, refusal for everyone past the cap. The dual-controlled, time-limited exception itself is preserved as a legitimate act. |
| SEAL-12 [7I] | **Availability of the deciders.** The roster holds at least three people with `retention.hold.manage`, so that two are available with one absent; the named privacy owner may be one of the two. If the authorization issuer or the tooling is down, no decision can be recorded: the content stays sealed and the incident stays open, with that cause appended. Nothing is decided by default when the system returns, and no decision is dated earlier than it was taken. |
| SEAL-13 [7I] | **Scope, stated.** Sealing is designed here for the content-bearing event stores. An owner-context row (a deal, a recording, a document) that is uncertain at its erasure is skipped, gets its decision record and, past its limit, its incident, by HLD-14 and HLD-18. **How an owning context seals its own row is not designed in this document.** It is owed by that context, and it blocks the execution of data-subject erasure there (AB-7I-14; HE-7L-7I-11). |
| SEAL-14 [OD-7I-30, conditions 1, 6, 10] | **Every row whose content outlives its deadline is sealed, whatever keeps it.** Until the seventh remediation only uncertain rows were sealed, and a row kept by a proven hold stayed in its ordinary store, readable by the tenant, for as long as the hold lasted. A hold requires preservation; it does not authorize continued ordinary use (HLD-06). At the first pass after the deadline the sealing function therefore also seals a row that HLD-11 reports as held by a current path, by an explicit reference or under `HOLD_APPLIES`, and a row under an unexpired `EXCEPTION_AUTHORIZED`. Its seal record carries the basis, `HELD` with the holds concerned or `EXCEPTION` with the exception record. **No incident is opened for it:** the retention is authorized by a hold, and the status says so truthfully; the unauthorized-retention incident of SEAL-04 remains reserved for a row that nothing authorizes. Everything else is as SEAL-01 … SEAL-13: one transaction, journaled intent, idempotent, restore-safe, no obligation resolved, one-way. When the last hold that reaches it ends, the content is erased by disposition (SEAL-10 iii). Before that, the one way to its content is the inspection function of SEAL-08, bound to the hold's record, for a legal or privacy purpose from the closed list, under two operator proofs. The frozen 7G rule that a parked case has replay-complete material is met by the vault copy; that reading is part of ERR-7I-26. |

### 14.7b Content access guard (OD-7I-30; P1-7I-R21)

Nothing in this section exists. It is a requirement on a future governed migration and on every service that returns or uses stored event content (IR-52), with a controlled erratum to frozen read behaviour (ERR-7I-26). A scheduled pass and an alert do not prohibit anything at the moment of a read. This section is the prohibition.

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| CAG-01 [OD-7I-30, conditions 1, 11] | **The invariant.** Content of a content-bearing event-store row is returned to, or used by, an ordinary path only while the row is *eligible*: the database clock is before the row's content deadline. From that instant every ordinary path obtains nothing, whether a hold keeps the row, a decision record exists, an exception is in force, the row has been sealed, or no retention pass has run at all. A stopped worker, an unreachable journal and a failed vault write each leave the content physically where it was and ordinarily unreachable. "Ordinary" is every path except the dual-controlled inspection of SEAL-08. |
| CAG-02 [condition 4] | **The content deadline is one database function.** It is owned by the migration role, is executable by no login role directly, and is called by the guard, by the selection predicate of every retention pass and by the sealing and erasure functions. It reads only committed lifecycle fields of the row and of the lineage anchor or case it depends on. *Delivery body and preview:* for a terminal row, the earliest of the clocks RET-04 … RET-07 apply to it, that is the row's 30 / 90-day limit, the lineage deadline of LBE-01 and, for `CANCELLED`, 30 days from `completed_at`; for a `PENDING` or `DELIVERING` row, none, because the body is owed work (ERA-11, RET-08). *Replay material and captured source:* 90 days from `parked_at` while unresolved, 7 days from `resolved_at` once resolved; while an `APPROVED`, `RUNNING` or `PAUSED` operation references it (RET-14, ERA-15), the deadline for that operation's own fetch is the end of the reference, and for every other reader it is unchanged. *Callback processing input:* 7 days from the transition to terminal `FAILED`; for a non-terminal receipt, none (RET-18). *Outbox payload of a `FAILED` row:* the limit of RET-02, 90 days from the publisher case's `parked_at`; for `PENDING` and `CLAIMED`, none (ERA-S1). A `PUBLISHED` outbox row is transport under RET-01, has no ordinary content reader, and is outside this function. **No approved period is changed by this rule**; it only names, per row, the instant RET-01 … RET-30 already fix. A row for which an input is null, absent or inconsistent (a terminal row with no completion time, a descendant with no anchor, a state the table does not know) has an **unknown** deadline, and unknown is not eligible. |
| CAG-03 [conditions 4, 7] | **One clock.** Eligibility is decided on the primary's clock, read with `clock_timestamp()` inside the function, after the row lock where one is taken. No session setting, argument or application clock is an input. A content-returning function raises on a standby (`pg_is_in_recovery()`), because a replica that lags can show a terminal row as non-terminal and so as having no deadline; replicas serve metadata. The retention pass and the sealing function read the same clock in the same way. |
| CAG-04 [conditions 1, 6] | **What each state allows.** Before the deadline: ordinary access, under the path's own authorization. At or after the deadline, in every one of these conditions: ordinary access denied. *Not yet seen by a pass:* no restricted path either, until the pass has written a status. *Held by a proven hold* (explicit reference, current path, `HOLD_APPLIES`): preserved; sealed at the pass with basis `HELD` (SEAL-14); inspection only. *`EXCEPTION_AUTHORIZED`:* preserved until the expiry; inspection only. *`OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED`:* preserved, sealed, an incident; inspection only. *`ERASURE_DETERMINED`, or no hold applies:* erased at the pass. *Sealed:* nothing in the store. *Erased:* nothing anywhere. The effective hold, the exception, the decision and the seal therefore each have a defined effect on access, and in no case is that effect to re-open an ordinary path. |
| CAG-05 [conditions 2, 5] | **The guarded inventory.** Every function that can return or copy content is listed in a governed inventory and contains the guard; a function that is not listed has no privilege that reaches a content column (CAG-06). As read from the frozen sources: (1) the tenant delivery read of 6J §23.2 (`payload_json`) and the preview field of §23.1, through one new read function for `app_api` (CAG-07); (2) the public replay of 6J §23.3, in the superseding replay function (7H MR-7H-08), which evaluates the guard on the parent row under its `FOR UPDATE` lock before any copy, where the installed body (`101_5I1` L1292 – L1340) checks status only; (3) the dispatcher's fenced body load (IR-05), which serves only a held claim on a non-terminal row and asserts that the row has no deadline; (4) the material fetch for an operation item and for the material view (IR-12; §13.5), before any ciphertext or wrapped key is returned; (5) the callback processing claim (7H MR-7H-09), which serves a non-terminal receipt only; (6) the relay's outbox claim, `PENDING` rows only, and the redrive of a `FAILED` row (7G R5), which evaluates the guard before the payload is read; (7) the capture of a published row for an unaccounted obligation (ACC-05), which is bounded by its own precondition and by RET-01. The sweeper, the maintenance principal and the platform administrator obtain no content from any function (PRV-07, PRV-08, PRV-14). No export and no support diagnostic reads an event store in the frozen design; one added later must use these functions and no other. A webhook send, a plugin callout and a provider call transmit only what one of these functions returned in the same operation (CAG-10). |
| CAG-06 [condition 5] | **Raw privileges are reconciled, because a guard that a direct statement can go around is not a guard.** *Physical facts:* `063_5I` L75 grants `SELECT, INSERT` on `webhooks.webhook_deliveries` to `app_api` and `app_worker`; L76 grants `SELECT` to `app_readonly`; `066_5I` L4 grants `SELECT` on every table of the schema, partitions included, to `app_readonly`. Forced RLS confines these roles to a tenant context and is silent about deadlines. *Target:* `REVOKE SELECT` from the three roles on the parent and on every partition, found by a recursive walk of `pg_inherits`; `GRANT SELECT (columns)` on the parent only, for the columns the frozen 6J and 7H statements read, **excluding `payload_json` and `last_response_body_preview`**. `INSERT` is unchanged. PostgreSQL has no column-level denial under a table-level grant (§8.6), so a column `REVOKE` alone is not an implementation. Afterwards, for each of the three roles: `SELECT payload_json …`, `SELECT * …`, `COPY … TO`, an `INSERT … RETURNING` of a content column and a predicate on one each fail with `42501`; a query of a partition fails outright. Replay material, callback inputs, the sealed vault and the outbox payload already carry no table privilege for these roles in the target state (INV-06, CBI-06, SEAL-01, IR-04). *Assertion block:* no login role holds `SELECT` on a content column of the parent or any privilege on a partition; every function executable by a login role whose body or result type can carry a content column is in the inventory of CAG-05; no view exposes one; the same assertion in every partition-creating migration (PRV-22). Rolling back restores the bypass, so the downgrade is gated. |
| CAG-07 [conditions 3, 5] | **The tenant read function.** `SECURITY DEFINER`, owned by the migration role, fixed `search_path`, executable by `app_api` only, with a `session_user` check and the tenant-context check of `101_5I1`: the caller's context must equal the row's organization. It returns the metadata the frozen DTO carries and, in the same statement, the body and the preview when the row is eligible and SQL null when it is not, with an internal access code: `ELIGIBLE`, `EXPIRED`, `SEALED`, `ERASED` or `DEADLINE_UNKNOWN`. A read takes no row lock: the result is correct for the statement's snapshot and the clock read in it. The list route gets the preview by the same function, row by row, so a page can hold eligible and expired rows together. **Metadata is not content:** identity, status, counts, times, the response code and the failure category stay readable under their own grants and their own retention, and audit rows are untouched. |
| CAG-08 [conditions 12, 13] | **What a denied path sees, and what it does not do.** The tenant read returns `payload_json: null` and a null preview, which is what PBR-06 already emits for an erased body; no field, state or error code is added (APF-03 as extended; ERR-7I-26). Replay is refused with the existing `422 WEBHOOK_REPLAY_NOT_ALLOWED`. An operation item whose material is denied ends as a missing source, as for erased material (ERA-09), and a redrive is refused. **Nothing is thereby resolved.** The delivery keeps its status. The case keeps its state, its history and its obligation: it is not `RESOLVED`, not rejected, not moved by the RPM-12 transition, because nothing was erased. The receipt keeps its status. The owning domain's reconciliation stays available on its own frozen terms (ERA-03; SEAL-02). |
| CAG-09 [conditions 7, 8] | **Fail closed, without a wider outage.** The denial needs the row and the clock and nothing else. It does not read the hold registry, the subject index, an index key, an exception record, the journal, the vault or the key service, so none of them can make it fail open, and none of them being down denies anything that is still inside its retention. A deadline that cannot be computed, a deadline function that raises, a standby, and a database whose activation row does not match its incarnation (JRN-12) each give no content. There is no fallback to a raw read: no role has one (CAG-06). The restricted path is the opposite: inspection needs the registry, the decision or hold record, both proofs, the audit path and the key service, and any of them missing gives no output (MAT-09). |
| CAG-10 [condition 9] | **The deadline can pass while an operation is in progress.** (i) *In the database:* a path that makes a durable copy (replay, an operation item, redrive) evaluates the guard and writes the copy in one transaction under the row lock. The copy is new owed work with its own clocks (LBE-05), and the frozen replay window already closes seven days before the lineage deadline (LBE-03). (ii) *Every content result carries the eligibility instant and the database time at which it was computed.* (iii) *Before the first byte of an external handoff*, an HTTP response body, a webhook send, a provider or plugin callout, a stream publish, the service computes the time remaining from those two values and its own monotonic clock, and aborts if less than a margin remains. A path whose handoff has a timeout uses a margin at least that long, so a transfer that starts is expected to finish in time. The margin and the timeouts are 7K values; no rule depends on their size. (iv) *Content does not outlive the operation that fetched it:* no cache, queue, task argument or log carries it (INV-07, RED-01). **Not claimed:** atomicity with the network. What cannot be prevented is RR-12. A non-terminal delivery has no deadline, so ordinary dispatch never meets this rule. |
| CAG-11 [conditions 4, 10] | **The guard and the sealing transaction cannot disagree.** Both call the deadline function of CAG-02 on the same row and read the clock of CAG-03. The pass selects and the sealing or erasure function acts only when the clock has reached the deadline; the guard returns content only while it has not. The sealing function re-evaluates the deadline under the row lock, so a row whose lifecycle changed since selection, for example one that an operation now references, is left alone. Hold applicability and decision status decide what the pass does with an expired row: erase, seal as held, or seal as undecided. They are not inputs to eligibility, so a late or contested decision cannot open a window. An exception's expiry and a hold's release change the status the decision function reports and never the deadline. |
| CAG-12 [condition 11] | **The pass is down, the journal is unreachable, or the vault write fails.** The content stays in its store, undestroyed and denied. Nothing is erased, no hold is released, no obligation is resolved, and nothing is reported complete. A guarded count function for the sweeper returns, by identifier only, the rows whose deadline has passed and whose content is still present, with their age, and that is an alert from its first row (HE-7J-7I-16). When the pass resumes it erases or seals each row and writes the incident, where one is due, **with the original deadline as its occurrence time** (SEAL-04). A sealing transaction that fails at the vault insert rolls back whole; the row is unsealed and still denied. Stated: between the deadline and the pass the row has no retention-decision status of its own unless one was opened earlier (HLD-18 opens it before the deadline for an uncertain row); the access denial does not wait for one. |
| CAG-13 [condition 10] | **Restore.** Grants and functions are schema and return with the database; eligibility is computed from the restored row and the present clock. A row restored to before its seal or erasure is therefore denied from the first statement, before the reconciler has reached it, in addition to the quarantine of INV-18. A row restored as non-terminal is owed work in the restored database and is handled by JRN-15 and JRN-25, not by this rule. Sealing and disposition stay idempotent and journaled (SEAL-03, SEAL-07, SEAL-10). |
| CAG-14 [condition 6] | **Inspection** is SEAL-08 unchanged in mechanism and now the only way to any content past its deadline: one function, two different holders of `retention.hold.manage`, each with an operator action proof, bound to one decision record or one hold record, a purpose from a closed list of privacy and legal purposes, at most 60 minutes, audit before release, a tenant-scoped access row, no download. It reaches sealed content only; a row past its deadline that no pass has sealed is reachable by nobody. |
| CAG-15 [7I] | **Evidence.** A denied read is counted, by path and access code, and is not audited row by row. A denial on a path that creates work is recorded where that path records its result: the replay refusal on the route's audit row, the item result on the operation, the redrive refusal on the case history. `DEADLINE_UNKNOWN` raises an integrity alarm, because it means a lifecycle field the design requires is missing. Inspection is audited as SEAL-08 says. |
| CAG-16 [7I] | **Tenant isolation.** Each function takes the organization from the row it locks or reads and compares it with the caller's tenant context where the caller has one. The guard adds no cross-tenant read and no argument that selects another organization's row. |
| CAG-17 [7I] | **Not covered, and stated.** (a) A subject's erasure request that is due and is waiting on the journal is JRN-29, unchanged: this guard keys on the retention deadline, not on a pending request-driven step. (b) Content already in a stream entry leaves by trim (RR-05). (c) Backups are ERA-20. (d) The guard is designed for the content-bearing event stores. Whether an owning context's own content (a recording, a transcript, a document) is readable after its `RetentionProfile` limit is that context's design, and it is handed on, not claimed (HE-7L-7I-12). |
| CAG-18 [7I] | **Compatibility.** This rule narrows what three frozen grants and three frozen read behaviours allow, and changes no state machine, route, DTO field, error code, event or retention period. The narrowing is ERR-7I-26. Before IR-52 exists the executed schema permits every read this section forbids (§22.1). |

### 14.8 Restore-safe erasure journal (OD-7I-13; P1-7I-R03)

Nothing in this section exists. The store's provider capabilities are **not assumed**; JRN-19 lists what must be verified before activation.

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| JRN-01 [OD] | **Independent store.** The journal lives in the existing approved in-region object storage, under a dedicated bucket or prefix with its own credentials, its own encryption key and its own lifecycle, separate from the database-backup target and from every other prefix. It is not in PostgreSQL and is outside the point-in-time-recovery and snapshot lineage of the primary database. No other database product or managed service is introduced. |
| JRN-02 [OD] | **Record types**, one object per record, append-only: `INTENT`, `COMPLETED`, `WITHDRAWN` (erasure steps); `TIMED_INTENT`, `TIMED_COMPLETED`, `TIMED_WITHDRAWN` (time-based erasure batches, JRN-21); `HOLD_PLACED`, `HOLD_RELEASED`; `KEY_DESTROY_INTENT`, `KEY_DESTROYED`; `CHECKPOINT`. **Every irreversible privacy erasure is journaled, request-driven and time-based alike (OD-7I-16).** The first remediation excluded time-based erasures on the ground that they are recomputed from each row's own clock. That holds only while the restored row is still in the lifecycle state the clock is measured from. A restore can return a terminal row to a non-terminal state, in which no clock runs and the terminal-only erasure function refuses to act (P1-7I-R08; JRN-21 … JRN-30). |
| JRN-03 [OD] | **Minimized content.** Sequence number; hash of the previous record; type; region; time; `organization_id`; the request, hold or key reference; store code; the set of resource references (identifiers only), encrypted; for `COMPLETED`, counts; and for every erased row of any store, in `INTENT` and `TIMED_INTENT` records alike, its **lifecycle evidence** (JRN-22). Never a name, a number, an address, a payload, a body, material, an input, a URL or a secret. Class `PID`. The journal is not a second store of personal information: it can re-identify nothing without the database it protects. |
| JRN-04 [OD] | **Encryption and authenticity.** The reference set is encrypted under the per-region platform key, purpose `ERASURE_JOURNAL`. The journal writer holds generate-only; the restore reconciler holds decrypt; nobody else holds either. Every record is authenticated, with the region, the sequence number and the previous record's hash as associated data, so a record cannot be altered, reordered, moved between regions or spliced. Transport is TLS; the bucket is storage-encrypted. |
| JRN-05 [OD] | **Sequencing.** One monotonic, gap-free sequence per region. The object name is derived from the sequence number, and an append succeeds only if no object of that name exists. Where the provider has no atomic create-if-absent, a single writer with a fencing token gives the same property (JRN-19). Each record chains to its predecessor by hash. |
| JRN-06 [OD] | **Write-ahead protocol.** Step journal states: `NOT_JOURNALED → INTENT_REQUESTED → INTENT_DURABLE → ERASED → COMPLETION_JOURNALED → VERIFIED`, or `→ WITHDRAWN`. (1) *Prepare:* a transaction checks authorization (the request's state, no hold) and sets `INTENT_REQUESTED` with a database-issued nonce. (2) *Intent:* the journal writer appends `INTENT` carrying the nonce and reads it back. (3) *Confirm:* a guarded function, callable by the journal-writer principal only, records the sequence number and sets `INTENT_DURABLE`. (4) *Erase:* the erasure function, run by the maintenance principal, requires `INTENT_DURABLE`, re-checks authorization and holds under its locks, erases, sets `ERASED` and writes its audit row, in one transaction. (5) *Complete:* after reading `ERASED`, the writer appends `COMPLETED`; a transaction sets `COMPLETION_JOURNALED`. (6) *Verify:* a pass confirms that no targeted row still holds content and sets `VERIFIED`. |
| JRN-07 [OD] | **Consistency boundary.** There is no distributed transaction. The invariant is one-directional: **every erasure committed in PostgreSQL has a durable `INTENT` in the journal**, enforced by the precondition of step 4. The converse is not required: an `INTENT` without an erasure is owed work, visible in both places. |
| JRN-08 [OD] | **An intent followed by an aborted transaction** never becomes a completion and never becomes an unauthorized deletion. `COMPLETED` is appended only after the database shows `ERASED`. The step stays `INTENT_DURABLE` and is retried through step 4, which checks authorization again. If the erasure is no longer authorized (a hold was placed, the request was withdrawn or rejected), a guarded, audited function appends `WITHDRAWN` with the hold or withdrawal reference and closes the step. A pending intent is executed only through that same function path, in normal operation and in a restore alike. |
| JRN-09 [OD] | **Crash points.** After (1), before (2): nothing erased; the step resumes. After (2), before (3): the writer finds its record by nonce and confirms; a duplicate `INTENT` is harmless. After (3), before (4): owed, retried. During (4): the transaction is atomic. **After (4) commits, before (5): the journal holds a pending intent for an erasure that happened; the completion reconciler reads `ERASED` and appends `COMPLETED`. If the database is lost in that interval, the pending intent is replayed on restore and the erasure is applied again, which is correct because it was authorized and committed.** After (5), before the state update: the writer finds its `COMPLETED` and updates. |
| JRN-10 [OD] | **Holds.** `HOLD_PLACED` is appended before the registry row commits; `HOLD_RELEASED` after the release commits. On a crash between the two actions the journal errs toward the hold, and reconciliation applies it. In a replay, records are applied in sequence order, so a hold placed before an erasure's completion prevents it and one placed after finds the data already gone (HLD-03). |
| JRN-11 [OD] | **Checkpoints.** The database stores `journal_applied_through`, the highest sequence number up to which every record's effect is present in it, updated in the transactions that apply them; every backup therefore carries its own lower bound. The writer periodically appends an authenticated `CHECKPOINT` naming the head sequence and chain hash. |
| JRN-12 [OD] | **Quarantine.** Activation is bound to the **database incarnation**: an identifier that changes on every restore, point-in-time recovery and promotion (in PostgreSQL, the system identifier together with the timeline). An activation record for exactly one incarnation is held outside the database. A recovered database has a new incarnation and no activation record, so it is quarantined by default, without relying on an operator remembering a step. Only the restore reconciler can issue an activation record. **A check at workload start is not enough** (second review): a worker that was running before the database was replaced reconnects without restarting, and a session open on a replica survives that replica's promotion. Fencing therefore has four layers, each sufficient against the case it names. (a) **Inside the database.** A single-row activation relation stores the incarnation the database was last activated as. Every guarded function of the event pipeline (outbox claim and mark, delivery claim, admission and body load, ledger worker and operator functions, completion, accounting, erasure) compares it with the incarnation the running instance reports and raises if they differ. The row is restored together with everything else, so in a recovered database it names the *old* incarnation and every such function refuses by default; only the restore reconciler's activation function rewrites it, in the transaction that ends the reconciliation. A reconnecting relay, dispatcher, consumer or tooling process therefore cannot claim, load, complete or erase, whatever it believes. (b) **At every connection and every pool checkout.** The checkout hook of TCX-07 also compares the connection's database incarnation with the external activation record, cached for no longer than a 7K bound, and refuses to begin a transaction on a mismatch. This covers plain tenant statements of the API, which pass through no guarded function. The incarnation is read per checkout, not once per connection, because a promotion changes it under a live session. (c) **Session termination and endpoint isolation.** The recovery procedure terminates every pre-existing session on the recovered or promoted instance and keeps it unreachable under the service endpoint until activation (7K runbook, HE-7K-7I-09). (d) **At start,** as before. Where a deployment cannot supply an incarnation identifier, or supplies one that lags a fast promotion (the timeline recorded at the last checkpoint is not sufficient by itself), the fallback is a check of the journal tail against the database at every checkout, or the gate stays closed (JRN-19). |
| JRN-13 [OD] | **Reconciliation, in quarantine, in this order.** (1) Authenticate the journal and prove completeness: the chain is contiguous from the restored `journal_applied_through` to the head; every record authenticates; the head agrees with the latest `CHECKPOINT` and with a consistent listing. (2) Refuse a backup whose recovery point is older than the start of the journal's guaranteed coverage (JRN-17). (3) Re-apply every record after the lower bound in sequence order: holds as they occur; `COMPLETED` erasures unconditionally, since the journal is authoritative that they happened; pending `INTENT`s through the erasure function with its authorization check; `WITHDRAWN` not at all; `KEY_DESTROYED` by confirming the version is absent at the key service and destroying it if a key-service recovery brought it back; **`TIMED_COMPLETED` and pending `TIMED_INTENT` records row by row through the lifecycle comparison of JRN-24 and the store treatments of JRN-25**; `TIMED_WITHDRAWN` not at all. (4) Run every time-based erasure pass to completion; these now cover only rows whose clocks elapse in the restored state, and they journal as in normal operation. (5) Run verification, which includes the assertion of JRN-26. (6) Write the audit row, the reconciliation report (JRN-27) and a `CHECKPOINT`. (7) Rotate the two verification keys of STP-10, rewrite the in-database activation row and issue the activation record. Every step is idempotent, so a crash restarts the procedure from (1). **Running the time-based passes over restored rows is no longer relied on to reconstruct earlier deletions**; that was the defect. |
| JRN-14 [OD] | **What a reconciliation covers.** Every store that has an erasure step: owner tables (the owning contexts' erasure functions, registered as steps; 7I requires their registration and does not design them), replay material and recovery-ledger copies, captured sources, webhook bodies and previews across each lineage, callback processing inputs, outbox rows of an erased subject (JRN-15), key versions, and object versions (the orphan reconciliation of ERA-22 runs after step 5, because a restored row may point at an object deleted since, and an object may exist with no row). Replicas are rebuilt from, or attached only to, the reconciled primary. |
| JRN-15 [OD] | **Stale obligations of an erased subject.** A restored database can hold, as non-terminal, work that in the lost timeline was finished before the erasure. It must not be re-emitted with the erased content. (a) A webhook delivery restored as `PENDING` or `DELIVERING` for which a `COMPLETED` **or `TIMED_COMPLETED`** record names the row: the reconciler sets the terminal status and completion time the record carries, and erases body and preview (JRN-25, row 1). The status is evidence from the journal, not an invention, and it is never derived from the mere passing of a deadline. (b) An outbox row restored as `PENDING` or `CLAIMED`, of a PII-bearing type (CLS-03), whose aggregate reference is in a `COMPLETED` subject erasure: it is not published. Its payload is replaced by a tombstone with the digest recorded, its status is set to `FAILED` with a safe category code, and a publisher recovery case is opened in `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` for the producing owner (the ERA-07 mechanism). Nothing is resolved, rejected or discarded (INV-09). In normal operation ERA-S1 is unchanged: a pending row is published as it is. |
| JRN-16 [OD] | **Fail closed.** If the journal store is unreachable, a record fails authentication, the chain has a gap, the head cannot be confirmed, the backup predates coverage, any re-application fails, **a restored row's state contradicts its journaled evidence (JRN-24 v), or a store treatment of JRN-25 cannot complete**, the environment stays quarantined and an alert is raised. Nothing is partially activated. There is no override in V1. |
| JRN-17 [OD] | **Retention.** RET-24. A record must outlive every backup that could bring its subject back. A backup older than the journal's coverage start is not eligible to be restored into service. Lifecycle expiry removes all versions of an expired record object; no identity can delete a record earlier. The residue this implies (encrypted identifiers of erased subjects for the backup horizon, about one year under 3F's current schedule) is stated in the request's completion evidence (ERA-18) and is part of LR-05. |
| JRN-18 [OD] | **Access and tamper resistance.** The journal writer can create objects and cannot overwrite or delete. The restore reconciler can read. No database role, database administrator, application worker, platform administrator, tenant principal or backup job holds any credential for the prefix. Immutability or object-lock features are used where the provider is verified to have them; where it does not, the minimum is denial of overwrite and delete to every runtime identity, versioning that preserves an overwritten object, and the chain, authentication and checkpoint checks, which turn tampering into a fail-closed quarantine instead of a silent loss. The store's access log is kept apart from application logs, and a delete or overwrite attempt is an alert. |
| JRN-19 [OD] | **Validation before activation**, on the actual provider and the actual managed database: atomic create-if-absent or an equivalent fenced single writer; read-after-write consistency for reads and for listings; enforceable denial of overwrite and delete; versioning and lifecycle behaviour for all versions; in-region placement (RSY-13); a failure domain distinct from the database-backup target; and that the database incarnation identifier of JRN-12 really changes on restore, point-in-time recovery and promotion. A capability that is absent is replaced by the stated fallback or the gate stays closed. |
| JRN-20 [OD] | **Normal-operation availability.** If the journal is unavailable, request-driven erasure steps **and time-based batches** wait at `INTENT_REQUESTED`. No erasure, hold release or key destruction proceeds without its record. Nothing is lost; the open steps and their age are visible (HE-7J-7I-08). Publication, consumption and delivery do not depend on the journal. The consequences for deadlines are JRN-29. |
| JRN-21 [OD-7I-16] | **Time-based erasure is journaled, write-ahead.** Every time-based erasure of this document runs as a **batch step** with the journal states of JRN-06: lineage-deadline and `CANCELLED` body erasure (RET-04, 05, 07), **the 30 / 90-day purge of a delivery row that still holds its body** (RET-04, RET-05: for a root delivery the body leaves with the row, and that purge is then the erasure), the material cap and post-resolution erasure (RET-12, RET-13, RET-15), `FAILED` processing-input erasure (RET-17) and the `FAILED` outbox payload tombstone (RET-02). (1) *Prepare:* a transaction selects rows by the frozen predicate, reads each row's committed lifecycle evidence, and stores the batch with its row identities, that evidence and a nonce, state `INTENT_REQUESTED`. (2) The journal writer appends `TIMED_INTENT` and reads it back. (3) Confirm: `INTENT_DURABLE`. (4) *Erase:* one transaction; for each row, under its lock, the function **re-verifies that the row's current evidence equals the journaled evidence**, re-evaluates the predicate and the hold exclusion (HLD-03), and erases only then; a row that changed is skipped and left for a later batch with fresh evidence. (5) `TIMED_COMPLETED` names exactly the rows erased. (6) Verify. Crash points are those of JRN-09. A batch whose intent is durable and whose erasure became unauthorized for every row is closed by `TIMED_WITHDRAWN` (JRN-08). |
| JRN-22 [OD-7I-16] | **Lifecycle evidence per row** (identifiers, states and times only; class `PID`). *Webhook delivery:* delivery ID and partition key, `organization_id`, `event_id`, endpoint ID, lineage root, terminal `status`, `completed_at`, `failure_reason` category, final `attempt_count` and claim sequence, `payload_hash`, the clock applied (`LINEAGE_DEADLINE`, `CANCELLED_BODY_LIMIT`), and for a lineage erasure the root's creation time and terminal status as held on the anchor. *Replay material and captured source:* case identity, group, `organization_id`, case state and `resolved_at` or `parked_at`, resolution kind where resolved, material digest, the clock applied. *Processing input:* receipt ID, `organization_id`, receipt status `FAILED` and the time of that transition. *`FAILED` outbox payload:* outbox ID, `event_type`, aggregate reference, payload digest, publisher case identity and its `parked_at`. *Request-driven steps* carry the same evidence for each row they erase. |
| JRN-23 [7I] | **The evidence was true before it was published.** The prepare transaction reads committed rows, so each terminal outcome in a `TIMED_INTENT` committed before that transaction's snapshot and therefore before the append. Step 4 erases only rows whose evidence is unchanged. Hence for every row named in `TIMED_COMPLETED`, and for every row of a pending `TIMED_INTENT`, the journaled status was a committed state of that row in the timeline that produced the record. Evidence is never written from a deadline, a schedule or an expectation. |
| JRN-24 [OD-7I-16] | **Lifecycle comparison on restore.** For each row named by an applied erasure record the reconciler compares the restored row with the evidence: (i) **absent** (created after the recovery point): nothing to do; (ii) **same lifecycle state, content present**: erase through the ordinary erasure function; (iii) **already erased**: no change; (iv) **an earlier lifecycle state on a path to the evidence** (for example `PENDING` where the evidence says `DELIVERED`): the store treatment of JRN-25; (v) **a state from which the evidence is unreachable**, or an identity mismatch (a different `payload_hash`, digest, organization or event): a contradiction; fail closed (JRN-16). A later `HOLD_PLACED` for the row, applied first because records are applied in sequence order, prevents (ii) and (iv) exactly as it would have prevented the erasure. |
| JRN-25 [OD-7I-16] | **Store treatments for a row restored to an earlier state.** The table below. Two principles decide every row. First: **content that was erased is erased again and is never transmitted, published, processed or shown.** Second: **a terminal status is restored only where the journaled outcome is a fact that the restore did not undo**; where the outcome depended on database state that the restore also rewound, the obligation is preserved through the owning domain's frozen reconciliation contract and nothing is marked done. |
| JRN-26 [7I] | **Verification.** Before activation the reconciler asserts, by query: no row named in an applied erasure record holds content; no such delivery is `PENDING` or `DELIVERING`; no such outbox row is `PENDING` or `CLAIMED`; no such receipt is non-terminal with an input; no such case holds material. Any counter-instance keeps the environment quarantined. |
| JRN-27 [7I] | **Atomicity, idempotence, report.** Each row's treatment is one transaction through restore-only guarded functions granted to the restore reconciler alone; each is forward-only and idempotent (a second application finds case (iii)), so a crash at any point is recovered by restarting the reconciliation. Every row treated under JRN-25 is listed in a reconciliation report by identifier, store, evidence and treatment, written to the audit trail and handed to the owning domains. The functions refuse to run while the database is activated. |
| JRN-28 [7I] | **Batching and scale, for 7K (HE-7K-7I-09).** One journal object per batch; the batch size, cadence and writer concurrency are 7K's values. Traceability is per row, not per batch: each row is individually listed with its evidence and is addressed by (sequence number, ordinal). Sequencing stays gap-free under batching because a batch is one record. Reconciliation reads every record after the recovery point, so its duration grows with the number of erasures since that point; 7K bounds it by the checkpoint interval and states the resulting recovery-time cost. Journal volume now scales with deliveries and cases, not with requests; that is stated for sizing and for RET-24. |
| JRN-29 [OD-7I-16] | **Journal outage and deadlines.** When an append cannot be durably confirmed, the batch or step stays at `INTENT_REQUESTED`: an explicitly tracked pending state, never a silent skip. A critical alert is raised at once. The writer retries with bounded backoff; the retry is idempotent because the record is found by its nonce (JRN-09). The owner-approved limits (OD-7I-01, 02, 03, 09, 10) and any legal deadline of a subject request **remain obligations**: an outage does not suspend or extend them. Each pending item carries its deadline; an *approaching* deadline (a 7K threshold before the limit) and a *missed* deadline are distinct escalations into the organization's privacy-incident procedure, whose content is not designed here (LR-09). **There is no fallback to unjournaled deletion,** by configuration, by operator action or by break-glass; the erasure functions cannot run without `INTENT_DURABLE` (INV-23). |
| JRN-30 [7I] | **Deletions that are not privacy erasures, and are not journaled.** (a) Cleanup of a `PUBLISHED` outbox row (transport; the fact lives in the owner table). (b) Deletion of a processing input in the transaction that makes its receipt `PROCESSED` or `SKIPPED` (7H CBK-18). (c) Purge of whole rows whose content was **already erased** or that hold identifiers only (delivery metadata whose body is `ERASED`, case metadata, accounting, position and completion records). A purge that removes a row still holding content is an erasure and is journaled (JRN-21). After a restore, a row of kind (a) or (b) that reappears non-terminal is owed work in the restored database, because the effect it stands for was rewound with it; it is published or processed once more under the at-least-once contract and then removed by its own lifecycle. It is not content that an erasure decision had removed. If a subject's erasure covered it, the request-driven record does (JRN-15). A delivery that was terminal but **not yet erased** when the database was lost is likewise re-sent as a duplicate with content the platform still lawfully held; receivers deduplicate by `event_id` (6J). |

**Restore matrix (JRN-25).** "Evidence" is what the journal record says the row was when its content was erased. "Restored as" is the earlier state found in the recovered database.

| # | Store | Evidence | Restored as | Treatment | Why this and not a terminal status / why a terminal status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Webhook delivery | `DELIVERED` | `PENDING` / `DELIVERING`, body present | Set `DELIVERED`, `completed_at`, attempt count and category from the evidence; clear the claim; append a closure record with disposition `RESTORED_FROM_JOURNAL`; erase body and preview, reason `RESTORE_RECONCILIATION`. One transaction | The receiver accepted the request in the lost timeline. That is an external fact the restore did not undo, and the tenant already saw the row as delivered. Sending again would transmit erased content |
| 2 | Webhook delivery | `DEAD_LETTER` | `PENDING` / `DELIVERING` | As row 1 with `DEAD_LETTER` | The attempts were made and failed against the receiver: external facts. A replay is refused, as it was before the loss, because the body is erased (LBE-13) |
| 3 | Webhook delivery | `CANCELLED` (`ORG_CANCELLED` or `HOLD_EXPIRED`) | `PENDING` | As row 1 with `CANCELLED` and its reason. Listed in the report for the Integrations and Organization owners, because the organization's own status was rewound too | The cancellation was a committed, tenant-visible outcome and the body was erased under OD-7I-02. The delivery cannot be made without the body. Whether the organization's cancellation itself is re-applied is that owner's recovery decision, outside 7I; the report makes the dependency explicit |
| 4 | Replay descendant | Its own terminal evidence | Absent, or `PENDING` | Absent: nothing. Present: as rows 1 – 3, on its own evidence. Every row with the same (`organization_id`, `event_id`) named in any record is treated in the same pass (ERA-S9) | Each row carries its own evidence; none is inferred from its parent |
| 5 | Lineage anchor | Root terminal status and creation time | Anchor older, or root non-terminal | Root row by rows 1 – 3; the anchor's terminal status is then set forward from the same evidence, insert-if-absent and forward-only | LBE-01 reads the anchor; it must not be recomputed from a descendant |
| 6 | Recovery case, material erased 7 days after resolution | `RESOLVED`, resolution kind, `resolved_at` | `PARKED` or `REPLAYING`, material present | Erase the material by the frozen RPM-12 path; case → `RECONCILIATION_PENDING`, reason `PRIVACY_MATERIAL_ERASED`; the journaled resolution is written to the case history as information. **Not** set `RESOLVED` | The resolution meant a handler effect committed in owner tables, and those were rewound to the same point. Marking it resolved could drop a valid obligation (INV-09). The owning domain reconciles (7G R6) against its restored state |
| 7 | Recovery case, material erased at the 90-day cap or on a subject's request | `PARKED` / `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` | `PARKED`, `REPLAYING`, `OPEN_RETRY` or `HOLD`, material present | From `PARKED` / `REPLAYING`: as row 6. From `OPEN_RETRY` / `HOLD` with held material: the frozen parking transition first, then row 6 | The case was unresolved when the material went; it stays unresolved. No new 7G transition is invented (ERA-13) |
| 8 | Captured R4 source | As rows 6 – 7 | Present, possibly referenced by an operation restored as `APPROVED` or `RUNNING` | Erase; items that need it get `SOURCE_MISSING` (ERA-S6). The tooling is quarantined, so no item ran meanwhile | A source is never fabricated |
| 9 | Callback processing input | Receipt `FAILED` at *t* | Receipt non-terminal, input present | Delete the input; set the receipt `FAILED` through the fenced status function, category `RESTORE_INPUT_ERASED`. It is not processed | `FAILED` is the frozen state that means "processing did not complete; the owning domain reconciles with the provider" (7H CBK). It preserves the obligation and is what the evidence says |
| 10 | Outbox row, payload tombstoned at the cap | `FAILED`, publisher case parked | `PENDING`, `CLAIMED` or `FAILED` with payload | Tombstone the payload, record the digest, status `FAILED` with a safe category, publisher case `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` (the mechanism of JRN-15 b). Not published | The producing owner reconciles; nothing is resolved or discarded |
| 11 | Any store | Any | A state the evidence cannot follow from, or a different hash / digest | None. Quarantine persists | JRN-24 (v) |

**The Day-40 counterexample, re-run.** Day 0: delivery `D` is `PENDING`; backup B0. Day 1: `D` is `DELIVERED`. Day 31: the retention pass prepares a batch containing `D` (for a root delivery this is the 30-day purge of RET-04, which removes the body with the row; for a descendant it would be the lineage pass) with evidence (`DELIVERED`, `completed_at` = day 1, its hash); `TIMED_INTENT` is appended and confirmed; the erasure transaction re-verifies the evidence under the row lock and erases; `TIMED_COMPLETED` follows. Had the journal been unreachable on day 31, `D` would have kept its body, tracked and alerted, and no unjournaled erasure would exist (JRN-29). Day 40: the database is lost and B0 is restored. `D` is `PENDING` with its body. The restored database carries the old incarnation in its activation row, so the dispatcher's claim function raises for any process, restarted or merely reconnected (JRN-12 a), and the dispatcher's pool refuses the connection at checkout (JRN-12 b). The reconciler proves the chain complete from B0's `journal_applied_through`, reaches the day-31 record, compares: case (iv). It applies row 1: `D` becomes `DELIVERED` with the journaled completion time, a `RESTORED_FROM_JOURNAL` closure is appended, body and preview become `NULL`. The time-based pass of step 4 then finds a `DELIVERED` row older than 30 days and purges it, journaled as usual. The verification of JRN-26 finds no named delivery non-terminal. Only then is the database activated. The dispatcher never saw `D` as `PENDING`; the terminal-only restriction of ERA-10 was never asked to erase a non-terminal row; the body was not sent, published, read by a tenant route or shown to an operator. The statuses came from evidence whose truth JRN-23 establishes, not from the elapsed 30 days. The same walk for the other reviewed cases is rows 2 – 10. Tests: VT-74 … VT-77.

**The first-review counterexample, closed.** T0: backup. T1: a contact's data and the PII-bearing replay material of a parked case are erased; before either erasure transaction could commit, `INTENT` records with sequence numbers after the T0 lower bound were durable in the journal (JRN-07), and `COMPLETED` records followed. T2: the database is lost. T3: the T0 backup is restored. Its erasure-step ledger knows nothing of T1; that is expected and irrelevant. The restored database has a new incarnation and no activation record, so no API process, relay, consumer, dispatcher or tooling starts (JRN-12). The reconciler proves the chain complete from the backup's `journal_applied_through` to the head and re-applies the T1 records: the owner rows are tombstoned, the material is erased and its case moves to `RECONCILIATION_PENDING`, bodies and inputs are erased, stale outbox rows of the subject are tombstoned and handed to the owner (JRN-15). Only then is an activation record issued. At no moment did a serving component hold a database that contained the T1 data. If the journal cannot be read or proved complete, activation never happens (JRN-16). The copy inside the T0 backup medium still exists until that backup expires; that is the stated residue of RR-05. Tests: VT-66 … VT-68.

## 15. Replay Lineage and Privacy (OD-7I-01)

This closes 7H HE-7I-7H-08 as a policy. Production replay stays blocked until the implementation exists (§24).

### 15.1 Alternatives considered

| | A. Per-row retention with safeguards | **B. Lineage-anchored body erasure (decided)** | C. Lineage-anchored row purge | D. Per-lineage key destruction with an external body store |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rule | Each row by its own 30 / 90 days; approve the 120 / 180-day consequence | Body erased at the lineage deadline once terminal; row metadata keeps its own 30 / 90 days | Whole descendant rows deleted at the lineage deadline | Bodies encrypted under a lineage key that is destroyed at the deadline |
| Reliability | No effect | No effect: a body is never removed from a non-terminal row | No effect on delivery; loses evidence | No effect; adds a key dependency to every send |
| Data minimization | Weakest: up to 120 / 180 days | Strong: root + 30 / 90 + 7 days, plus only an in-flight tail | Strong | Strong, including backups |
| Replay eligibility | Unchanged | Unchanged: the deadline is after the window closes | Unchanged | Unchanged |
| In-flight deliveries | Untouched | Untouched | Must not delete a non-terminal row; same tail | Untouched |
| Legal holds | Simple | Hold pauses erasure per row | Hold pauses purge | Hold must preserve the key |
| Compliance risk | Unapproved retention period | Low | Loss of the frozen 90-day dead-letter diagnostic history for replays | Low |
| Database complexity | None | One guarded erasure, a body-state marker, a reconciled immutability trigger | A changed purge predicate | A new store, key lifecycle, dual-write protocol |
| Operational burden | None | One more cleanup pass | Same | Highest |
| Migration | None | Columns and function; erratum to body immutability | Function; erratum to frozen per-row retention | New store and migration |
| Frozen contract touched | None | 5I INV-WH-04 wording (erratum) | 6J §22.6 for replay rows | 7H MR-7H-06 … 08 shape |

### 15.2 Rules

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| LBE-01 [OD] | **Lineage deadline.** For a lineage whose root ended `DELIVERED`: root `created_at` + 30 days + 7 days. For a root that ended `DEAD_LETTER`: root `created_at` + 90 days + 7 days. The root's creation time and terminal status are those held on the lineage anchor (7H LIN-01), not recomputed from a descendant. |
| LBE-02 [OD] | A row's body and preview are erased when **both** hold: the row is terminal (`DELIVERED`, `DEAD_LETTER` or `CANCELLED`), and the lineage deadline has passed. The erasure is ERA-10. |
| LBE-03 [OD] | The frozen replay-eligibility window (7H LIN-03: root + 30 / 90 days) is unchanged. The deadline lies 7 days after it closes, so no eligible replay ever finds its parent's body erased by this rule. |
| LBE-04 [OD] | The frozen per-row metadata and history retention (RET-04, RET-05) is unchanged. A descendant row, its hash and its claim / admission / abandonment / closure records stay for the row's own 30 / 90 days. Only the body and preview leave early. |
| LBE-05 [OD] | **A non-terminal row is never touched.** A replay created on the last eligible day and still `PENDING` or `DELIVERING` after the deadline keeps its body until it is terminal. It then loses it in the same pass. |
| LBE-06 [OD] | **Resulting bound.** A body copy exists no later than: the lineage deadline, or, for a row that was still non-terminal at the deadline, the moment that row became terminal plus the cleanup cadence. The non-terminal tail is bounded by the frozen retry schedule (at most ten attempts; 7H §13.2) or, for an organization that is not `ACTIVE`, by the 90-day hold expiry (RET-08). In the common case that is root + 37 or + 97 days, against 120 / 180 days under the per-row rule. The suspended-organization case can reach the hold expiry; it is the only way past the tail, it ends in `CANCELLED`, and the body is then erased at once because the deadline has already passed. |
| LBE-07 [OD] | The 7-day tail is a cleanup limit for eligible terminal bodies. It authorizes neither the destruction of outstanding work nor any retention beyond it. Cleanup runs at least daily ([REC]; cadence 7K); lag beyond the deadline is an alert (HE-7J-7I-08). |
| LBE-08 [OD] | **Earlier erasure.** A data-subject erasure (ERA-S8, S9), an organization erasure (ERA-17) or the `CANCELLED` body clock (RET-07) removes a body before the deadline. Whichever comes first applies. |
| LBE-09 [OD] | **Holds.** HLD-03 applies per row. |
| LBE-10 [OD] | **All payload-bearing copies.** The body exists in `payload_json` of the root and of each descendant, and its echo may exist in `last_response_body_preview`. No other primary copy exists: bodies are not logged (RED-01), not placed in object storage (STO-04), not in analytics projections (`webhook_delivery_stats_daily` is aggregate), and not in the recovery ledger (7G WHB-02). Secondary copies are read replicas (ERA-19) and backups (ERA-20). The erasure function is idempotent across all rows of a lineage. |
| LBE-11 [OD] | **What remains.** Delivery identity, `event_id`, `event_type`, endpoint reference, `payload_hash`, status, attempt counts, timestamps, `failure_reason` category and origin, history records, lineage fields, and the audit rows of replays. |
| LBE-12 [OD] | **The immutability trigger.** Frozen 5I INV-WH-04 and `fn_wd_identity_immutable` make `payload_json` immutable. That stays true for the whole active life of a delivery: signing, retry and replay always see the original bytes. Privacy-authorized erasure of a **terminal** row's body is a separate, one-way, guarded operation: `body PRESENT → ERASED`, reachable only through the erasure function, never reversible, never applicable to a non-terminal row, and leaving `payload_hash`, `event_id`, `event_type`, `webhook_endpoint_id` and `organization_id` untouched. How the trigger admits exactly that transition is specified in §15.4 (PBR-04). This is controlled erratum ERR-7I-01; 5I, 6J and 7H are not edited. |
| LBE-13 [OD] | **Replay of an erased row is refused** with the existing `422 WEBHOOK_REPLAY_NOT_ALLOWED`, checked inside the replay function under its locks. No new public error code is introduced. |
| LBE-14 [OD] | A tenant reading a delivery whose body was erased receives the delivery DTO with `payload_json` as JSON `null`, which is the stored SQL `NULL` of PBR-01 passed through (PBR-06). That the field can be `null` after erasure is an additive response note recorded as APF-03 (§21.4). |

### 15.3 What this closes and what it does not

| Item | State |
|---|---|
| 7H HE-7I-7H-08 | **Resolved**: the policy is recorded here by owner decision OD-7I-01 |
| 7H OD-7H-14 (delegation to 7I) | **Discharged** |
| 7H AB-7H-08 "DEFERRED 7I DECISION REQUIRED" | **Design-policy gate closed.** Its condition was "7I's recorded decision". That now exists |
| Production activation of the public replay route | **Still blocked**, now by AB-7I-05: the erasure mechanism (IR-21), the reconciled trigger, the retention worker, the restore procedure and the privacy verification tests must exist and pass. Documenting the policy makes nothing production-ready |

### 15.4 Physical representation of an erased body (Minor-7I-R01)

**Physical facts (`063_5I`).** `payload_json` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with `chk_wd_payload_nonempty CHECK (length(payload_json) > 0)`. `fn_wd_identity_immutable` compares with `<>`, which yields SQL null when either side is null, so it would not by itself stop a change to `NULL`; today the `NOT NULL` constraint does. `fn_replay_webhook_delivery` copies `payload_json` into the new row. The table is range-partitioned with a default partition. A `null` response is therefore not reachable in the executed schema, and correctness depends on the following.

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| PBR-01 [7I] | **Stored state after erasure:** `payload_json IS NULL`, `last_response_body_preview IS NULL`, `body_state = 'ERASED'`. No sentinel string, no empty object and no tombstone text is stored, so nothing can be mistaken for, signed as, or replayed as a body. `payload_hash`, `event_id`, `event_type`, `webhook_endpoint_id`, `organization_id` and every status and history field are unchanged. |
| PBR-02 [7I] | **New columns** on the parent, inherited by every partition: `body_state TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PRESENT'`; `body_erased_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL`; `body_erasure_reason TEXT NULL` from a closed set (`SUBJECT_ERASURE`, `ORGANIZATION_ERASURE`, `LINEAGE_DEADLINE`, `CANCELLED_BODY_LIMIT`, `RESTORE_RECONCILIATION`); `body_erasure_ref UUID NULL` (the erasure step, or null for a time-based pass). |
| PBR-03 [7I] | **Constraints.** `payload_json` loses `NOT NULL` (issued on the parent; it propagates to partitions and cannot be issued on a partition alone). `chk_wd_payload_nonempty` is dropped and replaced by a state-coupled check: either `body_state = 'PRESENT'` and `payload_json` is not null and non-empty and `body_erased_at` is null; or `body_state = 'ERASED'` and `payload_json` is null and `last_response_body_preview` is null and `body_erased_at` and `body_erasure_reason` are not null and `status` is `DELIVERED`, `DEAD_LETTER` or `CANCELLED`. A present row with a null body, and an erased row with a body, are both unrepresentable. [REC] The new check is added `NOT VALID` and then validated, to bound lock time on large partitions. |
| PBR-04 [7I] | **Trigger.** `fn_wd_identity_immutable` is superseded by `CREATE OR REPLACE` in the governed migration (the `101_5I1` precedent; `063_5I` is not edited; PRV-28 applies). It compares with `IS DISTINCT FROM`. It rejects any change to `payload_hash`, `event_id`, `event_type`, `webhook_endpoint_id` or `organization_id`. It permits a change of `payload_json` in exactly one shape: old `body_state = 'PRESENT'`, new `body_state = 'ERASED'`, new `payload_json` null, old `status` terminal and unchanged. It rejects every change of an `ERASED` row's `body_state`, `payload_json`, erasure time, reason or reference. The transition is one-way in the trigger itself, whoever the caller is. |
| PBR-05 [7I] | **Reachable only through the erasure function.** No runtime role holds `UPDATE` on the relation (`063_5I`, `109_5B7`; INV-05). The body-erasure function of IR-21 is the only `SECURITY DEFINER` function that sets `body_state`, and it is granted to the maintenance principal and the restore reconciler only. The trigger takes no flag and no argument that asserts authority (PRV-18). |
| PBR-06 [7I] | **Serializer.** The 6J §23.2 serializer emits `payload_json: null` when `body_state = 'ERASED'` and never substitutes a placeholder. It emits the stored body otherwise. `body_state` and the erasure time are not added to the tenant DTO by 7I; whether to expose them is part of APF-03. |
| PBR-07 [7I] | **Replay refusal without reconstitution.** The superseding replay function (7H MR-7H-08) reads the parent row under its lock and refuses with the existing `422 WEBHOOK_REPLAY_NOT_ALLOWED` when `body_state = 'ERASED'`, before any insert. Independently, an insert that copied a null body into a `PRESENT` row would violate PBR-03. No function rebuilds a body from an event, a hash, a log or domain state (ERA-21). |
| PBR-08 [7I] | **Partitions.** Columns, the nullability change, the check and the row trigger are defined on the parent and apply to every existing and future partition. The migration walks `pg_inherits` and asserts, per partition, the column set, the validated check and the trigger; a partition attached later is brought to the same shape before `ATTACH`. |
| PBR-09 [7I] | **Signing and retry are unaffected.** A body is null only on a terminal row, and no attempt is ever made on a terminal row; the dispatcher's fenced load returns a body only for a held claim on a non-terminal row. The original bytes are intact for the whole active life of a delivery, as 5I INV-WH-04 intends. |
| PBR-10 [OD-7I-28] | **A sealed body** (SEAL-01) is a third value of `body_state`: `SEALED`, with `payload_json` and the preview null and the status terminal, coupled by the check of PBR-03 in the same way as `ERASED`. The trigger of PBR-04 permits `PRESENT → SEALED` and `SEALED → ERASED` only, the first through the sealing function and the second through the erasure function; `SEALED → PRESENT` is not expressible. The serializer emits `payload_json: null` as in PBR-06, and replay is refused as in PBR-07. `body_state` is a column this document designs (PBR-02), not a frozen one. A tenant sees for a sealed body what it would have seen had the body been erased at the same limit. |
| PBR-11 [OD-7I-30] | **A body past its content deadline that is still `PRESENT`.** `body_state` records what a pass has done, not what the clock says. The serializer therefore never reads `payload_json` from the relation. It receives the body from the guarded read function (CAG-07) and emits `payload_json: null` and a null preview whenever that function returns none, whatever `body_state` is; the replay function refuses on the guard before it looks at `body_state` (CAG-05). No value is added to `body_state` for this condition, and a tenant cannot tell an expired body from a sealed or an erased one, as PBR-10 intends. |

Test: VT-64.

## 16. Provider Callback Data Security (OD-7I-03; closes HE-7I-7H-07)

The three callback routes and their ingress sequence are 7H §11 and are unchanged. Billing's `payment_webhook_receipts` contract (`102_5H2`) is preserved as it is and needs nothing from 7I.

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| CBI-01 [FROZEN] | Verification precedes every write. An unverified callback writes nothing (7H CBK-01). The tenant comes from platform-held state (CBK-03). |
| CBI-02 [7I] | **Classification of a processing-input schema.** Each adapter's closed schema is entered in the classification manifest. Permitted classes: `OPS` (normalized event kind, coded states), `PID` (the provider's reference to a platform call, connection or payment; provider timestamps; numeric measures), and `PII` **only** for the two numbers of a provider-originated inbound call, where the command cannot be built without them (7H CBK-15). Never: `SEN`, `SEC`, `FIN-P`, a raw payload, a signature, a token, media, a URL, free text. A schema with a field outside these classes is not admitted. |
| CBI-03 [OD] | **Encrypted at rest**, field-level, purpose `CALLBACK_INPUT`, under §12.1. The whole input is one encrypted record; its plaintext SHA-256 and the hash of the verified raw bytes are stored beside it. |
| CBI-04 [7I] | **Key ownership.** The organization's `CALLBACK_INPUT` KEK. The ingress workload can only obtain a wrapped data key; the callback-processing workload can unwrap (KEY-08). |
| CBI-05 [FROZEN] | **Write before acknowledgement.** Receipt and encrypted input commit in one transaction before the 2xx (7H CBK-04). If the input cannot be encrypted, the transaction does not commit and the route answers 5xx (§12.2). |
| CBI-06 [OD] | **Processing-only access.** The input relation has no table privilege for any role. It is returned only by the guarded processing claim, to the caller that won the claim, under that receipt's tenant context (PRV-11). It is decrypted in the processing workload's memory and is never logged, traced or exported. |
| CBI-07 [FROZEN] | **No raw provider payload** is retained by default (5I ADR-5I-010; 6J §40.4). OD-7I-03 does not change that. |
| CBI-08 [FROZEN] | **Recovery after a crash following the 2xx.** The sweep finds the stale receipt by a guarded cross-tenant function that returns identifiers only; the processor loads and decrypts the stored input and rebuilds the command (7H CBK-10). |
| CBI-09 [FROZEN] | **Terminal deletion.** The input is deleted in the transaction that moves the receipt to `PROCESSED` or `SKIPPED`. |
| CBI-10 [OD] | **`FAILED` diagnostic retention.** At most 7 days from the authoritative transition to terminal `FAILED`. Then erased by the maintenance principal's guarded function, promptly. Earlier under an erasure that is due; later only under a recorded hold. |
| CBI-11 [OD] | The 7-day clock never applies to a receipt that is not terminal. Such an input is owed work and is never deleted by age (7H CBK-18). |
| CBI-12 [OD] | **No tenant and no platform-admin read path.** `GET /inbound-webhook-events` returns the receipt's observability fields only (6J §40.2). `app_platform_admin` has no privilege on the input relation and no key-service permission for it. A diagnostic need within the 7 days is met by the processing workload's own category codes, not by a human reading the input. |
| CBI-13 [OD] | **Organization erasure** deletes that organization's inputs (7H CBK-20; ERA-17). A subject's erasure follows ERA-S10. |
| CBI-14 [7I] | **Audit.** The receipt row is the evidence of the callback (7H CBK-13). Erasure runs write one audit row per run with counts. Domain audit is written by processing, as frozen. |

Fault-injection requirements for this section are VT-45 and VT-49 (§28.3).
