## 17. Consent / DNC Applicability (closes HE-7I-7H-03)

### 17.1 Four different things

| Activity | What it is | Governed by |
|---|---|---|
| A telemarketing or campaign call | An outbound contact attempt to a person | Purpose- and channel-scoped consent; suppression and DNC; calling windows; evaluated at enqueue and again at dispatch (4I §6.3, §8.9; 6H) |
| Delivering an event to the tenant's own configured webhook | The platform passing the tenant's own data to a system the tenant designated | The tenant's configuration; the 19-topic catalogue; egress policy |
| Revealing customer data to an unrelated external party | A disclosure to someone the tenant did not designate | Not a platform function. No event path does it |
| Processing suppression and consent events internally | Internal facts consumed by internal contexts | 7B: EV-029 … EV-032, EV-088, EV-098 are internal-only |

### 17.2 Conclusion

**No consent- or DNC-dependent restriction applies to any of the 19 webhook topics.** The boundary and the evidence:

| Evidence | Source |
|---|---|
| The catalogue lists no condition on consent or suppression for any topic | 6J §19.1; 4F §8.4 |
| Consent is scoped to a purpose and a channel (`OUTBOUND_CALL` / `VOICE`, `MARKETING`, …). Delivery to the tenant's own system is not one of those purposes or channels | 4I §8.1, §8.2; 6G §20 |
| Suppression gates outbound contact attempts, at enqueue and at dispatch | 4I §8.8, §8.9 |
| 7H found no frozen contract conditioning a topic and defined no suppression rule | 7H ELG-07, §14.3 |
| Consent, DNC and suppression events themselves have no topic | 7B Rule G-1; 7H §5.2 |

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| CNS-01 [7I] | A change of a contact's consent or suppression state does not suppress, delay, cancel or alter any webhook delivery. 7I invents no rule that withholds webhooks when marketing consent is withdrawn. |
| CNS-02 [7I] | Equally, the tenant's ownership of the data is **not** treated as removing every purpose-limitation or sharing consideration. What the platform does about it technically: minimal projections (§11); personal fields only on the topics 6J names; no disclosure to anyone the tenant did not configure; egress policy (§18.4); erasure of retained bodies (§14, §15). Whether the tenant may lawfully send a given contact's data to a given receiver is the tenant's determination (4I §7.1). |
| CNS-03 [FROZEN] | Preserved unchanged: purpose-and-channel-scoped consent; append-only consent evidence (no update or delete; withdrawal is a new record); DNC and suppression authority; dispatch-time enforcement; auditable compliance changes (`SUPPRESSION_ADDED`, `SUPPRESSION_LIFTED`, `COMPLIANCE_POLICY_UPDATED`); tenant-specific compliance policy. |
| CNS-04 [7I] | Consent evidence and suppression records are not erased by contact erasure (6G §22.1). EV-032's fields are class `PID` and travel internally only (FLD-13 … FLD-15). |
| CNS-05 [7I] | An observed inconsistency is passed to 7L and not acted on: 4I §7.3 lists "Webhook" among the consumers of `compliance.consent_withdrawn` and `compliance.campaign_blocked`, and says a tenant "can opt in" to `compliance.eligibility_denied`; the governed 19-topic catalogue contains none of them (HE-7L-7I-04). Under 7A AUTH-02 the catalogue governs. No topic is added. |

### 17.3 Questions for legal review, not answered here

| ID | Question |
|---|---|
| LR-01 | Whether, for a given tenant and deployment, the tenant and the platform stand in the relationship ASM-05 assumes, and what that implies contractually |
| LR-02 | Whether delivering a contact's direct personal data (`lead.*`, `appointment.booked`) to a tenant-designated receiver needs any notice or consent basis beyond the tenant's own, in the tenant's jurisdiction and sector |
| LR-03 | Precedence between a preservation duty (a hold) and an erasure request, and the permitted duration of a hold; and, since OD-7I-28, what the organization and the platform owe when uncertain material is kept past its limit with no authorization (HLD-22) |
| LR-04 | Treatment of `actor_name` and similar values in immutable audit rows under an erasure request (5J ODD-5J-01, carried) |
| LR-05 | Acceptability of erased data persisting inside encrypted backups until backup retention ends, and inside transport until trimmed |
| LR-06 | Whether the approved retention figures (30 / 90 days, the 7-day tails, the 90-day material cap) meet any sector-specific minimum or maximum that applies to a given tenant |
| LR-07 | Telecom-regulatory obligations attaching to call-related event data (numbers, call records) and any statutory retention that would override an erasure |
| LR-08 | Incident-notification duties when event data is exposed, and their timelines |
| LR-09 | The privacy-incident procedure that an approaching or missed erasure deadline enters when the erasure journal is unavailable (JRN-29): who is notified, within what time, and what is recorded |
| LR-10 | The regulatory consequences of an unauthorized-retention incident (HLD-22; RR-10): whether and to whom it is notifiable, within what time, what the tenant as controller must be told, and what record is required. Recording the incident answers none of these |

No statutory deadline, effective date, approval or certification is asserted anywhere in this document.

## 18. India Residency and External Egress

### 18.1 Preserved

`STANDARD`, `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` and `REGIONAL`; the abstract `RegionRef`; the contracted `ResidencyScope` (`PRIMARY_DATABASE`, `CACHE`, `OBJECT_STORAGE`, `RECORDINGS`, `BACKUPS`, `LOGS`, `ANALYTICS`, `VECTOR_STORE`); no global cross-region event bus (4I §9; 7A §32). No region name appears in this document. The frozen regional topology is not modified.

### 18.2 Two cases that are not the same

| | **Data stored or processed outside the region** | **Tenant-directed delivery to an external destination** |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides | The platform's deployment | The tenant, by configuring an endpoint or installing a plugin |
| What it is | A platform-held copy | A transfer the tenant instructed, to a system the tenant chose |
| Covered by the residency commitment | Yes: every platform-held copy stays in region | No: it is outside the platform's stores; it must never be described as in-region storage |
| Control | Region tags; deployment conformance | Contract authorization; egress policy; all egress security controls |

### 18.3 Matrix 10 — Regionality by store

For an `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` organization. "In region" means the contracted region resolved from `RegionRef` by infrastructure configuration.

| ID | Store or path | Rule | Enforcement point | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RSY-01 | PostgreSQL primary and replicas | In region | Deployment; region tag of the database | VT-40 |
| RSY-02 | Relay, consumers, dispatcher, sweeper, maintenance, tooling | Each carries a region tag for its database and its transport and refuses to start if they differ (7D RES-7D-02 pattern, extended to every worker) | Startup check | VT-40 |
| RSY-03 | Redis (durable and SIGNAL), including persistence files and PEL state | In region; no cross-region replica carries stream keys (7E RSD-03, RSD-04) | Deployment | VT-40 |
| RSY-04 | Outbox; recovery ledger and all six components; replay material | In region; one ledger per region (7G RSD-7G-03) | Same database | VT-40 |
| RSY-05 | Webhook delivery rows, bodies, history records, fan-out claims, lineage anchors | In region (7H RES-7H-01) | Same database | VT-40 |
| RSY-06 | Callback receipts and processing inputs | In region | Same database | VT-40 |
| RSY-07 | Object storage and backups | In region; backup target and backup-encryption key in region. 3F §11 describes a weekly snapshot "replicated to secondary region"; for an `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` organization that replica is permitted only inside the contracted region, which is a 7K deployment item (HE-7K-7I-06) | Deployment (7K) | Restore-drill evidence |
| RSY-08 | Key service and secret manager | Keys and secrets of the organization exist only in region (KEY-05) | Key-service and secret-manager configuration | VT-40 |
| RSY-09 | Operator access and tooling | The tooling runs in region. An operator's workstation may be elsewhere; what reaches it is the redacted view, and unmasked material only under §13.5. Whether unmasked viewing from outside the region is itself a transfer is LR-06-adjacent and is recorded as a contract item (HE-7L-7I-06) | Tooling deployment; MAT rules | VT-24 |
| RSY-10 | Audit rows | In region with the database; cold archive in region | Deployment | VT-40 |
| RSY-11 | Logs, traces, metrics | In region (`LOGS` is a residency scope item). They carry no payload (RED-01), so a telemetry sink is never a path for event content | Sink configuration (7J, 7K) | HE-7J-7I-02 |
| RSY-12 | Egress path and proxy | In region regardless of where the destination is (7H RES-7H-02) | Deployment (7K) | VT-41 |

| RSY-14 | The residency profile itself (`data_residency_profile`, `region_ref`) | Fixed in the transaction that creates the organization. A non-default pair only by the governed provisioning change, in a deployment whose conformance with RSY-01 … RSY-13 is recorded; unwritable at runtime; never updated; no existing organization converted (CRF-01 … CRF-15) | Column privileges; triggers; provisioning creation function | VT-101, VT-102, VT-115, VT-116 |

Rows: 14.

### 18.4 Outbound destination policy (OD-7I-04; closes HE-7I-7H-04)

| Alternative | Security | Usability | Contractual | Implementation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strict in-region-only destinations | Strongest on paper; no reliable technical test of "in region" exists | Breaks most hosted receivers | Simple promise that cannot be verified | Needs attested host lists |
| Tenant-directed transfers under contract | Relies on contract and on existing egress controls | Unrestricted | Must state plainly that delivery is not storage residency | None beyond a server-held permission |
| **Per-tenant policy: tenant-directed under contract, plus an enterprise lock (decided)** | Adds a real, enforceable host restriction where a contract requires it | Unrestricted by default; restricted where contracted | Two clear statements | A policy store and enforcement, future |

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| EGR-01 [OD] | **Mode 1 — tenant-directed.** A tenant-configured webhook or plugin destination, including one outside the contracted region, is permitted only where the organization's contract and transfer permissions authorize it. For a `STANDARD` organization that is the default. For an `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` organization it requires a server-held, platform-set permission recorded on the organization's egress policy; without it the organization has no outbound webhook or plugin egress. The profile this rule reads is written by no runtime role (§8.11; OD-7I-22), so it cannot be downgraded to obtain the default. |
| EGR-02 [OD] | A tenant-directed delivery is never represented, in product, contract or documentation, as storage or processing inside the region. |
| EGR-03 [OD] | **Mode 2 — enterprise egress lock.** The platform may lock an organization to an approved set of destination hosts. The lock is a platform-controlled contractual security policy: set and changed only through a platform-side guarded operation; not visible as an editable setting to, and not bypassable by, any tenant administrator. |
| EGR-04 [OD] | The policy applies identically to webhook destinations and plugin destinations. It does not apply to provider callbacks (inbound), telephony or other separately governed network boundaries, which are unchanged. |
| EGR-05 [OD] | **Enforced twice.** At configuration time (endpoint create, `PATCH` of `target_url`, enable; plugin installation and activation), and at **every** network request by the egress adapter, against the policy in force at that moment. A destination edit, a retry, an internal replay or a public replay cannot bypass it: each ends in a request, and each request is checked. |
| EGR-06 [OD] | Every existing egress control stays in force in both modes: `https` only, address blocking, resolve-then-pin, TLS verification against the hostname, no redirect following, port 443 for webhooks (7H §14.4). The lock is an additional restriction, never a relaxation. |
| EGR-07 [OD] | **A host allow-list is not proof of where the recipient's data resides.** The platform makes no residency statement about a destination, and IP geolocation is never used as a compliance guarantee. |
| EGR-08 [7I] | **Outcomes use the frozen vocabulary.** A request refused by policy is a failed attempt `DESTINATION_BLOCKED`, `NOT_SENT`, origin `DESTINATION`, with an internal rule code identifying the policy (7H HTP-19; the rule code is internal, TVF-02). A configuration refused by policy is the existing `422 WEBHOOK_URL_UNSAFE`. No public error code and no closure category is added. For plugins the refusal is the existing normalized egress failure class of 6J §35.2. Whether a distinct tenant-facing code would serve tenants better is API follow-up APF-01. |
| EGR-09 [OD] | **Server-authoritative.** The policy is read from platform state by the adapter. No request parameter, header, endpoint field or plugin manifest value can set or widen it. |
| EGR-10 [OD] | **Audit.** A policy change writes an audit row in its own transaction: organization, old and new mode, count of hosts, actor, reason reference. It carries no URL path or query. A refused configuration writes the existing endpoint or plugin action with outcome `FAILURE`. A refused request is evidenced by its closure record and a security signal; it is not audited per attempt, to avoid an audit flood from a retrying delivery. Hosts are recorded; paths, queries, secrets and payloads never are. |
| EGR-11 [OD] | **Not implemented and not to be claimed.** The policy store, the permission of EGR-01 and the lock of EGR-03 do not exist. No strict destination-lock commitment is activated or marketed for any tenant until the enforcement is implemented, verified and approved (AB-7I-07). Until the permission of EGR-01 exists, no `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` organization's outbound webhook or plugin egress is enabled in production (AB-7I-06). |
| EGR-12 [7I] | The policy store needs a governed migration and a platform-side administration surface; 6J classifies a host allow-list as FUTURE (J2). Both are recorded as IR-27, IR-28 and API follow-up APF-04, and the capacity cost of a per-request policy read is handed to 7K (HE-7K-7I-05). |

## 19. Audit Integrity and Recovery

### 19.1 Three kinds of record

| Kind | What it is | Durability | Is it audit evidence? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Synchronous audit** | A row written by `audit.fn_insert_audit_event()` in the transaction of the change | Commits or rolls back with the change | Yes |
| **Mandatory asynchronous audit** | A mandatory audit written after commit | — | **This category is empty.** OD-7D-02 = A moved all 84 `AUDIT_ASYNC` routes and every worker-origin mandatory audit into the originating transaction (7D §36) |
| **Operational evidence** | Delivery rows, history records, receipts, execution rows, case history | Durable, with its own retention | Evidence of processing, not an accountability record |
| **Observability logs** | Logs, traces, metrics | Best-effort | **No** |

### 19.2 Rules

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| AUD-7I-01 [FROZEN] | Every mandatory audit record is written inside the originating PostgreSQL transaction. An audit failure rolls the change back (7A AUD-03; 7D AUD-7D-01, AUD-7D-07). |
| AUD-7I-02 [7I] | **7I introduces no asynchronous audit.** Every action this document adds is audited in the transaction of its state change, or, for a read, before its result is released (AUD-7I-06). |
| AUD-7I-03 [FROZEN] | The only write path is `audit.fn_insert_audit_event()`. No role has insert, update or delete on audit tables (`072_5J`). The hash chain is computed nightly and is not a write-time control (5J §15). |
| AUD-7I-04 [7I] | **Content of a recovery audit row** (closes HE-7I-7G-04): actor identity and type; capability used; operation identity and mode; plan fingerprint; reason code and ticket reference; source and target scope; candidate counts; outcome. For an approval, the approver and the assertion reference. Never a payload, material, a secret, or free text with tenant data (7G AUT-05). |
| AUD-7I-05 [7I] | **Scope of an audit row.** An action on a case with a trusted organization is a tenant-scoped audit event written under that organization's context, so it is attributable to the tenant's data; whether a tenant may read it follows 6L and DEC-6M-03. An action on a platform-scoped or untrusted case is a platform event. |
| AUD-7I-06 [OD-7I-07] | **Audit before release.** For an unmasked material view and for a destination-fingerprint verification, the audit row commits first and the result is produced only afterwards. A crash between the two leaves an audit row for an access that did not happen, never an access without a row. |
| AUD-7I-07 [7I] | **Refusals are audited** (OPA-14). A refusal has no state change to share a transaction with, so its audit row is written in its own transaction before the refusal is returned. If that fails, the action stays refused. |
| AUD-7I-08 [7I] | **Bulk system actions** are audited once per run and per organization, with counts and identity ranges: cancellation sweeps (7H §14.6), purges, body erasures, material erasures, input erasures. Never per row, and never with content. |
| AUD-7I-09 [7I] | **Not audited per occurrence, by design:** an ordinary delivery attempt (its history records are the evidence); a consumer's tenant-scope mismatch (it produces a recovery case and a security signal); a delivery-time egress refusal (closure record and signal). These are evidence and signals. They are not relied on as audit. |
| AUD-7I-10 [7I] | **The platform-event caller list is a schema gap.** `fn_insert_audit_event` accepts a platform-scoped event only from sessions of `app_worker` or `app_platform_admin` (`072_5J`). The new principals of §7.3 would be refused. A guarded function running as its owner does not help, because the check is on `session_user`. The governed migration therefore supersedes the function with one whose caller list names exactly the principals that have a platform-scoped action to record (IR-15). Until then no operation of §13 can write its audit row, and therefore cannot run (AB-7I-03). |

### 19.3 Proof that no mandatory audit is lost after a crash

The case to exclude is: business commit, then a process crash before a broker enqueue.

1. A mandatory audit that depended on a post-commit enqueue would be lost in that case (7A FM-13).
2. Frozen 7D §36 leaves no such audit: every one is written by the function inside the transaction that commits the change (AUD-7D-01, AUD-7D-02).
3. Every action added by 7I is covered by AUD-7I-02: same transaction, or commit-before-release.
4. Therefore, for every mandatory audit, either the change and its audit both committed, or neither did. No point exists between them at which a crash could separate them.
5. What remains is conformance: the 84 routes must actually be implemented that way and the documents that still print "Async" must be aligned (7D IO-7D-16). That is an implementation dependency already frozen as a blocker for those routes; it is restated as AB-7I-03 (d) for the event operations of this document.

This is an architectural argument from frozen rules. No runtime test of it was executed.

## 20. Security Failure Scenarios

### 20.1 Principle

**Fail closed, and never by turning a valid durable obligation into a terminal failure.** Where a check cannot be made, the operation is not performed and the obligation stays where it is: pending in the stream, `PENDING` in a delivery row, `RECEIVED` in a receipt, `PARKED` in the ledger.

### 20.2 Matrix 13 — Failure modes

| # | Failure | Safe outcome | What is **not** done | Recovery mechanism | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FS-01 | PostgreSQL unavailable | No handler runs; no `XACK`; no delivery is claimed; callbacks answer 5xx | No acknowledgement on assumption; no in-memory substitute for the ledger | Entries stay pending and are redelivered (7G FC-10); claims lapse and are released by the sweep | VT-57 |
| FS-02 | Redis unavailable | Publication stops with rows `PENDING` / `CLAIMED`; consumers idle; plugin callouts refused (7H PLG-15) | No direct delivery around the transport; no limiter bypass | Outbox drains when Redis returns (7D §25) | VT-57 |
| FS-03 | Secret manager unavailable | Webhook attempts end `SECRET_UNAVAILABLE`, `NOT_SENT`; plugin callouts fail normalized; endpoint URL changes refused if the evidence key is unreachable | Nothing sent unsigned; no cached secret beyond the attempt | Frozen retry schedule | VT-57 |
| FS-04 | A data key or KEK temporarily unavailable | §12.2: parking not attempted; receipt not committed; replay and callback processing paused; material view denied | No plaintext storage; no acknowledgement without stored material | Retried when the key service returns | VT-45 |
| FS-05 | Worker crash during tenant-context setup | The transaction never commits; the setting dies with it | No statement runs before the assertion of step 4 (TCX-03) | Redelivery | VT-03 |
| FS-06 | Worker crash after a privileged read | Whatever was read existed only in that process's memory; nothing was written | No partial effect | Redelivery; a claim lapses | VT-03 |
| FS-07 | Replay submitted while the requester's capability is being revoked | The request is checked under the grant's row lock: it either precedes the revocation and is then stopped at approval or at execution (OPA-10), or follows it and is refused | No execution on a capability that was valid only at request time | OPA-12 | VT-23 |
| FS-08 | Erasure request arrives during a consumer retry | The entry is redelivered and the handler sees the tombstoned owner state; its true result is recorded | No acknowledgement, park or resolution caused by the erasure | ERA-S3 | VT-46 |
| FS-09 | Erasure request arrives during an HTTP send | The send completes or fails as any attempt. The body is erased in the transaction that makes the row terminal | No aborted request; no body erased under a claim | ERA-S7 | VT-47 |
| FS-10 | A recovery item is awaiting authorization | The case stays `PARKED`; its material is retained inside its limits; an expiring approval lapses | No execution; no automatic approval | A new approval | VT-21 |
| FS-11 | Audit write fails, or the process crashes before any enqueue | The change rolls back (same transaction). Nothing was enqueued for audit, because nothing is | No unaudited change; no audit "later" | The caller retries the whole operation | VT-30, VT-31 |
| FS-12 | Object-storage deletion partially fails | The owner's reference is already cleared (frozen best-effort step); the object is an orphan | Not reported as fully erased | Orphan reconciliation (ERA-22); the erasure step stays open (ERA-23) | VT-52 |
| FS-13 | A destination is found, after DNS resolution, to be outside what the egress policy permits, or to resolve to a blocked address | `DESTINATION_BLOCKED`, `NOT_SENT`; one attempt spent | No connection; no "good address" picked from a mixed answer | Frozen schedule; tenant corrects the endpoint | VT-41, VT-42 |
| FS-14 | A plugin returns sensitive content, a credential or an organization identifier | The response is data returned to the invoking node, capped and normalized; previews are sanitized (PVW-07); no field is used as an identifier, permission or credential | No privilege change; nothing forwarded to another tenant | — | VT-58 |
| FS-15 | An envelope with forged tenant information | If the payload organization differs from the envelope: contract-invalid, parked. If a referenced resource is not visible: handler failure, no effect | No "repair" of the organization; no cross-tenant lookup | Recovery case; security signal | VT-02 |
| FS-16 | Material view without the required permission or approval | No output; the denial is audited | No masked-to-unmasked fallback; no partial bytes | A proper approval | VT-24 |
| FS-17 | KEK rotation during a recovery | Stored records name their KEK version and stay readable (KEY-10) | No re-encryption race; no failed replay because of rotation | — | VT-45 |
| FS-18 | A retention purge and a replay run concurrently | The purge and the replay both lock the row (and, for webhooks, the lineage anchor). One wins. A replay that finds the body erased is refused; a purge that finds a replay open skips the row | No replay of an erased body; no purge of a row a replay just read | Lock order of 7H ADM-04, to which the erasure function conforms (IR-21) | VT-47 |
| FS-19 | A hold is introduced during an erasure | Completed steps stand; unstarted steps do not start; the request shows what was erased | No reversal claimed; no silent continuation | HLD-04 | VT-53 |
| FS-20 | A malformed or unknown classification value | The manifest does not load; the dependent producer or serializer does not start | No default to a lower class | Corrected manifest, redeploy | VT-14 |
| FS-21 | Day-83 re-validation job crashes or runs twice | The result is appended once per run; an equal second result is harmless; no state changed | No disposition by the job | Next scheduled run | VT-50 |
| FS-22 | Day 90 reached while a disposition is in progress | The row lock serializes them: either the disposition commits first and the material follows MRL-12, or the erasure commits first and the disposition then fails DAU-09 and is refused | No rejection without re-validation | MRL-14 | VT-51 |
| FS-23 | The erasure function crashes midway through a lineage | Each row's erasure is its own short transaction; erased rows stay erased, the rest are picked up by the next run | No half-erased row | Idempotent rerun | VT-47 |
| FS-24 | An ACL parity check fails on a Redis node | The node takes no traffic | No worker connects to a node with a divergent ACL set | Re-apply the governed set | VT-19 |
| FS-25 | Every stream gateway instance is unavailable | Consumers idle; entries stay pending and pin the trim watermark; publication continues | No direct Redis access by a consumer; no acknowledgement on assumption; no publication blocked | Gateway returns; workers read again; the sweep reclaims idle entries | VT-73 |
| FS-26 | The gateway crashes after committing an accounting row and before `XACK` | The entry is still pending; it is redelivered and takes the duplicate path; the accounting insert is a no-op | No second effect; no lost obligation | 7F XAK-09; GWY-11 | VT-71 |
| FS-27 | A group's entry is acknowledged, or read with `NOACK`, with no durable evidence (gateway defect or compromise, Redis regression, break-glass) | The outbox row is held by the interlock; once the group's trim bound passes it the pair is an unaccounted obligation; the row is captured and a `PARKED` class `V` case opened | No handler outcome invented; no row cleaned up; no rejection possible | R2 through the owner's handler (ACC-05) | VT-72 |
| FS-28 | The obligation reconciler does not run | `PUBLISHED` rows are held past 7 days; alert on watermark age | No cleanup of an unaccounted row | Next run | VT-72 |
| FS-29 | The erasure journal is unavailable when an erasure is due | The step waits at `INTENT_REQUESTED`; nothing is erased; the open step is visible | No erasure without a durable intent; no completion reported | Journal returns; the step resumes | VT-67 |
| FS-30 | Crash after a journal `INTENT` is durable, before the erasure transaction commits; or the transaction aborts | The step is `INTENT_DURABLE` and owed; it is retried with authorization re-checked, or withdrawn with a reference | No `COMPLETED` record; no deletion that is no longer authorized | JRN-08 | VT-67 |
| FS-31 | Crash, or loss of the database, after the erasure transaction commits and before `COMPLETED` is journaled | The pending intent is completed by the reconciler from `ERASED`; after a database loss it is re-applied on restore | No erasure forgotten by a restore | JRN-09 | VT-66, VT-67 |
| FS-32 | A database is recovered to an earlier point and the journal is unreachable, has a gap, fails authentication, or the backup predates journal coverage | The environment stays quarantined; no workload starts | No partial activation; no override | Repair the journal access or choose an eligible backup | VT-68 |
| FS-33 | The cost port returns a result with basis `PROVIDER_COST`, or with no basis | Outcome row and EV-097 carry `null` cost and `null` ROI; a non-null value is rejected by PV-7I-01 and the transaction rolls back | No provider-derived figure in a row, an outbox payload or a stream | The outcome is recomputed when a billed-basis port exists | VT-69 |
| FS-34 | Key retirement is requested while a held record, an open operation or a restorable backup still references the version | Refused by the reference check; the version stays decrypt-only | No destruction that strands a record or defeats a hold | KEY-19 | VT-65 |
| FS-35 | The relay crashes after claiming rows | The rows stay `CLAIMED` and are reclaimed after the lease timeout by the next claim, as `077_5J1` specifies; a late mark by the crashed worker is a no-op | No change to 7D recovery semantics; no second principal needed to recover | 7D claim and lease rules, unchanged | VT-60 |
| FS-36 | The platform authorization issuer, or the key relation's current key version, is unavailable | No platform or tenant lifecycle transition happens; the organization keeps its committed status; deliveries are admitted or held by that status | No fallback to the frozen three-argument call, to the session setting alone, or to a direct `UPDATE` | The request is retried when the issuer returns; a suspension that must not wait is an incident for the operating organization, not an unproven call | VT-99 |
| FS-37 | An organization-erasure step is due while the journal is unreachable, a hold is active, the approval has expired, or the audit insert fails | The erasure does not run; the operation stays `APPROVED` or moves to `EXPIRED`; a failed audit insert rolls the mutation back | No unjournaled, unaudited or unapproved anonymization | Retry under JRN-09; a fresh approval after expiry; release of the hold | VT-105, VT-106 |
| FS-38 | A residency provisioning change runs with the deployment-conformance record absent, stale or naming a region other than the contracted one; or with an owner user that does not exist or is not `ACTIVE`; or fails at any statement | Nothing is created: no organization, membership, event or audit row; the authorization stays unconsumed | No organization set ahead of the infrastructure; no `ACTIVE` organization without its profile; no conversion of an existing organization | Complete the deployment conformance and run the change again with the same authorization | VT-115, VT-116 |
| FS-39 | A tenant places a request hold while the journal is unreachable | The hold function fails; the request is not `ON_HOLD`; no erasure can commit either, because every erasure needs the journal (INV-23) | No `ON_HOLD` without its registry row; no unjournaled hold | The tenant retries; a hold placed after the journal returns precedes any erasure that then runs, by the gate | VT-114 |
| FS-40 | A request hold's subject matches no contact, several contacts, or a `subject_contact_id` that names no row | The hold commits with the contact set the resolver returned (empty, or several) and its keys; rows of other subjects erase on their clocks; a row that later carries one of the keys is held from its own commit | No refusal of the hold; no pending or "unresolved" hold; no organization-wide pause | None needed. An empty contact set is reported to operators as an indicator, not as a failure | VT-113, VT-117 |
| FS-41 | A status and the registry are found to disagree (a request `ON_HOLD` with no `REQUEST` hold, or the reverse) | That request is treated as a hold scoped, at that moment, from its own subject fields (HLD-11 e); integrity alarm | No erasure on the less restrictive reading; no organization-wide pause | Investigation; the pairing is restored through the guarded functions | VT-113 |
| FS-42 | An uncertain row reaches its retention limit while a request hold it is assessed against exists, and nobody has recorded a decision | The row is not erased and no hold is released. Compromised: rotate, re-derive, keep verifying | Reading a missing key as "no match"; retiring a version that edges still use | The key is restored; rotation; retirement only at zero references | VT-128 |

No reviewer: nothing is decided, and the incident records the cause | Automatic renewal; a scheduled exception; a single-person decision; a decision dated before it was taken | A decision by two people when they are available | VT-131 |

### 21.2 Protections confirmed

### 21.3 No tenant surface for internal recovery

There is no route, DTO, webhook topic, WebSocket message or export that returns a recovery case, an observation, an operation, a history entry or material to a tenant principal (7G TEN-7G-07). The only tenant-visible trace of the recovery system is the audit row of MAT-06 and tenant-scoped recovery audit rows, which name an action and a purpose category and nothing about the case.

### 22.2 What 7I does not claim

No role, function, column, trigger, ACL user, key, policy record or worker described in §6 – §21 exists unless §22.1 marks it **EXISTS**. A reader must not infer from a rule's present tense that anything was built.

---

## 23. Implementation and Migration Requirements

A register of logical requirements. It is not a migration. Names, DDL, signatures and the migration number are chosen by the governed migration and its owner; no migration 113 is created or named here. Kinds: **SQL** (governed PostgreSQL migration), **REDIS** (ACL and provisioning configuration), **APP** (application authorization or behaviour), **KEY** (key-management integration), **AUD** (audit or observability dependency), **POL** (policy or legal prerequisite).

VT-146 … VT-149 pass. **Opening this gate for a `FROM_T0` organization does not remove RR-11** |

OD-7I-13 … OD-7I-15 were raised during the first freeze-gate remediation, for the three findings whose correction needed a retention, availability or contract trade-off the frozen sources do not settle. OD-7I-23 … OD-7I-25 were put to the owner in the same way on 2026-10-11 during the fourth remediation; the owner chose option A for each and confirmed in writing with numbered conditions, mapped below. Open owner decisions: **0**.

### OD-7I-01 — Lifetime of replayed webhook body copies — **decided: lineage body erasure**

1. 7H left the retention, erasure and lineage purge of replay copies to 7I and blocked replay activation on it (LIN-04; AB-7H-08).
2. 6J §22.6, §23.3; `063_5I`, `101_5I1`; 7H OD-7H-10, OD-7H-14, LIN-01 … LIN-05; 5I INV-WH-04.
3. **A.** Body erased at root + 30 / 90 + 7 days once the row is terminal; metadata keeps its per-row retention.
4. **B.** Keep the per-row rule and approve 120 / 180 days.
5. **C.** Delete whole replay rows at the lineage deadline. (A fourth, per-lineage key destruction with an external body store, was analysed in §15.1 and not offered: highest complexity for no additional benefit in V1.)
6. A and C bound personal data in bodies; B leaves it up to 180 days.
7. None affects delivery. A adds one cleanup pass.
8. A and B keep 90 days of dead-letter diagnostics for replays; C loses most of it.
9. A: marker, function, reconciled trigger, erratum. B: none. C: a changed purge predicate and an erratum to frozen retention.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied: windows and per-row metadata retention preserved (LBE-03, LBE-04); a non-terminal body never erased (LBE-05, ERA-11); prompt erasure once eligible (LBE-07); evidence preserved (LBE-11); earlier erasure, holds and idempotence across all copies (LBE-08 … LBE-10); schema changes identified (IR-21); trigger reconciled (LBE-12); erratum recorded (ERR-7I-01); migration, worker, backup and verification as activation requirements (AB-7I-05).

### OD-7I-02 — `CANCELLED` delivery retention — **decided: metadata 90 days, body 30 days**

1. `CANCELLED` rows had no retention and were never purged (7H §13.4, HE-7I-7H-05).
2. 5I §13; 6J §22.6; 7H OD-7H-02, T-10, T-11.
3. **A.** Metadata and history 90 days from cancellation; body at most 30 days.
4. **B.** 90 days including the body.
5. **C.** 30 days including the body.
6. A removes personal data from an unreplayable body soonest while keeping evidence.
7. None.
8. A and B give a tenant 90 days to ask why deliveries were cancelled; C gives 30.
9. A: two predicates (IR-22). B, C: one.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: state and replay prohibition preserved; reason and evidence kept; no replay from a metadata-only row (RET-07); idempotent, tenant-isolated cleanup (ERA-16); earlier erasure applies; distinct clocks (RET-06, RET-07); no new state or route.

### OD-7I-03 — `FAILED` callback processing input — **decided: 7 days**

1. 7H CBK-18 left the diagnostic period after `FAILED` to 7I.
2. 7H OD-7H-08, CBK-15 … CBK-20; 6J §40.4; 5I ADR-5I-010.
3. **A.** 7 days.
4. **B.** 30 days.
5. **C.** Delete at failure.
6. Shorter is less exposure of numbers and provider facts; all options are encrypted.
7. None.
8. None; no tenant surface.
9. A timestamp and an erasure function (IR-23).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**, matching the frozen 7-day TTL of the optional raw-payload debug store. Conditions applied: clock from the terminal transition (CBI-10); encryption (CBI-03); processing-only access (CBI-06); no tenant or administrator read (CBI-12); never logged; holds; never for non-terminal receipts (CBI-11); delete on `PROCESSED` / `SKIPPED` preserved (CBI-09); recovery and no-raw-payload preserved (CBI-07, CBI-08).

### OD-7I-04 — Destinations outside the region — **decided: tenant-directed under contract, plus an enterprise lock**

1. No frozen source says whether an `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` tenant's destination may be outside the region (7H RES-7H-02).
2. 4I §9; 7A §32; 7H §14.4, RES-7H-01, RES-7H-02; 6J §30.3, J2.
3. **A.** Tenant-directed transfers permitted.
4. **B.** Strict in-region only.
5. **C.** Tenant-directed, plus a platform-set host lock for a specific tenant.
6. B is strongest on paper and unverifiable in practice; C adds an enforceable restriction.
7. C adds a policy read per request (7K).
8. B breaks most hosted receivers; A and C do not.
9. C needs a policy store and enforcement (IR-27, IR-28) and an administration surface (APF-04).
10. Recommended: A. **Chosen by the owner: C**, with conditions applied: Mode 1 only where the contract authorizes it, with a server-held permission for `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` (EGR-01); never represented as residency (EGR-02); platform-controlled and not bypassable (EGR-03, EGR-09); both destination kinds (EGR-04); configuration and every request (EGR-05); existing controls kept (EGR-06); no residency inference from hosts or geolocation (EGR-07); audited without URLs or payloads (EGR-10); a future capability, not to be claimed or marketed (EGR-11; AB-7I-06, AB-7I-07).

### OD-7I-05 — Requester ≠ approver — **decided: hard, no override**

1. 7G AUT-04 said the approver SHOULD differ and left enforcement to 7I.
2. 7G §40, §41, AUT-02 … AUT-06.
3. **A.** Hard control, no override.
4. **B.** Hard with a time-boxed emergency self-approval.
5. **C.** Advisory.
6. A removes solo high-risk replay; B's override is the control most likely to be abused.
7. A can delay an incident recovery until a second person is reachable; nothing is lost meanwhile.
8. None.
9. Approval records and identity comparison in the ledger (IR-11); a roster (IR-32).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: different authenticated humans, across roles and sessions (OPA-07); no override; re-validation at approval and execution (OPA-10); binding to the immutable plan (OPA-08); stale or mismatched approvals refused; full audit (AUD-7I-04); 7G restrictions preserved; roster (OPA-18); no alternate path (OPA-16).

### OD-7I-06 — Erasure touching an unresolved case — **decided: erase PII-bearing material when due**

1. 7G PRT-06 fixed that erasure never resolves an obligation and left to 7I which material is erased and when.
2. 7G RPM-12, PRT-06, T-13; 6G §22.1; 4I §9.3.
3. **A.** Material with direct personal data erased when erasure is due; identifier-only material kept until resolution.
4. **B.** All linked material erased at once.
5. **C.** A 72-hour resolve-first window, then erase.
6. A and B remove direct personal data at once; C holds it 72 hours longer.
7. B forces more reconciliations; A the fewest for the same privacy effect.
8. None directly.
9. Classification by type (CLS-03); step ledger and aggregate reference (IR-24); erasure function (IR-25).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: holds and retention exceptions (HLD); 7G semantics preserved (ERA-03, ERA-12); `RECONCILIATION_PENDING` with `PRIVACY_MATERIAL_ERASED`; minimum metadata kept (ERA-01); identifiers classified by re-identification risk (ERA-02; `PID`); erasure is not success or rejection; dependent replay disabled (ERA-09); hand-off to the owner; idempotent and recoverable (ERA-05); backups and copies (ERA-19, ERA-20); no indefinite exception (OD-7I-09).

### OD-7I-07 — Plaintext access to replay material — **decided: redacted default, dual-control plaintext**

1. 7G AUT-07 separated material view from metadata and left its control to 7I.
2. 7G RPM-11, AUT-07; 6M DEC-6M-03.
3. **A.** Redacted by default; unmasked under a second approver, a ticket and a time-boxed per-case grant.
4. **B.** Single operator, audited.
5. **C.** No plaintext in V1.
6. A prevents one operator reading tenant personal data alone; C prevents all reading.
7. C makes value-dependent defects hard to diagnose.
8. A adds a tenant-visible audit entry per unmasked access.
9. View grants, view service, key-service policy (IR-12, IR-18).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: MAT-01 … MAT-11 one for one.

### OD-7I-08 — Tenant-visible failure detail — **decided: category and origin**

1. 7H left to 7I whether platform-side categories and the secret role are tenant-safe.
2. 7H HTP-14, HTP-19; 6J §23.
3. **A.** Category and origin.
4. **B.** Also the secret role.
5. **C.** One generic platform-error code.
6. B discloses secret-store state; C discloses least.
7. None.
8. A lets a tenant tell a receiver fault from a platform fault; C does not.
9. A DTO allow-list; APF-02.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: TVF-01 … TVF-05; RED-12; no change to public codes or routes.

### OD-7I-09 — Maximum material lifetime, case unresolved — **decided: 90 days from parking**

1. OD-7I-06 forbids an indefinite exception; frozen 7G keeps material while a case is non-terminal and never ages a case out.
2. 7G RPM-10, RPM-12, PRT-02, PRT-06; 7F §31.
3. **A.** 90 days.
4. **B.** 180 days.
5. **C.** 30 days.
6. Shorter is less parked personal data.
7. A converts some replayable events of state-guarded consumers into reconciliations (MRL-03); C does so for Billing and Analytics too.
8. None.
9. Erasure function and alert (IR-25).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: 7G invariants preserved through RPM-12 (MRL-02, MRL-07); a minimization limit, not an entitlement and not a closure (§14.5); clocks distinguished; the trade-off stated (MRL-03); earlier erasure and holds (HLD-05); cases never deleted by age (RET-11); erratum recorded (ERR-7I-03); shared material protected (MRL-08).

### OD-7I-10 — Material after resolution — **decided: 7 days**

1. 7G RPM-10 allows up to the metadata's 90 days and lets 7I shorten it.
2. 7G RPM-10, PCL-02, PCL-03, T-18, BKL-14.
3. **A.** 7 days.
4. **B.** Erase at resolution.
5. **C.** 90 days with the metadata.
6. A and B remove payloads that are no longer needed.
7. B leaves no window to examine a wrong resolution.
8. None.
9. Erasure function with a reference interlock (IR-25).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: clock from `resolved_at` (MRL-05); metadata keeps 90 days; reference interlock with a bounded path (ERA-15); earlier erasure and holds; idempotent and crash-safe (ERA-12); backfill captures fresh material (MRL-06); storage, keys, replicas, backups (§12, ERA-19, ERA-20); no recreation (ERA-21); cleanup verification (HE-7J-7I-08).

### OD-7I-11 — `CONSUMER_UNIDENTIFIED` at the limit — **decided: re-validate, reject only if permanence is proven**

1. After erasure at the cap, 7G offers no way to close such a case: rejection needs the erased bytes (DAU-09).
2. 7G §10, §19 PID-05, §24.4, DAU-03, DAU-06 … DAU-09, IMP-07.
3. **A.** Re-validate at day 83; reject only on proof.
4. **B.** Erase; two operators close later using the digest.
5. **C.** Exempt from the cap until reviewed.
6. A keeps the frozen proof rule; B weakens it; C extends retention of unknown bytes.
7. A needs a scheduled job and a human disposition in a 7-day window.
8. None.
9. Job and result record (IR-25, IR-14).
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: 7G class-`I` rules preserved; governed re-validation (MRL-09); success routes to R2 (MRL-10); a decoder failure alone is not proof (MRL-11); the scheduler has no disposition authority (OPA-17); no auto-rejection of owed or recoverable cases; concurrency safety (MRL-13); unknown content treated as sensitive (CLS-04, MAT-01); the remaining gap raised as OD-7I-12 rather than decided silently.

### OD-7I-12 — Day 90, unproven or undispositioned — **decided: erase; owner-window reconciliation**

1. A case still failing at day 90 without proof of permanence, or not dispositioned, has no frozen terminal path: class `I` admits neither rejection without the bytes nor `OWNER_RECONCILED` (7G §24.4, MR-18).
2. 7G §24.2 T-13, T-14; §24.4; DAU-04, DAU-09; MR-18; LC-2.
3. **A.** Erase; the consuming group's owning domain reconciles its observation window; controlled erratum to §24.4.
4. **B.** A bounded, dual-controlled retention exception.
5. **C.** Erase and record an "unproven" rejection.
6. A keeps the limit and invents no proof; B extends retention; C records a terminal rejection without proof.
7. A can leave a metadata-only case open for a long time.
8. None.
9. One guarded transition, once governed (IR-14); ERR-7I-04.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Conditions applied: MRL-14 … MRL-17 one for one; evidence-bound resolution only; otherwise the case stays open with no terminal deadline; the erratum is narrow and is not active until governed (AB-7I-08).

### OD-7I-13 — Independent store for the erasure journal — **decided: existing in-region object storage**

1. An erasure ledger inside the database is rewound by a restore, so it cannot say which erasures followed the backup (P1-7I-R03). A record outside the backup lineage is needed, and the frozen architecture names no store for it.
2. 3F §11 (point-in-time recovery 7 days; daily snapshots 30 days; weekly snapshots 1 year; restore drill); 4I §9 (residency scopes); 5A §19 (object storage); 6C §13.
3. **A.** Write-once, chained journal records in the existing in-region object storage, under a dedicated prefix, credential and key.
4. **B.** A second PostgreSQL instance with its own backup lineage.
5. **C.** Fix the properties only and choose the product at 7K or implementation.
6. A and B both give an independent failure domain; B's own backups need the same restore-safety argument again. C leaves the gate closed with no design.
7. All options: an erasure waits when the journal is unavailable, and a recovered database cannot be activated until the journal is read. A adds one object write before each request-driven erasure commits.
8. All options keep encrypted identifiers of erased subjects for the backup-restorability horizon, about one year under 3F's schedule.
9. A: no new product; a prefix, identities, a key purpose, journal states on the step ledger (IR-24, IR-31, IR-34). B: a new managed instance.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied: independence from the backup lineage (JRN-01); dedicated credentials, keys and isolation (JRN-01, JRN-04, JRN-18); tamper resistance preferred and the provider's capabilities verified, not assumed (JRN-18, JRN-19); intent durable before the erasure commits (JRN-06, JRN-07); a crash-safe state protocol (JRN-06, JRN-09); an aborted transaction never becomes a completion or an unauthorized deletion (JRN-08); a missing completion marker reconciled from the pending intent (JRN-09); sequencing, checkpoints, authenticated reads, replay and verification (JRN-05, JRN-11, JRN-13); replay before traffic (JRN-12, JRN-13; INV-18); fail closed (JRN-16); minimized, encrypted, in-region, separately auditable (JRN-03, JRN-04, RSY-13); retention against the backup horizon with holds and object versions (JRN-17; RET-24); no deletion or tampering by administrators, workers or tenants (JRN-18); configuration, validation, recovery testing and implementation requirements (JRN-19; IR-31, IR-34; VT-66 … VT-68); no other database product or managed service (JRN-01).

### OD-7I-14 — EV-097 `total_cost` and `roi_pct` — **decided: customer-billed basis only, otherwise `null`**

1. The frozen sources disagree on whether the campaign cost is provider procurement cost or the customer's billed spend (§10.3a). If it is the former, the event carries platform-confidential economics into the outbox, the campaign family stream and backups (P1-7I-R04).
2. 4D §4.6, §11.4, §17.10; 4F §2, §11; 4G §7.2; 6H §26, ADR-6H-08, DEP-6H-13; 6L §26.2, DEC-6L-02; 7A BIL-05; 7B §24; 7C EV-097 binding.
3. **A.** Billed spend only; `null` until the cost port attests that basis.
4. **B.** Always `null` in V1; remove the fields in a future 7C version.
5. **C.** Keep provider cost internally and restrict the campaign family's consumers.
6. A and B keep provider economics out of every event store. C needs INV-07 amended and contradicts DEC-6L-02.
7. None. `null` is valid under the frozen binding for both fields.
8. A: campaign cost and ROI stay absent until 6K supplies a billed-basis port. B: they never travel by event.
9. A: a basis value on the port result, a producer gate and a validation rule (IR-37); an erratum to upstream wording (ERR-7I-11). No schema change.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied: DEC-6L-02 preserved (FIN-02, FIN-07); the 4D, 6K, 6L, 7B and 7C contracts verified (§10.3a table; 6K contains no port implementation, DEP-6H-13 open); both fields confirmed nullable, so no emission needs blocking for the `null` case (FIN-03); confidential with no consumer (FIN-07); enforced before the outbox insert (FIN-05); no unverified value emitted until the port is correct (AB-7I-09); server-authoritative (FIN-08); no provider-cost field and no platform economics on a general-purpose stream (FIN-09); erratum and gate recorded without editing a frozen document (ERR-7I-11; CNF-7I-12).

### OD-7I-15 — Consumer-group acknowledgement integrity — **decided: accounting plus a group-authorizing stream gateway**

1. Redis ACLs cannot scope a command to a consumer group. A credential that can issue `XACK`, `XAUTOCLAIM` or `XREADGROUP` on a shared family key can remove or take another group's pending entry; `XREADGROUP … NOACK` does so without any acknowledgement. For the consumers whose only durable intent is the pending entry, the obligation is then gone (P1-7I-R05).
2. 7E MF-11, MF-14, TRM-02, GRP-07, GRP-08, SCY-05, OD-7E-03; 7F §13, §18, EID-08, RDL-03, EXT-04; 7G RCL-04, RCL-06, PAT-01 … PAT-11, DSR-12, DGL-04, ILK-06.
3. **A.** PostgreSQL-side accounting and recovery only.
4. **B.** Accounting, and a gateway that holds the only consumer-side Redis credential. (Also offered: the gateway alone; formal acceptance of the risk with no new control.)
5. **C.** Per-group or per-tenant stream keys: not offered, because it changes the frozen topology.
6. A detects and recovers but does not prevent. B prevents misuse by any consumer and still detects and recovers a failure of the gateway or of Redis. The gateway becomes part of the trusted computing base for transport.
7. B adds one in-region round trip per read batch and per acknowledgement batch, an evidence read and an accounting insert per acknowledged (group, event), a new component to run redundantly, and a new availability dependency of consumption. Publication is unaffected. Both options can hold a `PUBLISHED` row past 7 days while a group is behind.
8. None directly.
9. B: a gateway workload and principal, a binding registry, an accounting relation, evidence functions, a reconciler, a cleanup interlock, nine fewer Redis users (IR-16, IR-35, IR-36); errata to 7E, 7F and 7G (ERR-7I-08 … 10).
10. Recommended: A. **Chosen by the owner: B**, with conditions applied: no consumer keeps a direct credential for group commands (RDS-03, RDS-05); a separately privileged workload of the modular monolith, not a business microservice (ROL-03, GWY-01); server-controlled authentication (GWY-02); identity bound to registered groups, keys and operations (GWY-03); no caller-supplied group or key trusted (GWY-04); reading, claiming, sweeping and acknowledging all mediated (GWY-05); `XACK` only after the frozen boundary and durable evidence (GWY-08, GWY-10); CON-01 and CON-08 covered without inventing an effect from a success claim (GWY-09, ACC-08); durable tenant-safe evidence (GWY-08 a; 7F EID-06); accounting and reconciliation retained for gateway or Redis failure (ACC-03 … ACC-09); acknowledgement only after the authoritative boundary (GWY-10); publication independent of consumers (GWY-15); availability, redundancy, replay, crash recovery, rotation, monitoring and alerts (GWY-11, GWY-13, GWY-15; §9.4; HE-7J-7I-09); shared streams kept, no per-tenant stream (§9 preamble); latency and throughput cost stated for 7K (GWY-17; HE-7K-7I-08); the gateway not a data-access mechanism and its credential hardened (GWY-12, GWY-13); a consumer cannot forge accounting, bypass the gateway or obtain its credential (ACC-10, GWY-13, GWY-14); no alternate Redis path (GWY-14); 7G authorization boundaries preserved (GWY-16); errata recorded and nothing claimed as already frozen (ERR-7I-08 … 10); consumer activation blocked until built and validated (AB-7I-10). The residual trust in the gateway itself is documented and not claimed away (T-7I-21, RR-02, GWY-18).
### OD-7I-16 — Journal unavailable; time-based erasure — **decided: journal every erasure; wait and alert**

1. A time-based erasure left no record outside the database, so a restore that returned the row to a non-terminal state brought the content back where no clock and no erasure function could reach it (P1-7I-R08). Journaling them makes time-based erasure depend on the journal's availability.
2. OD-7I-01, 02, 03, 09, 10, 13; 7G RPM-12, T-13; 7H DSM, CBK-18; 3F §11.
3. **A.** No erasure without a durable journal record; on an outage wait, track and alert.
4. **B.** Erase anyway and mark older backups ineligible for restore.
5. **C.** Do not journal time-based erasure; forbid restoring a backup older than the shortest clock (7 days).
6. A keeps restore safety unconditionally. B trades it for punctuality. C contradicts 3F's 30-day and one-year snapshots and leaves R08 open.
7. A: a journal outage can push a body, material or input past its approved limit; one journal object per batch of time-based erasures.
8. A: encrypted identifiers and lifecycle states of every time-erased row are kept for the backup horizon, about one year.
9. IR-43, with IR-31 and IR-34; ERR-7I-15.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied, in the owner's numbering: (1) every request-driven or time-based erasure journaled before it commits (JRN-02, JRN-21; INV-23); (2) no unjournaled erasure when the write is unconfirmed (JRN-20, JRN-29); (3) tracked pending state and critical alert (JRN-29; HE-7J-7I-10); (4) bounded, idempotent retry (JRN-09, JRN-29); (5) deadlines remain obligations (JRN-29); (6) approaching and missed deadlines escalated through the privacy-incident procedure (JRN-29; LR-09); (7) protection from tampering, deletion, rollback and unauthorized access (JRN-01, JRN-04, JRN-05, JRN-18); (8) terminal-state and erasure evidence sufficient against an older backup (JRN-22 … JRN-25); (9) intent followed by a failed transaction never becomes a completion (JRN-08, JRN-21 step 5); (10) erasure committed, completion marker missing, recovered durably (JRN-09); (11) completeness proved before traffic (JRN-12, JRN-13, JRN-26; INV-18); (12) the in-region object storage of OD-7I-13 kept (JRN-01); (13) batching and scale defined for 7K without weakening per-row traceability (JRN-28; HE-7K-7I-11); (14) no silent fallback (JRN-29; INV-23). The Day-40 counterexample is re-run in §14.8.

### OD-7I-18 — Forged completion evidence — **decided: per-context principals and delivery-bound evidence, both**

1. Consumers share `app_worker`. A holder of that credential can write another context's guard row; the genuine delivery then takes the duplicate path and the gateway acknowledges on the forged row (P1-7I-R11). The first remediation recorded this as RR-06 for 7L.

6. A stops cross-context writes at the database. B stops a guard row from serving as acknowledgement evidence. Neither alone covers both a foreign credential and a same-context credential without its gateway identity. C prevents nothing; monitoring is detective only.
7. A: nine roles, nine credentials and up to nine more pools; a missing grant is a handler failure, never a loss. B: one insert per (group, event) in each handler transaction, one token per delivery, one verification per acknowledgement.

Recommended: B. **Chosen by the owner: A and B.** Conditions applied. *A:* (1) separate least-privilege principals (CTX-01); (2) only its own tables, guards and effect objects (CTX-02, CTX-03); (3) no forging of another context's evidence (CTX-03; CEV-05; INV-22); (4) no account per tenant or event (CTX-01); (5) modular monolith preserved (ASM-01; §7.1); (6) `app_worker` grants, inheritance, definer functions, tenant context and pools reconciled (CTX-05, CTX-06, CTX-07, CTX-09); (7) no alternative credential with equivalent privileges (CTX-08; ROL-04); (8) 7F idempotency semantics preserved (CTX-11; CEV-04); (9) errata to 5B and 7F recorded without editing them (ERR-7I-14). *B:* (1) unforgeable, purpose-bound token for an actual delivery (CEV-01); (2) bound to identity, group, event, organization, transport reference and generations (CEV-01); (3) a guard record is not evidence because a worker supplied an event ID (GWY-08; CEV-09); (4) committed atomically with the effect (CEV-06); (5) verified by the gateway before acknowledgement (CEV-08; GWY-10); (6) replay, substitution, cross-group use and stolen-credential forgery prevented (CEV-10, CEV-14); (7) consumers cannot mint tokens or reach the key (CEV-02); (8) crashes, duplicates, stale claims, version changes and expiry reconciled without loss (CEV-11, CEV-12); (9) external-write and attestation-only consumers keep their frozen handling and attestation is not presented as proof (CEV-07; GWY-09; ACC-08); (10) accounting and recovery kept as defence in depth (ACC-01 … ACC-20). Both required before activation (AB-7I-11). Costs documented, not used to downgrade (CTX-09, CTX-10, CEV-15; HE-7K-7I-10). What the two controls did not cover was raised as RR-08 and decided separately (OD-7I-19).

### OD-7I-19 — RR-08, state-keyed guards — **decided: mitigate; do not accept**

1. Five consumers decide on business state that a legitimately privileged credential can write directly. A stolen owning-context or `app_api` database credential could advance that state so the genuine handler finds nothing to do (RR-08 as first written).
2. `003_5B`, `004_5B`, `028_5E`, `030_5E`, `031_5E`, `035_5F`, `036_5F`, `078_5F1`, `090_5F10`, `098_5E1`; `001_5B` (`pgcrypto`); 6C §7.7; 6H §13, §24; 7F §13, §28 (CON-02, 03, 05, 09, 11), EID-08, TXA-05.
3. **A.** Accept as a stated residual of the frozen tenancy model.
4. **B.** Mitigate: guard columns behind owning-context functions that verify an authorized cause in the database.
5. **C.** Leave open and report the phase blocked.
6. A prevents nothing. B prevents direct mutation and forged calls by a stolen database credential; it cannot prevent a fully compromised authorized workload.
7. B: one keyed-digest verification per guarded transition; one provenance insert; a proof minted per mutating API request on these paths.
8. None: no route, shape, permission, error code or event changes (STP-14).
9. IR-44; ERR-7I-17 (5B, 5E, 5F, 6C, 6H, 7F).
10. Recommended by the author: A. **Chosen by the owner: B.** Conditions applied, in the owner's numbering. *§1 design:* (1) unnecessary direct `UPDATE` on state columns removed (STP-02); (2) guarded least-privilege transition functions (STP-04 … STP-08); (3) verification of the authenticated API action or producing-domain event (STP-05, STP-06); (4) provenance committed atomically (STP-11); (5) per-context principals and restricted `EXECUTE` (STP-05, STP-15; CTX-03); (6) a stolen credential cannot forge tenant context, actor, event provenance or completion evidence to obtain the mutation (STP-05, STP-06, STP-16; CEV-05); (7) audit and anomaly detection as support only (STP-11, STP-16). The requirement that a definer function not be sufficient by itself is met by in-database verification of a code the caller cannot compute (STP-05, STP-06, STP-10). *§2:* no event-ID guard added; compare-and-swap, unique constraints and lock-then-recompute preserved; CON-03 and CON-09 recompute from authoritative state (STP-08, STP-12). *§3:* the two consumer tables of §8.9, from the migrations. *§4:* legitimate workflows and frozen contracts preserved (STP-14). *§5:* attackers A, B and C distinguished; A and B prevented; C stated (STP-16; RR-08). *§6:* roles and grants (STP-02, STP-15), transition rules (STP-04), function requirements (STP-05 … STP-08), audit and provenance (STP-11), scenarios (VT-91 … VT-95), errata (ERR-7I-17), requirement (IR-44), gate (AB-7I-11), handoffs (HE-7J-7I-11, HE-7K-7I-10, HE-7L-7I-07). Scope kept to the guard columns of five consumers (STP-01); RR-01 is not reopened.

### OD-7I-20 — Organization integration erasure — **decided: dual control, `CANCELLED` only**

1. `integrations.fn_integrations_anonymize_org(UUID)` is a definer function that irreversibly disconnects and redacts every integration connection of the organization it is given, checks nothing and audits nothing, and is executable by `app_platform_admin` (P1-7I-R12). No frozen source says who may start an organization erasure or what record authorizes it.
2. `061_5I` L166 – L178; 5I §23; 6J §11, §31 ("platform-admin/break-glass-only"); 6M (no erasure route, no erasure purpose); `105_5B4` (six purposes); 6C §7.1, §13, §15.7; OD-7I-05, OD-7I-13, OD-7I-16, OD-7I-17 condition 8.

4. **B.** The same record and executor, with one operator holding a break-glass grant and a proof.
5. **C.** As A without the `CANCELLED` precondition.
6. A: no database credential, alone or combined, reaches the mutation; a live organization cannot be erased. B: one compromised operator session can erase a cancelled tenant's integration identity. C: a live tenant's integrations can be severed by two operators.

9. IR-47; ERR-7I-18.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied, in the owner's numbering: (1) `CANCELLED` required (OEA-02); (2) authorized, active, organization-bound, free of blocking holds (OEA-06; the state table of §8.12); (3) different authenticated requester and approver (OEA-03); (4) no emergency self-approval (OEA-03); (5) approval database-verifiable and bound to operation, organization, purpose and scope (OEA-04); (6) neither a raw UUID nor a stolen `app_platform_admin` credential authorizes (OEA-01, OEA-15; INV-27); (7) direct `EXECUTE` revoked (OEA-01); (8) only through a narrowly guarded maintenance operation (OEA-05); (9) the executor cannot mint or approve (OEA-05); (10) authorization, hold status and state verified at the mutation boundary (OEA-06); (11) replay, duplicate execution, cross-tenant substitution and expired approvals prevented (OEA-08); (12) audit atomic with the mutation (OEA-07); (13) legitimate erasure and idempotent crash recovery preserved (OEA-10, OEA-11, OEA-16); (14) separately authorized subject-level erasure on an `ACTIVE` organization not prohibited (OEA-13). The 6J compatibility erratum is ERR-7I-18; the migration requirement IR-47; the stolen-credential test VT-103.

### OD-7I-21 — Platform lifecycle authorization — **decided: database-verified platform action proof**

1. The platform suspend and reactivate functions authorize on `session_user = 'app_platform_admin'` plus a session setting the same session can set, and take the administrator's identity as an unverified argument. 5. (No further option.)
6. A: a stolen `app_platform_admin` password cannot change a status. B: it can, audited under an identity it invents. Under both, direct `UPDATE` by `app_api` and `app_worker` is closed.
7. A: one keyed-digest verification, one session read and one consumed-proof insert per platform lifecycle action; a dependency on the issuer for these two routes.

Owner conditions applied, in the owner's numbering: (1) 6M endpoints preserved (OLC-10); (2) 6B authentication and platform-admin authorization remain mandatory (OLC-07, OLC-10); (3) a trusted issuer creates a short-lived, single-use, purpose-bound proof (OLC-07, OLC-09); (4) bound to administrator identity, session, organization, exact action and expiry (OLC-07); (5) unforgeable with the database credential alone (OLC-07, OLC-16); (6) the functions verify independently (OLC-08); (7) consumed atomically with the transition (OLC-09); (8) no reuse across action or organization (OLC-09); (9) replay, cross-session substitution, expired proofs and revoked authorization prevented (OLC-08, OLC-09); (10) row locking, legal transitions, audit atomicity and outbox requirements preserved (OLC-10, OLC-13); (11) `CANCELLED` terminal (OLC-04); (12) no trust in a caller-controlled setting, actor UUID or unverified argument (OLC-08); (13) every direct status `UPDATE` privilege removed (OLC-02); (14) crash recovery, concurrency and deterministic tests defined (OLC-14; VT-96 … VT-100). The 6M §16 / `107_5B5` compatibility requirements are ERR-7I-19. The tenant edges of 6C were moved behind API-proof functions under the already approved mechanism of OD-7I-19 (OLC-06); that restates frozen edges and was not a separate decision.
