3. **A.** Revoke every privilege, `SELECT` included, on the ten relations; no platform membership or role function in V1.
4. **B.** Revoke writes; keep `SELECT` on the six relations that hold no personal data or credential material.
5. (No further option.)
6. A removes every administrator path to tenant authorization state and to the two identity relations. B leaves cross-tenant membership readable without break-glass.
7. None for any frozen route: no 6M route reads or writes these relations.
8. None tenant-visible. Tenant membership, role, team, identity and request workflows are unchanged.
9. IR-48; ERR-7I-21.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied, in the owner's numbering: (1) the ten relations verified against the executed migrations (the §8.13 matrix; ARA-01); (2) direct privileges revoked on each (ARA-01); (3) 6B and 6C tenant workflows preserved (ARA-06); (4) no new platform membership or role capability (ARA-05); (5) `PUBLIC`, inheritance, sequences, views and definer functions checked (ARA-02, ARA-03, ARA-04); (6) no indirect creation of an `ACTIVE` membership, promotion or authorization change (ARA-03, ARA-08, ARA-10, ARA-12; INV-28); (7) guarded maintenance operations only where a frozen contract requires one, and none does (ARA-05); (8) tenant RLS, trusted identity, audit and permission evaluation preserved (ARA-06, ARA-07); (9) cache invalidation and session effects defined (ARA-07); (10) the complete before / after relation and function inventory (§8.13); (11) deterministic adversarial tests (VT-107, VT-108); (12) no public route added (ARA-05, ARA-06). The closure is the ACL, not audit or monitoring. While applying it one further administrator path to a tenant's destination was found in the plugin catalogue and closed without changing who manages the catalogue (ADM-15; F-7I-30).

### OD-7I-24 — Request hold lifecycle — **decided: tenant-controlled, registry-backed**

1. Any of three database credentials can move a request out of `ON_HOLD` by a direct update, and the design did not prove that a request-level hold is always present in the protected registry or that erasure cannot proceed around it (P1-7I-R15). Frozen 5B §27 and 6C §13 define how a request enters `ON_HOLD` and no way out.
2. `004_5B` L53 – L86; `008_5B` L38; 5B §27; 6C §13, §15.31 – §15.37; 4I §8.6, §9.3; `081_5F4`; HLD-01 … HLD-09; OD-7I-05, OD-7I-13, OD-7I-16, OD-7I-19.
3. **A.** The frozen hold route creates a registry hold in its transaction; the frozen reject route is the only V1 exit and ends that one hold; platform holds are separate and dual-controlled.
4. **B.** The tenant places; only two platform operators release.
5. **C.** A, plus a later tenant resume transition with a second tenant approver.
6. Under all three, erasure reads the protected registry and `status` is a guarded column. A leaves release of a tenant's own request hold with the tenant; B removes it from a compromised API process at the cost of the tenant's control; C needs a new API.
7. A: one gate lock per erasure transaction per organization; erasure for an organization waits while a new hold's subject is being resolved.
8. A: a held request cannot be resumed; a new request is filed. No new route, state or error code.
9. IR-49; ERR-7I-22.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied, in the owner's numbering: (1) the hold operation atomically establishes the protected request-scoped hold (DSH-06); (2) status, hold record and audit share one transaction (DSH-06, DSH-07); (3) rejection is the only V1 exit, subject to the frozen contract (DSH-05); (4) rejection releases that request's hold and never a platform hold (DSH-07; HLD-02); (5) platform holds separate, authoritative and dual-controlled (HLD-02, HLD-05); (6) no removal by direct update, forged setting, unauthorized call or unguarded registry write (DSH-01, DSH-02, DSH-04, DSH-08; HLD-02); (7) erasure checks the effective hold state including platform holds (HLD-03, HLD-11, HLD-14; OEA-06); (8) deterministic locking for placement, rejection, release and erasure eligibility (HLD-10, HLD-15); (9) no window under concurrency or partial failure (HLD-10, HLD-12; DSH-09); (10) request and subject scope kept apart, without legal claims (HLD-12, HLD-13); (11) rejection cancels, erases and releases nothing outside its scope (DSH-07); (12) the frozen diagram does not draw `ON_HOLD → REJECTED`, so it is recorded as a controlled correction and a held request has no exit until that is consolidated (DSH-05; ERR-7I-22; AB-7I-14); (13) no new endpoint or state (DSH-05); (14) SQL requirements, audit, fault injection and a gate (IR-49; DSH-04; VT-111 … VT-114; AB-7I-14). The three counterexamples are worked in §28.7. **Amended in mechanism by OD-7I-26:** item 7's statement that "erasure for an organization waits while a new hold's subject is being resolved" described HLD-12 as first written. That rule had no enforceable bound (P1-7I-R17) and is withdrawn. Conditions 9 and 10 are now met by HLD-10, HLD-11, HLD-12 and HLD-16 … HLD-19: the scope is fixed in the hold's transaction and no organization-wide wait exists. No condition of this decision is weakened.

### OD-7I-25 — Enterprise residency — **decided: born enterprise**

1. OD-7I-22 as first applied assigned `INDIA_ENTERPRISE` to an existing organization after checking under its row lock that it held no data. Only five relations lock that row on insert, so a tenant write can commit between the check and the assignment (P1-7I-R16).
2. `003_5B`, `004_5B` (the five foreign keys); `062_5I`, `077_5J1` (no foreign key); 6C §7.7, §15.1; 5B §26; 4I §9; OD-7I-04, OD-7I-22; CRF-06 as reviewed.
3. **A.** The governed provisioning change creates the organization already `INDIA_ENTERPRISE`, with its owner membership and creation event, in one transaction; no existing organization is converted.
4. **B.** Fence an existing empty organization with an internal admission state, a blocking trigger on every data-bearing relation, refusal of its API and worker activity, and a drain period.
5. **C.** Both.
6. A has no window to defend. B's correctness depends on every one of roughly 180 relations and every non-database writer taking part.
7. A: none at runtime. B: a tenant-visible unavailable period and a trigger on every data-bearing insert.
8. A: enterprise tenants are onboarded by the platform; one that already signed up as `STANDARD` receives a new organization. Self-service creation is unchanged.
9. IR-46 as amended; ERR-7I-20, ERR-7I-23.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**. Owner conditions applied, in the owner's numbering: (1) contract authorization, region and conformance established before creation (CRF-05, CRF-06 b, c); (2) the profile and region present from the first committed state (CRF-13; CRF-04); (3) the frozen organization-plus-owner-membership transaction and its durable creation event preserved (CRF-13); (4) asynchronous compliance-policy seeding preserved (CRF-13); (5) the authority not forgeable by `app_api`, `app_worker`, a tenant administrator or a platform-administrator credential (CRF-05, CRF-08); (6) no partially provisioned organization accepts operations, processing, delivery, callbacks or storage (CRF-14); (7) no create-as-`STANDARD`-then-update (CRF-04, CRF-07); (8) self-service creation stays `STANDARD` (CRF-03); (9) no online upgrade or relocation (CRF-07); (10) the OD-7I-04 egress contract and destination lock preserved (CRF-06 f, CRF-10); (11) fail closed on a region mismatch (CRF-06 c); (12) provisioning identity, region attestation and owner membership verified and audited (CRF-05, CRF-06 c, d, CRF-11); (13) a failed attempt leaves no `ACTIVE`, accessible, misclassified organization (CRF-14); (14) consumers cannot begin on a partially provisioned organization (CRF-14); (15) 6C and 5B compatibility recorded without editing them (ERR-7I-20, ERR-7I-23); (16) implementation, migration and validation requirements, including the creation event and outbox behaviour (IR-46; CRF-13; VT-115, VT-116). Endpoint, outbox and object-storage writes cannot race the assignment because no existing tenant undergoes conversion: §28.7.

### OD-7I-26 — Scope of a request hold — **decided: fixed at commit; no organization-wide pause**

1. The fourth remediation held every row of an organization while a request hold's subject was being matched to rows, and nothing guaranteed that the matching would finish. An unrelated subject's data could be kept past its approved limit indefinitely, with no recorded decision (P1-7I-R17). The alternatives trade minimization for unrelated subjects against certainty of preservation and against build cost.
2. `004_5B` (subject fields); `020_5D`, `093_5D2` (contact identity and merge); the contact-reference columns of `011_5C`, `012_5C`, `021_5D`, `023_5D`, `024_5D`, `030_5E`, `045_5G`, `098_5E1`; `062_5I`, `077_5J1`; 4I §9.3; 5B §27, ADR-5B-007; 6C §13; 7G RPM-12, PRT-06; 7H CBK-18, CBK-20; OD-7I-01, 02, 03, 05, 07, 09, 10, 11, 16, 24; HLD-11 and HLD-12 as reviewed.
3. **A.** Keep the organization-wide pause; add a resolution deadline and a dual-controlled decision when it is reached.
4. **B.** Resolve the subject to rows inside the hold transaction and store that snapshot.
5. **C.** Hold a conservative candidate set during resolution, then replace it atomically with verified references. **D.** A standing subject index; the hold commits already scoped; rows are decided one at a time when erased; only unattributable rows wait, under a per-row decision.
6. A protects held data and delays every unrelated subject in every hold. B protects what it finds and has no answer for rows created later or for rows that cannot be attributed. C's protection depends on how the candidate set is built, and partial matching can miss. D protects every indexed row and every later one, holds nothing of another subject, and is explicit about the rows it cannot classify. Erasing unattributable rows on their clocks regardless of holds was considered and rejected: it can erase held data because classification is incomplete.
7. D: one index write per contact-linked resource write; one index lookup per row erased; no asynchronous resolver to operate; a small, recurring human decision load for unattributed rows. A: lowest build cost, highest retention cost.
8. None tenant-visible in any option chosen: no route, state, response or error changes; a hold is never refused.
9. IR-50; ERR-7I-24.
10. Recommended and chosen: **D**, confirmed by the owner in writing with conditions, mapped here by the owner's sections. *§1 index:* (1) canonical subject from the frozen 5B / 6C identifiers and identity mappings (HLD-12); (2) existing and new resources across CRM, campaign contacts, call resources, webhook payloads, recovery material and object-storage references (HLD-16, HLD-17); (3) tenant isolation, no cross-organization matching (HLD-12, HLD-16); (4) duplicates, changed identifiers, aliases, merges and ambiguous identities (HLD-12); (5) transactional maintenance (HLD-16); (6) backfill and verification before activation (HLD-19; AB-7I-14); (7) least privilege, classification and audit (HLD-16, HLD-18); (8) an incomplete or unavailable index never read as empty or complete (HLD-19; HLD-17 default). *§2 placement:* (1) gate and lock order preserved (HLD-10, HLD-15); (2) tenant authorization and action proof (DSH-04, DSH-06); (3) subject resolved and scope established (HLD-12); (4) status, registry hold, subject binding, coverage evidence and audit commit together (DSH-06; HLD-12); (5) journal requirements kept (HLD-09); (6) no erasure between scope and commit, because the gate is held exclusively throughout (HLD-10); (7) no success while the index is incomplete (HLD-19 a); (8) a failure path inside the frozen error envelope, with no new state or code (HLD-19 a). *§3 later resources:* an authoritative write boundary that ingestion, replay, imports, merges and background work cannot bypass (HLD-16 triggers; HLD-12 merge widening; HLD-17). *§4 unattributable material:* (1) never classified unrelated by default (HLD-17, HLD-18); (2) item-level record (HLD-18); (3) the material's own deadline applies (HLD-18; RET-29); (4) a documented dual-controlled decision among lawful erasure, proven applicability and a narrow exception (HLD-18 outcomes 3, 1, 2); (5) never erased automatically (HLD-18); (6) no hold released automatically (HLD-05, HLD-18); (7) no recurring undocumented extension (HLD-18 renewal rule); (8) escalation with evidence and ownership (HLD-18); (9) unrelated subjects keep their schedules (HLD-11, HLD-13). *§5:* no organization-wide pause as a resolution mechanism (HLD-11; HLD-19 is a fault state that no hold can cause); no two-stage quarantine was substituted. The twelve invariants of the fifth review's brief are met by the same rules: (1) no held data erased because matching is incomplete (HLD-11 b, c; HLD-17 fail-safe default; HLD-18); (2) no undocumented indefinite retention of unrelated data (HLD-11, HLD-18; INV-31); (3) no unauthorized narrowing or release (HLD-12 immutability; HLD-16 accumulation; HLD-18 dual control; DSH-07); (4) effective-hold checks authoritative inside guarded erasure transactions (HLD-03, HLD-10, HLD-11, HLD-14); (5) gate and lock order deadlock-safe (HLD-10, HLD-15); (6) subject-resource mapping durable and updated for new resources (HLD-16); (7) a partial or failed resolver cannot report a hold as fully scoped (HLD-12: no resolver state exists); (8) no step reported complete that did not run (ERA-05, `SKIPPED_HELD`); (9) delayed retention work visible, audited and owned (HLD-18; HE-7J-7I-14); (10) approved retention periods and exceptions kept distinct (HLD-18); (11) rejection never releases a platform hold (DSH-07; HLD-02); (12) no new route or state (HLD-12; DSH-05). The values marked [REC] (30-day review of an authorization; 7 days to escalation) are recommendations for 7K and the operating organization; no rule depends on their size. **Amended in mechanism by OD-7I-27 and OD-7I-28:** the exception of §4 (4) is no longer a `PLATFORM` hold that stays in force past its review date but a record with a hard expiry; the resting state `DECISION_DUE` is withdrawn and replaced by the six statuses of HLD-18; a row past its limit with no decision is sealed and recorded as unauthorized retention (HLD-22); index entries are ended rather than only accumulated, and still link (HLD-16, HLD-21). §4 (5) and (6), no automatic erasure and no automatic release, are unchanged and are restated by OD-7I-28. No condition of this decision is weakened.

### OD-7I-27 — Historical associations and a hold — **decided: held by default; reviewed at the deadline; released only on evidence**

1. HLD-16 kept every index entry for ever, so that editing a reference could not take a row out of a hold. A resource re-pointed from held contact X to unheld contact Y was then held by X's hold indefinitely, on an association that may no longer describe its content. Removing the entry instead would let a tenant-path credential re-point a row out of a hold. Whether the resource still contains X's information cannot be decided mechanically (P1-7I-R18, counterexample C).
2. `020_5D` L61, L76 (identity columns; table-level `UPDATE`); `021_5D` L66, `022_5D` L88, L118, `023_5D` L41, `030_5E` L50 (table-level `UPDATE` on relations that carry a contact reference); `093_5D2` and `097_5D5` (merge body; lineage immutability); 6G §8.5, §10, §22; `004_5B`; OD-7I-24, OD-7I-26; HLD-16 as reviewed.
3. **A.** The ended association holds the row until the hold ends; no review.
4. **B.** Held by default; at the row's retention deadline two reviewers confirm the hold or release the association on evidence; nothing is automatic.
5. **C.** Only a hold that existed when the association ended reaches through it; a hold placed later does not.
6. A never loses held data and over-retains unrelated content with no review. B never loses held data and gives over-retention a lawful exit, at the price of a human decision. C needs no decision, can miss content that still contains the former subject's data, and lets a re-pointing made before a foreseeable hold defeat it.
7. B adds reviews to the decision queue of HLD-18 and, where nobody decides, incidents under OD-7I-28. A and C add none.
8. None tenant-visible: no route, state or CRM behaviour changes in any option.
9. IR-50 (ended edges with provenance, path classification, the release function); ERR-7I-24.
10. Recommended and chosen: **B**, confirmed by the owner in writing with conditions, mapped in the owner's numbering: (1) immutable historical evidence with original contact, replacement contact, transition and transaction provenance (HLD-16); (2) no indefinite retention from a historical link alone (HLD-21 (2), (3)); (3) no silent removal of a hold by reassignment, merge or identity change (HLD-11, HLD-16, HLD-21 (1)); (4) determination at the retention deadline (HLD-18, HLD-21 (2)); (5) two distinct reviewers for a release (HLD-21 (3)); (6) the four kinds of evidence (HLD-21 (3)); (7) a changed `contact_id` alone is insufficient (HLD-21 (2), (3)); (8) hold preserved where the information is still present (HLD-21 (3), `HOLD_APPLIES`); (9) normal processing when proven unrelated, subject to other holds (HLD-21 (3)); (10) uncertainty invokes OD-7I-28 (HLD-21 (3), HLD-22); (11) frozen merge semantics preserved, malicious reassignment cannot bypass an existing or a future hold (HLD-12, HLD-21 (1), (4)); (12) transitive matching through contact identity, historical aliases and versioned keyed digests (HLD-11 b1 – b3, HLD-20); (13) transaction boundaries, concurrency, crash recovery, tenant isolation and immutable audit evidence (HLD-11, HLD-15, HLD-16, HLD-19, HLD-20; RET-29); (14) no new public CRM or DSR endpoint (HLD-21 (5)). The tests the approval requires are VT-124 (a contact created after placement), VT-125 (changed phone and email), VT-126 (reassignment), VT-127 (merged contacts) and VT-128 (key rotation).

### OD-7I-28 — Uncertain material past its limit with no decision — **decided: preserve, seal and declare; residual accepted**

1. HLD-18 let a retention-decision record stay `DECISION_DUE` indefinitely and described the material as kept under "an open decision that is counted, aged, owned and escalated". An owner and an alert are not an authorization. A person cannot be made to decide; automatic erasure can destroy held data; silence is not approval. At the limit one of two approved requirements has to give: the retention limit, or no automatic erasure of possibly held data (P1-7I-R19).
2. OD-7I-01, 02, 03, 09, 10 (the limits); OD-7I-26 §4 (5), (6); HLD-05 and HLD-18 as reviewed; 7G RPM-12, PRT-06; 7H CBK-18, CBK-20; §15.4 (`payload_json NOT NULL`).
3. **A.** Preserve; seal; record as unauthorized retention and an incident from the deadline; never erase or release automatically.
4. **B.** As A, with automatic, journaled erasure after a fixed overdue period.
5. **C.** As A without sealing: the material stays under its existing access controls.
6. A destroys nothing and leaves an unbounded, visible, sealed breach of the retention limit. B bounds retention and can irreversibly destroy held evidence; it reverses OD-7I-26 §4 (5). C is A with the material still usable while overdue.
7. A and C: a decision queue and an incident process that depend on people. A additionally: a vault, a key purpose and a sealing pass. B: nothing beyond A, and no dependence on people at the end.
8. A: a tenant reading a sealed delivery sees a null body, as for an erased one, and replay is refused with the existing code. No route, state or error is added.
9. IR-51; PBR-10; ERR-7I-25.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**, confirmed by the owner in writing with conditions, mapped in the owner's numbering: (1) sealed condition at the deadline (HLD-22; SEAL-01, SEAL-03); (2) no normal read, replay, processing, delivery, export, diagnostics or support access (SEAL-01, SEAL-06, SEAL-08); (3) no re-entry to Redis, outbox publication, consumer recovery or webhook delivery (SEAL-06); (4) access only by an independently approved privacy or legal process (SEAL-08); (5) two distinct humans for inspection, applicability, exception and erasure (HLD-18, HLD-21, SEAL-08); (6) the missed deadline recorded as an incident from its actual occurrence time (SEAL-04); (7) evidence of deadline, material, reason, owning context, approvals and escalation history (HLD-18; SEAL-04); (8) alert and formal incident escalation, an alert never a resolution (SEAL-05); (9) mandatory review and escalation with no guaranteed resolution time (SEAL-05; HLD-22); (10) no automatic release of a hold (SEAL-10; HLD-05); (11) no automatic destruction because time has passed (SEAL-10; HLD-22); (12) no repeated generic exceptions or scheduled renewals (HLD-18; SEAL-11); (13) the legitimate time-limited, dual-controlled exception preserved (HLD-18; SEAL-11); (14) once applicability is established: hold, authorized exception, or lawful erasure (HLD-18 statuses; SEAL-10); (15) sealing enforced at the database, storage and service boundaries (SEAL-01, SEAL-09; PBR-10); (16) encryption, key custody, tenant isolation and access audit (SEAL-08, SEAL-09); (17) backups, restores, object versions and recovery workers cannot reactivate sealed material (SEAL-07); (18) idempotent, crash-safe sealing and disposition (SEAL-03, SEAL-10); (19) no recovery obligation silently made terminal (SEAL-02); (20) legal and regulatory obligations kept explicit (SEAL-05; LR-03, LR-10). **The owner's residual-risk acceptance is recorded as RR-10:** unauthorized retention may continue until an authorized determination is made; it stays documented, monitored and escalated; this document does not claim that the risk has gone or that a maximum retention period exists. The owner's instruction to be asked before any further material decision stands; none was taken in this remediation.

### OD-7I-29 — Subject-scoped platform holds — **decided: one attribution model for both kinds**

1. HLD-02 allowed a `PLATFORM` hold to be recorded by subject fields. HLD-11 (a) matched a platform hold by explicit reference only, and (b) and (c) read the subject index for `REQUEST` holds only. A legal hold placed for a phone number, with no row named, therefore protected no content-bearing row (P1-7I-R20). Correcting it by the request-hold model also brings unattributable rows of that organization into the decision procedure, which widens what a platform hold keeps.
2. HLD-02, HLD-10 … HLD-22 as reviewed; `004_5B` (subject fields); `020_5D`, `093_5D2`, `097_5D5`; 4I §8.6, §9.3; `024_5D` L78; OD-7I-24, 26, 27, 28.
3. **A.** One model: a platform hold's subject fields become a contact set and clear keys at placement and are matched by the same traversal, uncertainty rule and historical review as a request hold's; authority and release stay separate.
4. **B.** The same matching for attributed rows only; an unattributable row is never held by a platform hold.
5. **C.** Prohibit subject scope: a platform hold names explicit resources or rows only.
6. A protects every indexed row, every later one, and the rows whose attribution is broken. B can erase held evidence whose attribution failed. C cannot cover a row created later or a subject whose rows the operator cannot enumerate, and it changes approved HLD-02.
7. A: no new mechanism; more rows in the decision queue while a subject-scoped platform hold exists. B: fewer. C: none.
8. None tenant-visible in any option: no route, state, response or error changes.
9. IR-49 and IR-50 as extended.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**, confirmed by the owner in writing with conditions, mapped in the owner's numbering: (1) subject phone and email identifiers matched through the same subject-index traversal as request holds (HLD-11 b; HLD-23); (2) direct keys, contact identifiers, parent resources, current and historical associations, merges and versioned digests (HLD-11 b1 – b3, *Res*, *Id*; HLD-20); (3) resources created or linked after the hold commits (HLD-23; HLD-12; HLD-16); (4) explicit resource-reference holds preserved (HLD-02; HLD-11 a); (5) the OD-7I-27 review where a past link no longer proves applicability (HLD-21 (5); HLD-23 (4)); (6) unattributable records through the item-level decision and OD-7I-28 sealing (HLD-11 c; HLD-18; HLD-22); (7) no automatic organization-wide hold because a subject identifier is used (HLD-11, the closing rule; HLD-13); (8) distinct authorities, neither kind released by the other (HLD-02; HLD-11, one result; HLD-23 (1), (5); DSH-07); (9) platform release independently authorized, dual-controlled and audited (HLD-05; HLD-23 (3); §19.4); (10) the check inside each erasure transaction under the lock protocol (HLD-03, HLD-10, HLD-15); (11) identity changes, merges, key rotations and restores cannot bypass a platform hold (HLD-23, "what cannot bypass it"; HLD-16, HLD-20; JRN-10); (12) tenant isolation (HLD-11; HLD-12; HLD-23); (13) SQL requirements and deterministic tests (IR-49, IR-50; VT-132 … VT-137). The owner's instruction to close the finding without changing the approved public DSR or legal-hold APIs is met: HLD-23, "no route". The original counterexample is worked in §28.10.

### OD-7I-30 — Content past its retention deadline — **decided: no ordinary access, enforced at the database**

1. Sealing took content out of its ordinary store only when the retention pass ran, and SEAL-03 said that with the pass stopped an overdue row stayed there unsealed. Three roles hold table-level `SELECT` on the delivery relation, so a guard inside a function could be bypassed by a direct statement. OD-7I-28 authorized restricted preservation, not ordinary access after the deadline (P1-7I-R21). The correction needed a choice the earlier decisions do not make: whether content that a proven hold keeps stays ordinarily readable after its deadline.
2. `063_5I` L74 – L77; `066_5I` L4; `101_5I1` L1292 – L1356; 6J §23.1 – §23.3; 7G RPM-01, RPM-10; 7H MR-7H-06, MR-7H-08, MR-7H-09; HLD-06; SEAL-01 … SEAL-13; OD-7I-01, 02, 03, 09, 10, 28.
3. **A.** From the deadline no ordinary access for any row, whatever keeps it; held rows are sealed too; inspection only, under dual control.
4. **B.** Rows kept by a proven hold stay readable by the tenant; only undecided rows are denied; the guard evaluates the effective hold on every post-deadline read.
5. **C.** Held rows stay readable on the tenant's read route and are denied to every processing path.
6. A's denial needs only the row and the database clock, so it cannot fail open when the pass, the journal, the registry, the index or the vault is unavailable. B and C put the full effective-hold evaluation on the read path and must deny whenever it cannot run.
7. A: one function call per content read; no dependency of pre-deadline traffic on anything new. B, C: head locks and index reads on post-deadline reads.
8. A: a tenant reading a delivery that a hold keeps past its 30 / 90-day limit sees a null body, as for an erased one; replay is refused with the existing code. No route, field, state or error is added.
9. IR-52; ERR-7I-26.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**, confirmed by the owner in writing with conditions, mapped in the owner's numbering: (1) ordinary content access denied after the deadline for held or undecided material, even unsealed (CAG-01, CAG-04); (2) tenant APIs, workers, replay, redrive, external delivery, callouts, exports and diagnostics (CAG-05); (3) permitted metadata and immutable audit evidence stay available under their own contracts (CAG-07; ERA-01); (4) eligibility rechecked at the trusted boundary on the database clock (CAG-02, CAG-03); (5) grants, guarded functions and `SECURITY DEFINER` paths reconciled (CAG-06, CAG-05; PAS-10); (6) a narrow, independently approved inspection process (CAG-14; SEAL-08, SEAL-14); (7) fail closed when index, hold evaluation, exception evidence or policy service is unavailable (CAG-09); (8) valid pre-deadline processing and unrelated access preserved (CAG-09; CAG-02, the owed-work rows); (9) the deadline crossing during an operation, final handoff checks, the residual disclosed (CAG-10; RR-12); (10) the seal-to-vault architecture, encryption, journal and restore safeguards preserved (SEAL-01 … SEAL-14; CAG-11, CAG-13); (11) a stopped worker leaves nothing ordinarily accessible (CAG-01, CAG-12); (12) no unresolved recovery obligation marked completed because access is denied (CAG-08); (13) compatibility errata without editing frozen documents (ERR-7I-26; CAG-18); (14) SQL and application requirements, gates and failure-injection tests (IR-52; AB-7I-15; VT-138 … VT-145, VT-150). The failure trace is worked in §28.10.

### OD-7I-31 — Identity history from before the index — **decided: two certifications; index-first; accepted fallback**

1. HLD-19 said that identity history from before the backfill is not known to the index and is not claimed. It did not say when the index may be relied on, what an organization with older data is told, or how a row that depends on unknown history is classified. No frozen source records a contact's earlier identifiers or a resource's earlier contact.
2. `020_5D` (no version or history column; L72, L76); `093_5D2` (merge lineage immutable); `022_5D` L24; `072_5J`; HLD-16, HLD-19, HLD-21; OD-7I-26, 27, 28.
3. **A.** Index-first in production (`FROM_ORIGIN`); an organization with older data certified `FROM_T0` under a tenant-specific acceptance, with the limit recorded.
4. **B.** Every legacy resource uncertain against every subject hold, with no certification distinction.
5. **C.** No certification for legacy organizations: no hold and no data-subject erasure for them. **D.** `FROM_T0` for everyone, the limit stated once, no gate and no acceptance.
6. A never reads a missing edge as no history and prevents the gap where it can be prevented. B is A's fallback without the prevention. C leaves legacy tenants with no erasure at all. D overstates nothing and prevents nothing.
7. A: a per-organization certification, flags on heads, and in a `FROM_T0` organization a decision load that can cover most contact-linked rows while a subject hold exists.
8. None tenant-visible: no route, state or error changes. A `NOT_CERTIFIED` organization's hold request fails with the existing retryable error (HLD-19 a).
9. IR-53.
10. Recommended and chosen: **A**, confirmed by the owner in writing with conditions, mapped by the owner's two headings. *`FROM_ORIGIN`:* complete verified coverage from creation (HLD-24, creating-transaction evidence); all applicable relations, identity changes, merges, replay material and object references (HLD-16, HLD-17; the recorded inventory version); atomic index maintenance and completeness checks (HLD-16; HLD-19); no certification the evidence does not support (HLD-24, transitions and demotion). *`FROM_T0`:* an authoritative T0 (HLD-24); complete coverage of later operations (HLD-24 conditions 1 – 3); the unprovable earlier history preserved as a fact (legacy flags; RR-11); explicit, documented, tenant-specific acceptance (HLD-24, the acceptance); no silent promotion (HLD-24: not expressible); legacy rows with unverifiable identifiers, associations or provenance uncertain where a hold may apply (HLD-25; HLD-24 condition 4 for event-store rows); no inference of "unrelated" from a missing edge (HLD-25, the refusal); OD-7I-27 review and OD-7I-28 sealing where attribution cannot be established (HLD-25; HLD-21; HLD-22); nothing invented (HLD-24, what the backfill writes); capabilities restricted until the conservative controls exist and are verified (AB-7I-16; `NOT_CERTIFIED`); the acceptance cannot override a hold, a statutory duty or a retention limit (HLD-24: read by no hold, deadline, decision or guard). The fallback is recorded as a limitation and a rollout control (RR-11; CNF-7I-30), not as proof of complete historical attribution or of compliance with any law. **Applied as written, and stricter than the option text put to the owner:** that text matched legacy rows on current state and merge lineage; the owner's conditions make them uncertain, and HLD-25 follows the conditions. The owner's instruction to be asked before any further material decision stands; none was taken in this remediation.

## 28. Adversarial Verification

### 28.1 Attempted counterexamples

Each row is an attempt to break the design. "Prevented" means by the design as specified; where the control does not exist yet, the row says so and names the gate.

| # | Attempt | Does the design prevent it? | By what | Condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cross-tenant data exposure through an API or a consumer | Yes | Session-only tenant context; forced RLS; forgery guard; envelope-only scope (§6) | EXISTS |
| 2 | Privileged worker abuses SQL | Partly, and stated | Narrow principals with no table privilege (§8); payload stores unreadable by `app_worker`; decrypt withheld. A stolen `app_worker` credential still reaches that role's tables for any organization (RR-01) | AB-7I-01; RR-01 accepted at 7L |
| 3 | Forged tenant context in an event | Yes | INV-02; TEN-7F-02; A-2, A-4. The context-less insert (A-5) is closed by IR-03 | AB-7I-01 for A-5 |
| 4 | Redis ACL overreach | Yes for commands and keys. Group names cannot be scoped by ACL, so consumers are given no group command at all | Matrix 6; RDS-03, RDS-05 … RDS-07, RDS-10; the gateway (§9.5). Limits in §9.3 | AB-7I-02, AB-7I-10; RR-02, RR-03 |
| 5 | Operator replays without authorization | Yes | Capability grants; plan-bound approvals; no table privilege for the tooling role; no operator credential to either store (OPA-16) | AB-7I-03 |
| 6 | Self-approval of a sensitive recovery action | Yes | Human-identity comparison in the ledger (OPA-07); assertion evidence (OPA-09) | AB-7I-03; RR-04 |
| 7 | Raw personal data in logs | Yes | RED-01 … RED-06; category codes only; no payload logging | D0 redaction exists; scanner is 7J's |
| 8 | Sensitive transcript or media exposure through events | Yes | INV-07; FLD-28; 7C §19.3 | Contract |
| 9 | Personal data surviving erasure in DLQ material | Yes | ERA-08; 90-day cap; 7-day post-resolution; encrypted | AB-7I-05. Backups: ERA-20, §14.8, LR-05 |

**P0 open: 0. The sixth review found two more (F-7I-32, F-7I-33); the second was introduced by the fifth remediation, and its retention risk is accepted, not removed. The fifth review found one more (F-7I-31), introduced by the fourth remediation. The fourth review found three more (F-7I-27 … F-7I-29): two that this document had seen and handed to 7L with a reading that understated them, and one that the third remediation itself introduced. Before that, the third review found two (F-7I-24, F-7I-25); this document had seen both and handed them to 7L, one behind a sentence that was false (F-7I-26). Before that: the second review found four more (F-7I-18 … F-7I-21), two of which this document had seen and deferred. Twenty-seven P1-class items are now recorded: the eleven below, those four, F-7I-22 and F-7I-23, the two of the third review, the three of the fourth, F-7I-30, the one of the fifth, the two of the sixth, and F-7I-34. Of the earlier eleven: six from the original self-review and five from the independent review (three of which the self-review had seen and under-rated, F-7I-07, F-7I-10, F-7I-15; one it had closed with an invalid mechanism, F-7I-03; one it had missed, F-7I-14). Each is closed by a design rule or an owner decision and protected by an activation gate. "Closed in design" means the architecture is specified; no control in this document is running, and whether the closures hold is for the independent re-review to decide.

### 28.4 Independent freeze-gate findings ledger

The findings of the independent review of the 2,061-line version, each with what the review asks for. Every entry is a design closure reached by static reasoning. None is an executed control.

| Finding | Original counterexample | Revised invariant | Enforcement boundary | Trusted principal | Crash and concurrency semantics | Physical implementation requirement | Deterministic test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P1-7I-R01** Outbox privilege escape | `app_worker`, with outbox `SELECT` revoked, calls `fn_claim_outbox_events` and receives full rows of every tenant | INV-20; INV-04 as restated; PRV-17 (c) | The function's ACL, then a `session_user` check in the body | The relay role alone | 7D claim, lease, compare-and-swap and reclaim logic carried over unchanged; a crashed relay's rows are reclaimed after the timeout (FS-35) | IR-01, IR-04; OBX-01 … OBX-09; PRV-28 assertion block | VT-59, VT-60, VT-61 |
| **P1-7I-R02** Administrator `SELECT` model | A "revoke" of two columns leaves the table-level grant; the administrator still reads `payload_json` | INV-08; PRV-14 | Table and column privileges on the parent; none on any partition | Migration role; no runtime principal can re-grant | Privileges are transactional DDL; the migration asserts the end state or fails as a whole; partition creation repeats the assertion in its own transaction | IR-09; PAS-01 … PAS-10 | VT-62, VT-63 |

**P1-7I-R15: the three required failure traces.**

| Case | Trace | After IR-49 | Which independent authority prevents erasure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** Unauthorized release | A request is legitimately `ON_HOLD`. A holder of `app_platform_admin` or `app_worker` (or `app_api`) runs `UPDATE … SET status = 'IN_PROGRESS'`, bypassing the 6C workflow and its audit | The statement fails with `42501`: the administrator has no privilege on the table, the other two none on the column. Through the functions, no edge leaves `ON_HOLD` except rejection, and every function needs a proof the credential cannot compute | Two, each sufficient alone. The transition trigger refuses the edge for every caller. And the `REQUEST` hold is a separate row in a relation no login role can write: it is still unreleased, and the effective-hold function is a union (HLD-11), so an erasure reads the hold whatever the status says. If the two ever disagree, the disagreement is itself treated as a hold |
| **B** Hold placement race | An erasure function checks for a hold and finds none. A valid hold workflow places `ON_HOLD` concurrently. Both commit | Both transactions take the organization's hold gate, the erasure in share mode before it reads, the placement exclusively. Exactly two orders exist. Erasure first: the placement waits for the erasure's commit; the data was erased before any hold applied, and the request records that (HLD-04). Placement first: the erasure waits, and its hold check, a new statement after the wait, sees the committed hold and erases nothing | The gate. An erasure cannot complete after the hold "should apply", because the hold applies from the commit of the placement, and no erasure that has not yet read can commit before that commit without having waited on it |
| **C** Registry synchronization gap | A request is `ON_HOLD`; the registry has no corresponding hold; a time-based body cleanup or an owning-context erasure runs | The gap cannot be produced by a runtime path: the hold function writes both in one transaction and the deferred trigger refuses a commit that has one without the other (DSH-06, DSH-08); requests held before the migration are backfilled. If the gap were nevertheless found, HLD-11 (e) treats the request as an unresolved hold and every erasure for that organization waits | **What must be preserved:** every platform-held copy of the request's subject's personal content in the event stores (delivery bodies and previews, replay material, processing inputs, outbox payloads) and the subject's rows in the owning contexts, until the hold is released; while the hold is unresolved, every such row of the organization. **What prevents deletion:** HLD-03 and HLD-11 inside every erasure and purge function, time-based ones included, and HLD-14 for owner-context functions, the frozen `081_5F4` pair among them |

**P1-7I-R16: the seven required interleavings.** In V1 there are two kinds of organization and neither has a provisioning window.

| # | Interleaving | What happens | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | An endpoint is inserted during provisioning | For an existing `STANDARD` organization there is no provisioning: its profile is never assigned again. For an enterprise organization being created, no session other than the creating transaction knows the identifier, so no endpoint row can name it; a row planted with a guessed identifier makes the function raise (CRF-06 e) | CRF-04, CRF-07, CRF-13 |
| 2 | An outbox row is inserted during provisioning | The same. The only outbox row for the new organization is the `organization.created` row inserted by the creating transaction itself | CRF-13 |
| 3 | The organization-created consumer processes before the residency is final | It cannot. The event row commits in the same transaction as the profile; the relay claims only committed rows; the consumer's first read sees `INDIA_ENTERPRISE`. The asynchronous compliance seed is therefore always after the assignment, and is not moved into the creation transaction | CRF-13, CRF-14 |
| 4 | An object is created in storage concurrently | No object key, upload authorization or storage prefix exists for an organization that no request can yet authenticate into: every such operation starts from a tenant request, which needs a visible membership | CRF-14 |
| 5 | Provisioning aborts and is retried | The transaction rolls back: no organization, membership, event, audit row or consumed authorization. Nothing `ACTIVE` and misclassified remains. The retry uses the same authorization and succeeds once | CRF-14; FS-38 |
| 6 | An organization that already has data is to be made enterprise | Refused. No function accepts an existing organization; a direct `UPDATE` is refused by the trigger for every caller. The tenant is given a new organization, and moving its data is a separately approved process | CRF-04, CRF-07 |
| 7 | The contracted region and the deployed environment do not match, or the contract authorization is missing | The function raises before inserting anything; nothing is created | CRF-06 b, c |

The system therefore cannot certify a residency profile incorrectly through a race: the profile is never asserted of an organization that existed before the assertion. What the database does not verify is the contract itself (CRF-12).

### 28.8 Fifth independent freeze-gate findings ledger

The finding of the fifth review, of the 3,400-line version. A design closure reached by static reasoning from the SQL text and the frozen documents. Not an executed control; no gate named here is open.

**Superseded in part by §28.9.** Where this ledger says `DECISION_DUE`, "an open, owned decision", "entries accumulate" or an authorization that is a `PLATFORM` hold, the rules now in force are HLD-16, HLD-18, HLD-21 and HLD-22. The ledger is kept unchanged below as the record of the fifth remediation.

**The required counterexample, against the 3,400-line version.**

| Step | What that version did |
|---|---|
| 1 – 3 | Organization A has unrelated subjects X and Y. A tenant places a legitimate hold on X; the `REQUEST` hold commits (DSH-06) |
| 4 | The owning contexts are to resolve X to resource references and mark the hold `RESOLVED` (HLD-12). They do not: the resolver is not running, or X's identity data is inconsistent, or `subject_contact_id` names a contact that no longer exists |
| 5 – 7 | Y's terminal `FAILED` callback input reaches day 7 (CBI-10) and Y's `CANCELLED` delivery body day 30 (RET-07). Each erasure function takes the gate and evaluates HLD-11; clause (c), "an unreleased hold of either kind in the row's organization is not yet resolved", is true; neither row is erased |
| 8 | Resolution keeps failing. Nothing else ends clause (c): not a deadline, not a decision, not an operator act other than rejecting X's request, which ERR-7I-22 has not yet made possible |

**Maximum duration of the hold over Y's data under that version: unbounded.** It could retain an unrelated subject's personal data indefinitely, with no authorization and no recorded decision. Alerts, the JRN-29 escalation and the 7K handoff that HLD-12 cited report the condition; none of them ends it. The text's phrase "bounded by the resolution" was wrong.

**The alternatives, as put to the owner (OD-7I-26).**

| Criterion | A: bounded organization-wide pause | B: resolve inside the hold transaction | C: two-stage candidate quarantine | **D: scope fixed at commit; standing index (chosen)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Retention and minimization | Every unrelated subject delayed in every hold, up to the deadline and beyond if retention is authorized | Unrelated subjects unaffected | Unaffected only outside the candidate set | Unaffected; only unattributable rows wait |
| Genuine hold protection | Complete | Rows found at placement; nothing for later rows or unattributable rows | As good as the candidate set | Indexed rows, later rows, and unattributable rows |
| Unrelated subjects' rights | Suspended for the pause | Preserved | Partly | Preserved |
| Partial identity resolution | Whole organization waits | Must refuse the hold or commit it unscoped | Stalls, or the set grows | No partial state: several matches are all held; no match is a key-scoped hold |
| Cross-context availability | A resolver must run | One database: a query, not a call | A resolver must run | One database; no resolver process |
| Locking and concurrency | Gate; long-lived logical wait | Gate; short | Gate; an atomic swap of scope | Gate; short; no swap |
| Crash recovery | A stalled resolver is the failure mode | All or nothing | Two states to recover | All or nothing; no intermediate state |
| Legal-hold exceptions | Explicit at the deadline | None defined | None defined | Explicit, per row, dual-controlled |
| Operational complexity | Low | Low | High | Medium: an index and a small decision queue |
| Migrations | A deadline and a decision record | A snapshot relation | Candidate and verified sets | Index, triggers, backfill, attribution fields, decision record |
| OD-7I-24 and frozen 6C | Compatible | Refusing a hold would conflict | Compatible | Compatible; nothing tenant-visible changes |

**The twelve evidence items for P1-7I-R17.**

| # | Item | P1-7I-R17 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Original evidence | HLD-11 (c), HLD-12, FS-40 and VT-113 of the 3,400-line version; RET-06, RET-07, CBI-10, MRL-01; `004_5B` L56 – L59 and `chk_dsr_subject_present`; `020_5D` (contact identity); the eight migrations with a contact reference; `062_5I` (no reference on the receipt) |
| 2 | Failing scenario | The table above |
| 3 | Corrected invariant | INV-31; INV-29 as restated |
| 4 | Trusted principal and boundary | The hold function (scope, from the CRM resolver, in its own transaction); index triggers owned by the migration role; two holders of `retention.hold.manage` through the platform authorization issuer (decisions); the effective-hold function inside every erasure function |
| 5 | Privileges and guarded functions | No login-role privilege on the index, a hold's contact set and keys, or the decision record; one resolver returning identifiers only; the decision functions for the tooling principal, each verifying two operator action proofs; a superseding merge function |
| 6 | Transaction and lock ordering | Placement: gate (exclusive) → request row → resolver read → registry. Erasure: gate (share) → index lookup → data locks in the 7H order. Decision and merge widening: gate (exclusive). Unchanged order, no cycle (HLD-15) |
| 7 | Crash, retry, concurrency | No intermediate hold state exists to recover. A resource and its index entry commit together. A row is `SKIPPED_HELD` or erased, never both and never reported erased when skipped. Decisions are idempotent per (row, hold set, operators) |
| 8 | Frozen compatibility | The 6C `hold` route's request, response, permission, audit action and state are unchanged; a hold is never refused. Retention periods of OD-7I-01, 02, 03, 09, 10 are unchanged. Attribution is metadata on future records (ERR-7I-24) |
| 9 | Dependency | IR-50, with IR-49 |
| 10 | Gate | AB-7I-14 |
| 11 | Test | VT-113, VT-117 … VT-123 |
| 12 | Why the failure is prevented | The clause that held the organization is gone, and with it the state it depended on. Y's rows carry attributions that the index maps to Y; clause (b) is false for them; clause (c) does not apply because they are attributed. They are erased on day 7 and day 30 |

**The required scenarios, with expected results.** Rows 1 – 9 are the nine of the fifth review's brief; rows 10 – 13 complete the ten the owner's approval lists.

| # | Scenario | Expected result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unresolved subject matching: X's keys match no contact | The hold commits, scoped to its keys, contact set empty. Y's `FAILED` input is erased at day 7 and Y's `CANCELLED` body at day 30. No row of the organization is held except a row that carries X's key and any unattributed row. The empty contact set is an operator indicator |
| 2 | Resolver process crash | Not applicable as a state: there is no resolver process. A crash of the hold function before commit leaves no hold and no `ON_HOLD`; the tenant's retry places it. A crash after commit leaves a complete, scoped hold |
| 3 | Missing or inconsistent contact identity | `subject_contact_id` naming no row: as scenario 1. An email matching two contacts: both are in the contact set and both contacts' rows are held; a third subject's rows are not. A contact later corrected to carry X's phone number: its rows are held from that commit by the key |
| 4 | Concurrent hold placement and unrelated erasure | Y's erasure and X's placement serialize on the gate for the length of one transaction. In both orders Y's row is erased. The erasure's record shows it erased, on time |
| 5 | Resource creation while a hold is being placed | The resource's index entry commits with it. If it is X's, it is held from its own commit whether that is before or after the placement's commit, because the lookup happens when an erasure reaches the row, not when the hold was placed |
| 6 | Resolver timeout or prolonged outage | Not applicable as a state. The nearest failure is the CRM resolver query failing inside the hold function: the function fails, nothing commits, and no erasure of any subject is affected, because no hold exists. The tenant retries |
| 7 | Hold rejection or authorized release | Rejecting X's held request releases X's `REQUEST` hold and no other (DSH-07). X's rows and any unattributed rows return to their clocks and those past their limits are erased by the next pass, each journaled. A `PLATFORM` hold on any of them, including an exceptional-retention authorization, still holds that row. Releasing a `PLATFORM` hold needs two operators |
| 8 | Erasure deadlines reached during uncertainty | For attributed rows there is no uncertainty: they are erased or held by HLD-11 (b). For an unattributed row: it is not erased, the batch reports `SKIPPED_HELD`, a decision record opens as `DECISION_DUE` with an owner, and the row is then retained under a signed authorization, erased on a signed determination, or stays as an aged, escalated open decision. It is never erased or released by the clock |
| 9 | Restore of a hold from an older backup | The database is quarantined. Holds are re-applied before erasures (HLD-09; JRN-10). Each re-applied hold takes the union of its journaled contact set and a fresh resolver run against the restored data; widenings and authorizations are re-applied; a determination is not, so its row is held again unless its erasure was journaled, in which case the erasure is re-applied. The index must pass its completeness assertion before activation. No hold is ever restored with a smaller scope than the journal records. Every relation of the index is `UNVERIFIED` after a restore until re-verified, so an earlier index snapshot is never read as complete |
| 10 | The subject index is unavailable or unverified during hold placement | The hold function fails and nothing commits; the tenant sees the existing retryable server error. Erasure depending on the unverified relation is refused for that organization meanwhile, so nothing the hold would have covered is erased. After rebuild and verification the retry places a fully scoped hold. Rows attributed through verified relations, and other organizations, are unaffected |
| 11 | Journal outage and recovery | During the outage the hold function fails (HLD-09) and no erasure commits (INV-23), so neither can get ahead of the other. On recovery the gate orders them: a hold placed first is read by every later erasure |
| 12 | Resource created after the hold is active; identity merge after the hold is active | A new resource of X is indexed in its own transaction and is held when an erasure reaches it. X merged into Z: the merge adds Z to the hold's contact set under the gate; rows now attributed to Z are held; nothing is removed |
| 13 | Concurrent hold rejection and erasure | Serialized on the gate. Rejection first: the row is erased after the release, each journaled in that order. Erasure first: the row is skipped as held, then erased by the next pass after the release. Never erased while a covering hold is unreleased |

**What is and is not claimed.** *Prevented:* an unrelated subject's attributable data being held by another subject's hold, at placement or afterwards; a hold existing with an undetermined scope; a row passing its limit with no record of why. *Not prevented, and recorded:* an unattributable row can remain past its retention limit for as long as a request hold exists in its organization and two operators keep authorizing it, or nobody decides. That is a documented, owned exception, not a silent one, and its size is kept small by attributing rows at creation (HLD-17). Whether such an exception is acceptable in law is not decided here (LR-03). *Dependence:* the index is only as complete as its inventory; a contact-linked relation missing from it would make that relation's rows unattributed, which is the safe direction, never "unrelated". *Scope of "the subject's data":* a hold covers the resources linked to the subject, as ERA-06 defines them for erasure. A passing mention of X inside free text that belongs to another subject's resource is not attributed to X by any option considered; this document does not claim it is held.

### 28.9 Sixth independent freeze-gate findings ledger

The two findings of the sixth review, of the 3,542-line version. Design closures reached by static reasoning from the SQL text and the frozen documents. Not executed controls; no gate named here is open. For P1-7I-R19 the closure is of the ambiguity and of the mechanism. The retention it described is **not** prevented: it is an owner-accepted residual (RR-10).

**Frozen-source evidence, as read in this remediation.**

**P1-7I-R18, counterexample A, relation by relation.** Organization O; index key version 1 is `WRITE`.

| Step | Statement | Rows written in that transaction | State that matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A hold is requested for phone P; no contact has P | Registry: hold H, contact set empty, keys {(`PHONE`, P)} in clear. Journal: the placement | The index has nothing about P |
| 2 | `INSERT` contact C with `phone_e164 = P` | Head (O, `CONTACT`, C). Edge C —`KEY`→ (`PHONE`, *D(1, P)*, version 1), current | Written by the contact trigger, in C's transaction |
| 3 | `INSERT` deal D with `contact_id = C` | Head (O, `DEAL`, D). Edge D —`CONTACT`→ C, current | D has no number and no `KEY` edge |
| 4 | An event about D is delivered; a delivery row W records attribution (`DEAL`, D) | None in the index | HLD-17 |
| 5 | W's body reaches its limit. The erasure takes the gate (share), locks W, then head D, then head C, and reads | None | *Res* = {D}; *Con* = {C}; *Id(C)* = {C}; C's `KEY` edges = {*D(1, P)*}. H's key digested under version 1 is *D(1, P)*. Equal: **path (b3), current. W is held**, recorded `SKIPPED_HELD` |
| 6 | Unrelated contact Y (phone S) has deal E and delivery V | Edges E → Y, Y → *D(1, S)* | *Con* = {Y}; Y is not in H's contact set; *D(1, P)* ≠ *D(1, S)*; E has no key. **No path. V is erased on time** |

The comparison in step 5 is between a digest computed at that moment from the hold's clear key and a digest stored by C's own insert. Nothing has to have been "updated" on the hold or on D.

**Counterexample B, the transaction boundary.** C has phone Q: edge C → *D(1, Q)*. Hold H for P commits with an empty contact set. Then `UPDATE` C to P: the contact trigger locks head C exclusively, ends the edge to *D(1, Q)* with its provenance, and adds C → *D(1, P)*, all in the update's transaction. An erasure of a row linked to C takes head C in share mode before it reads C's edges.

| Order of head C | What happens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| The erasure locks it first | The update's trigger waits. The erasure commits. The update commits afterwards | The erasure preceded the identity change in every sense: C was not P's when it committed |
| The update locks it first | The erasure waits on the head. The update commits. The erasure's next statement reads the edges and sees C → *D(1, P)* | Held, path (b3) |
| The update commits before the erasure starts | The erasure reads the new edge | Held |

There is no fourth order: an erasure cannot read C's edges without the head, and the edge cannot change without it. If C later gives P up, the edge is ended, not removed, and C's rows stay held, now by a historical path under review (HLD-21).

**Counterexample C, a re-pointed resource.** R is attached to X: edge R → X, current. An authorized operation re-points R to Y: the edge to X is ended, carrying the original contact X, the replacement Y, the statement and the transaction; R → Y is current. X is held by H; Y is not; no merge link joins them.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does R still contain X's information? | **Not decidable from the index.** The reference changed; the title, notes, events already emitted and free text of R may or may not still describe X |
| What does the function do? | *Con(R)* = {X, Y}. X is in H's contact set, through an ended edge: a historical path. **R is held**, and a `HISTORICAL_ASSOCIATION` record opens (HLD-21) |
| How does X's association stop holding Y's content? | By an association release: two different reviewers, under the gate, on verified content, lawful purpose, the ended edges and the current associations. Then R follows Y's schedule. The edge itself is never removed |
| Why can a tenant-path credential not use the same transition to escape a hold? | It can re-point R. It cannot end the link's effect: the release function is not executable by any tenant-path role and needs two operator proofs. A hold on X placed after the re-pointing reaches R in the same way |
| And if nobody reviews? | R's event content is sealed at its limit and recorded as unauthorized retention (HLD-22). It is not erased and is not called held |

**Counterexample D, merge.** Held secondary S is merged into primary P. The frozen statements run unchanged; the triggers write, in the merge's transaction: for each re-pointed deal, task, note and appointment, the edge to S ended (provenance: the merge function) and an edge to P current; for S, an edge S —`MERGED_INTO`→ P; for P, `KEY` edges for a secondary phone or email it has just been given.

| Row | Evaluation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A deal moved from S to P | *Con* = {S, P}; through P, a current edge; *Id(P)* = {P, S}; S is in the contact set | Held, current path |
| An activity, a lead-score record, a campaign contact or a call left on S | *Con* = {S} | Held, current path |
| A deal created on P after the merge | *Con* = {P}; *Id(P)* contains S | Held, current path |
| The same three rows when the hold names P and not S | *Id(S)* contains P | Held: the link is followed in both directions |
| A hold by key on S's primary number, which P never acquires | S keeps its own `KEY` edge; *Id(P)* contains S; path (b3) | Held |

**Merge rules preserved:** the body, its refusals, its lock order among contact rows, its results and its grants are those of `097_5D5`. **The gate:** one statement before the body takes the organization's gate exclusively. The order is gate, then contact rows, which is the order every erasure uses for gate and data locks, so a merge and an erasure of one organization are serialized and cannot deadlock on one another. **Unification versus reassignment:** a merge writes a `MERGED_INTO` link, so the ended edge to S and the current edge to P name one identity and no review opens; a re-pointing between unlinked contacts has no such link and is reviewed. A merge cannot be used to narrow a hold: it only joins identities, and lineage is immutable.

**Counterexample E, key rotation.**

| Step | State | Comparison |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold H for P placed. Contact C1 with P: edge under version 1 | H's key digested under version 1 matches |
| 2 | Rotation: version 2 is `WRITE`, version 1 `VERIFY`. One transaction | Nothing on H changes |
| 3 | Contact C2 created with P: edge under version 2 | H's key digested under version 2 matches |
| 4 | A write that began before the rotation commits after it, under version 1 | Matches under version 1, which is still verified |
| 5 | A hold for P placed after the rotation | Digested under versions 1 and 2: reaches C1 and C2 |
| 6 | Retirement of version 1 requested while C1's edge exists | Refused by the reference count |
| 7 | Version 1 unreadable | Rows whose evaluation meets a version-1 edge are uncertain and are not erased. Never "no match" |

**No valid held resource is erased; no unrelated resource is retained on an obsolete association without an approved reason.**

| Direction | Why |
|---|---|
| A held row is not erased | Every path a subject's row can have to its hold is one of (b1) – (b3) over edges that are written with the row and never removed; the evaluation holds the heads it read until the erasure commits; where an edge cannot be read or verified the row is uncertain and is not erased |
| An unrelated row with no association to the held subject is not retained | It has no path, and is erased on its clock (step 6 above) |
| An unrelated row with only an ended association is not retained indefinitely *as a held row* | It is reviewed; released on evidence by two reviewers; or, if nobody decides, sealed and recorded as unauthorized retention, which is the owner-accepted residual and is not presented as a lawful reason (RR-10) |

**P1-7I-R19, the required failure trace, under the corrected rules.**

| Step | What happens now |
|---|---|
| 1 | An unattributable callback input is terminal `FAILED` |
| 2 – 3 | A request hold for another subject exists in the organization. On the first retention pass, days before the limit, a decision record opens: `PENDING_INVESTIGATION`, naming the input, its 7-day deadline, the reason and the hold |
| 4 | The platform cannot prove the input is the held subject's, or that it is not |
| 5 | The 7-day limit passes. The input is not erased. Its ciphertext and key leave the callback store for the sealed vault; the record is `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED`; an incident is opened whose occurrence time is the limit; the privacy and security owner is notified and the incident workflow entered |
| 6 – 7 | Nobody decides. At day 7 after the limit the incident is escalated again and the escalation appended. Nothing else changes |
| 8 | It was an incident from step 5, not from step 7 |
| 9 | At 30, 90 and 180 days: escalated again each time. No exception exists, so none is renewed. The content is still sealed and still present |
| 10 | The material remains in storage |

**What authority permits the retention after the approved deadline? None, and nothing in this document says otherwise.** The record says `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED`. It is not a legal hold: no hold has been shown to reach the input. It is not an approved exception: none was signed. It is not a longer retention period: OD-7I-03's seven days are unchanged. It is a breach of the retention limit that the owner has chosen to incur, knowingly and visibly, instead of destroying material that may be subject to a valid hold (OD-7I-28). What the design guarantees is narrower than a bound: the content cannot be used, the record cannot describe the condition as authorized, the incident cannot be closed by anything but a decision, and no exception can be repeated to make it look approved.

**The six conditions the brief requires to be kept apart.**

| Condition | Record | Authority | Ends |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pending investigation before the deadline | `PENDING_INVESTIGATION` | The approved retention period itself | At the deadline |
| Retention required by an established hold | `HOLD_APPLIES`; or held by HLD-11 (a), (b) with no decision record at all | The hold: a tenant-authorized request hold, or a dual-controlled platform hold | When that hold ends |
| Approved time-limited retention exception | `EXCEPTION_AUTHORIZED`, with an exception record | Two holders of `retention.hold.manage`; the privacy owner as well past the first bound | At its expiry; never past the cumulative cap |
| Overdue decision without approval | `OVERDUE_UNAUTHORIZED`, with a seal and an incident | **None** | Only by a decision or the end of the holds. Unbounded |
| Authorized erasure determination | `ERASURE_DETERMINED` | Two holders, on evidence; refused where a current path reaches a hold | At once: the row is erased |
| Retention governed by another independent obligation | No decision record: an owed delivery (ERA-11), a row named by a platform hold, the journal horizon (RET-24) | That obligation | With it |

**This solution challenged for new defects.**

| # | Challenge | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A tenant widens a hold over other people by merging contacts | True, and intended: a merge is the tenant's own declared unification of identities, it is recorded, and lineage is immutable. It can only widen. A hold whose identity closure spans more than one contact is an indicator (HE-7J-7I-15) |
| 2 | Deadlock between an erasure and an ordinary CRM write | Possible when an ungated transaction writes two indexed rows in the opposite head order. PostgreSQL aborts one; neither outcome erases a held row (HLD-15). Not claimed to be deterministic |
| 3 | Sealing hides a body from the tenant | At that moment the body would otherwise have been erased, and the tenant would see null in either case (PBR-10). Sealing shows the tenant nothing less than erasure would |
| 4 | Sealing destroys a replay source | The source had reached the limit at which it would have been erased (ERA-09). No obligation is resolved by it (SEAL-02) |
| 5 | Two reviewers record `HOLD_APPLIES` falsely to park material without an incident | Not prevented. It is a signed, evidenced, audited claim bound to a named hold, and it ends with that hold. This is the dual-control trust boundary already stated in OEA-15 |
| 6 | The cumulative cap forces a legitimate long investigation into "unauthorized" | Intended. A preservation duty that exists independently is recorded as a platform hold with its own reason; an uncertainty that only persists is not allowed to look approved |
| 7 | New states contrary to "no new database state" | The decision statuses, the seal record and `body_state = 'SEALED'` belong to relations and a column this document designs. No frozen state machine gains a value. The record shapes of 7G, 7H and 6J that must show a seal are a controlled erratum (ERR-7I-25) and block activation until consolidated |
| 8 | The retention pass is not running at the deadline | The content stays unsealed in its store until the next pass, as an unerased row would. The incident is still dated from the deadline (SEAL-03). Detection is HE-7J-7I-15 |
| 9 | Ended edges retain pseudonymous digests of former identifiers | True, for as long as the contact exists and is not erased (RET-28). It is the price of OD-7I-27 conditions 1 and 12, and is class `PID`, unreadable by any login role |
| 10 | A key version can stay `VERIFY` for years | True (HLD-20). A compromised version therefore stays in use for matching; the exposure is stated and is an incident, not a closed item |
| 11 | Owner-context rows are not sealed by this design | True (SEAL-13). Their erasure stays blocked by AB-7I-14 until the owning context provides it. Not claimed as designed here |

**What is and is not claimed.** *Prevented, in design:* erasure of a held subject's row because a contact was created, changed, re-pointed or merged after the hold, or because an index key was rotated; a re-pointing or an identifier edit taking a row out of a hold; a row past its limit in a condition whose record says or implies it is authorized when it is not; any ordinary read, replay, delivery or export of material past its limit with no decision; an exception renewed automatically, on the same evidence, or past the cap. *Not prevented, and recorded:* uncertain material stays stored past its approved limit for as long as nobody decides (RR-10); a pre-seal backup holds the content until it ages out; identity history from before the index backfill is unknown; two authorized reviewers can record a false applicability; an owning context's own sealing is not designed here. **Indefinite retention is not eliminated by this remediation.**

Not executed controls; no gate named here is open. Three owner decisions were needed and taken before any rule was changed (OD-7I-29 … OD-7I-31).

#### P1-7I-R20 — Subject-scoped `PLATFORM` holds

| # | Evidence | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Original failing interleaving | (1) Two operators place a `PLATFORM` hold for phone P in organization O; no row is named. (2) Contact C of O has `phone_e164` = P. (3) Delivery row W carries attribution (`CONTACT`, C), and replay material M belongs to a case with the same reference. (4) W's body clock runs out. (5) The erasure takes the gate, locks W and calls the effective-hold function. (6) Clause (a): no hold names W or a resource of W. Clauses (b), (c): only `REQUEST` holds are read. (7) Not held. W's body is erased; M follows at its cap |
| 2 | Physical SQL and frozen evidence | Facts 6 and 9: no registry exists and no frozen source defines the platform hold, so the defect is wholly in 7I's own rules. HLD-02 as reviewed ("resource references or subject fields") against HLD-11 (a) – (c) as reviewed |
| 3 | Corrected invariant | INV-31 as amended: a hold with subject scope, of either kind, holds the rows of its subject and no others; INV-29 unchanged |
| 4 | Authoritative enforcement component | The effective-hold function of HLD-11, one traversal for both kinds, called inside every erasure and purge function; the platform hold function of HLD-23 for placement and release |
| 5 | Transaction and locking | Placement: exclusive gate, resolver, registry row, journal record and audit row in one transaction. Erasure: share gate, row lock, index heads `FOR SHARE` in the HLD-15 order, then the edge read. A placement and an erasure of one organization serialize on the gate; an identity or association change and an erasure serialize on the head (§28.9, counterexample B, which does not depend on the hold's kind) |
| 6 | Privilege and tenant isolation | No login role has any privilege on the registry or the index. Placement and release need two operator action proofs of two holders of `retention.hold.manage`. The organization is part of every digest and every index key. A request function cannot name a platform hold, nor a platform function a request hold |
| 7 | Crash and recovery | The placement is appended to the journal before the registry row commits (HLD-09), so a crash errs toward the hold. After a restore the reconciler re-applies the hold with its scope, re-runs the resolver and takes the union, before any erasure record (HLD-23; JRN-10) |
| 8 | Future implementation requirement | IR-49 (registry scope and the platform placement function) and IR-50 (one traversal, one verdict), both as extended. No migration is created here |
| 9 | Activation dependency | AB-7I-14, extended; AB-7I-16 for the organization concerned |
| 10 | Deterministic test | VT-132 (this trace, both lock orders), VT-133 … VT-137 |
| 11 | The scenario re-run | Step 1 now stores contact set {C} and keys {(`PHONE`, P)}. At step 5 the function computes *Res* = {C's head}, *Con* = {C}, *Id(C)* = {C}; C is in the hold's contact set: path (b2), current. **W is held**, recorded `SKIPPED_HELD`. Had C been created after the placement, the contact set would be empty and C's own `KEY` edge *D(v, P)* would equal the digest of the hold's clear key under version *v*: path (b3), current, held. M is evaluated through its case's reference in the same way. Had W carried no usable reference, clause (c) would make it uncertain and open a decision record. At step 7 nothing is erased. Past the deadline each row is sealed with basis `HELD` (SEAL-14) |
| 12 | Residual limits | Rows nobody decides on: RR-10. A `FROM_T0` organization: RR-11. Two colluding operators can release a platform hold; that is the dual-control boundary, as for OEA. A compromised issuer: RR-09. Owner-context stores are bound only when their erasure functions call HLD-11 (HLD-14; AB-7I-14) |

#### P1-7I-R21 — Fail-closed access before physical sealing

| # | Evidence | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Original failing interleaving | (1) Delivery W of organization O is `DELIVERED`; its limit passes. No hold decision and no exception exists. (2) The retention pass is stopped. W's `payload_json` is still in the relation. (3a) A tenant user with `webhook:read` calls the 6J §23.2 route: the body is returned. (3b) A tenant user with `webhook:manage` calls replay: the function copies the body into a new `PENDING` row, and the dispatcher sends it. (3c) Any process holding the `app_readonly` credential sets a tenant context and runs `SELECT payload_json`: the body is returned. (3d) For material past its cap whose case is still `PARKED`: an R2 item, or a material view under an ordinary grant, obtains it |
| 2 | Physical SQL and frozen evidence | Facts 1 – 4. Under the sixth remediation's design the result of each of 3a – 3d is disclosure or re-use: SEAL-03 as reviewed said the row "stays in its store past the deadline, unsealed", and PAS-10 kept the three grants |
| 3 | Corrected invariant | INV-32 |
| 4 | Authoritative enforcement component | The content-deadline function and the guard inside every function of the CAG-05 inventory, in PostgreSQL; column privileges without the two content columns; the service-side pre-handoff check as a second line only |
| 5 | Transaction and locking | A read: one statement, no lock, correct for its snapshot and the clock read in it. A path that copies or creates work: the guard and the write in one transaction under the row lock. Sealing and erasure: the row lock and the same deadline function and clock (CAG-11). The pass acts only at or after the deadline; the guard permits only before it |
| 6 | Privilege and tenant isolation | No login role holds `SELECT` on a content column of the parent or any privilege on a partition (CAG-06). The read function checks `session_user` and the tenant context against the row's organization. Inspection needs two operator proofs (SEAL-08) |
| 7 | Crash and recovery | The denial has no state to lose: it is recomputed on every call. Worker, journal or vault down: the content is stored and denied (CAG-12). A seal that fails rolls back whole. A restored database denies from its first statement (CAG-13) |
| 8 | Future implementation requirement | IR-52; ERR-7I-26. No migration is created here |
| 9 | Activation dependency | AB-7I-15 |
| 10 | Deterministic test | VT-138 (this trace for every store, path and row condition), VT-139 … VT-145, VT-150 |
| 11 | The scenario re-run | Steps 1 and 2 as before; the body is still stored. (3a) The read function finds the clock at or past W's deadline and returns `payload_json: null` and a null preview, with W's metadata. (3b) The replay function evaluates the guard under its lock and refuses with `422`; no row is inserted, nothing is sent. (3c) `42501`: the role holds no privilege on the column. (3d) The fetch returns nothing; the item ends as a missing source; the case stays `PARKED`. When the pass resumes it erases W, or seals it if a hold reaches it or it is uncertain, and an incident, if due, is dated from the deadline |
| 12 | Residual limits | RR-12: bytes released before the deadline; a handoff in flight across it; a compromised authorized workload ignoring the pre-handoff check. Until the pass runs, the row is physically present and has no status record of its own. A due request-driven erasure waiting on the journal is JRN-29, unchanged (CAG-17 a). Owner-context content is not covered (HE-7L-7I-12) |

#### Activation clarification — pre-index identity history

| Question | Answer in this version |
|---|---|
| Which organizations have no gap? | Those certified `FROM_ORIGIN`: every inventoried relation carried its trigger before the organization's first row, established by the creating-transaction evidence of HLD-24 |
| Which authoritative history sources exist? | Merge lineage only. Not `updated_at`, not audit snapshots, not activities, not backups (facts 7, 8; HLD-24) |
| Is completeness claimed because every current row has a head? | No. A head proves current state. `FROM_T0` records that earlier history is unknown, and it cannot be promoted |
| How is an unverifiable legacy row classified? | Held if a path links it to a hold. Otherwise uncertain against any hold its unknown history could concern (HLD-25), with the decision procedure, review and sealing of OD-7I-27 and OD-7I-28. Never unrelated by default |
| When may the index be certified ready? | The six conditions of HLD-24, per organization; AB-7I-16 |
| What is not solved? | The history is not recovered. In a `FROM_T0` organization a subject hold can make most contact-linked rows wait for decisions (CNF-7I-30; RR-11) |

**Challenges to the new design, with the author's answer.**

| Challenge | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does a subject-scoped platform hold become an organization-wide exemption when its identifier matches nothing? | No. It is a hold with an empty contact set and its keys; it reaches rows carrying those keys and makes only unattributable rows uncertain |
| Can a tenant-path credential take a row out of a platform hold? | Not by any index write: edges are ended, never deleted, and still link. Not by the registry: no privilege |
| Can the guard be bypassed by a direct statement? | Not after IR-52: no login role holds the column privilege. **True today**, in the executed schema |
| Does the guard fail open when the registry or index is down? | No: it does not read them |
| Does denying access to held material strand an obligation? | The case stays unresolved and visible; raw replay is lost at the same instant erasure would have removed it (MRL-03). Nothing is marked done |
| Is the check atomic with the HTTP response? | **No.** RR-12 |
| Is a `FROM_ORIGIN` certification proof that the inventory is complete? | **No.** It is proof for the recorded inventory version. A relation found later demotes the organization; until it is found, its rows are unattributed, which is the fail-safe default |
| Does `FROM_T0` recover or approximate earlier history? | **No.** Nothing is inferred. RR-11 |
| Is the legacy rule wide? | **Yes**, in a `FROM_T0` organization while a hold with a key exists. Stated in HLD-25 and CNF-7I-30 |
| Was any of this executed? | **No.** No statement, trigger, grant, function or test was run |

### 29.4 What this document does not claim

It does not claim that any control is implemented, that any test passed, that any role, key, ACL user or migration exists beyond those marked **EXISTS** in §22.1, or that applying these controls makes the platform or any tenant compliant with any law.
